This is IgA nephropathy, considered an adult counterpart to Henoch-

rather than weeks after the onset of the upper respiratory tract infection.
Furthermore, there is no culture of on the throat swab pointing towards a
streptococcal infection.
IgA nephropathy is more common in coeliac disease

Primary polydipsia is a rare cause of polyuria in the general population

The plasma and urine osmolality results are not consistent with SIADH
or diabetes insipid us which can be caused by the drugs mentioned in
the incorrect stems. The patient has no obvious biochemical cause for
his polydipsia such as diuretic medication, diabetes mellitus,
hyperthyroidism or electrolyte abnormality. Lithium therapy can cause
polydipsia but this is unlikely given sub-therapeutic serum levels. There
is no history to suggest excess alcohol consumption.

What is the most likely cause of this patient's oedema?
explanation:
This patient is demonstrating the triad of oedema, low albumin, and
proteinuria suggesting nephrotic syndrome. Further quantification of
proteinuria via spot protein creatine ratio or 24-hour collection is
required. The above subacute nephrotic picture would suggest
amyloidosis or minimal change nephropathy as the most likely causes
out of the five options. This patient has chronic back pain and a raised
CRP suggesting poorly controlled ankylosing spondylitis. This would
support AA amyloidosis as the most likely cause of his nephrotic
syndrome. Amyloidosis is a rare disorder caused by deposition of
abnormal amyloid protein. It can affect multiple systems including the
kidneys, heart and peripheral nerves. AA amyloidosis occurs secondary
to a poorly controlled chronic inflammatory condition such as ankylosing
spondylitis or rheumatoid arthritis. The key to treatment is to address
the underlying condition.
AL amyloidosis is not linked to another condition and results from
abnormal plasma cells producing excessive amounts of light chains in a
process similar to multiple myeloma.

stem: An 8-year-old boy presents to his GP with swelling around his eyes and limbs, tiredness and weight gain. The GP performs a urine dip. What is the most likely underlying pathology in this child?
explanation:
Minimal change disease
Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in a child. Minimal change disease is the archetypal cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, responsible for roughly three-quarters of paediatric presentations. The triad of peri-orbital and peripheral oedema, lethargy and weight gain reflects heavy proteinuria with consequent hypoalbuminaemia and fluid retention. Most children are normotensive and have bland urine microscopy, which fits the vignette. On light microscopy the glomeruli look normal, but electron microscopy shows podocyte foot-process effacement; these structural changes explain the selective albuminuria. First-line treatment with oral corticosteroids induces remission in 80 % of cases, further supporting its primacy in this age group.

IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy usually manifests as macroscopic haematuria precipitated by an upper respiratory tract infection rather than overt nephrotic syndrome. Although proteinuria can occur, it is seldom sufficient to cause generalised oedema in children. A biopsy would demonstrate mesangial proliferation with IgA deposition, findings that do not align with the expected minimal-change picture in an otherwise well eight-year-old.

Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephritis is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults but is rare in young children. It classically produces massive proteinuria in middle-aged patients and may be secondary to autoimmune disease, malignancy or drugs. The histology shows a thickened glomerular basement membrane with sub-epithelial immune deposits, not the normal light microscopy seen in minimal change disease.

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows group A streptococcal infection by 1–3 weeks and presents with haematuria, hypertension and mild oedema, representing a nephritic rather than nephrotic picture. Complement C3 levels are typically low, and proteinuria is rarely heavy enough to cause the marked anasarca described in this stem.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis can indeed cause nephrotic syndrome and is an important differential when steroid resistance occurs, but it is less common than minimal change in children. It tends to affect older children and adolescents, may be associated with scarring from previous renal injury, and is often refractory to steroids. The likelihood, epidemiology and expected treatment response therefore make it a less probable explanation for this eight-year-old’s presentation than minimal change disease.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents for routine renal follow-up. He has a longstanding history of polyuria and polydipsia, since childhood, and has regular repeat testing. His heart rate is 108 beats/min and his blood pressure is 102/72 mmHg. His capillary refill time is 3 seconds. He is asked to perform another water deprivation test. After this, his urine osmolality remains low. He is then given desmopressin, after which urine osmolality still remains low. What is the most likely mutation causing this patient's medical condition?
explanation:
Vasopressin receptors
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus may be caused by genetic mutations: the more common form affects the vasopressin (ADH) receptor. This patient presents with polyuria, polydipsia, clinical dehydration, and laboratory tests show low urine osmolality following water deprivation and desmopressin administration. Given this, he likely has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (DI). In nephrogenic DI, the kidney is unable to respond to circulating antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the posterior pituitary, causing an inability to reabsorb water within the collecting tubules. This results in loss of water in the urine, causing low urine osmolality, high serum osmolality, hypernatraemia, polyuria, and excessive thirst. Because the kidneys are not able to respond to circulating endogenous ADH from thirst and water deprivation, polyuria continues during water deprivation and after administration of synthetic ADH (desmopressin). Nephrogenic DI has many causes, but in this patient, the cause is likely genetic considering his longstanding history. Most cases of genetic nephrogenic DI are caused by vasopressin (ADH) receptor mutations.

Aquaporin 2 channels
Aquaporin 2 channels are translocated to the luminal surface of the collecting tubule cells after activation of ADH receptors and they facilitate the reabsorption of water. Genetic nephrogenic DI can be caused by mutations affecting the gene that encodes aquaporin 2 channels; however, it is more commonly caused by ADH receptor mutations.

Epithelial sodium channels
A gain of function mutation affecting epithelial Na channels occurs in Liddle syndrome. In Liddle syndrome, excessive sodium reabsorption from the collecting tubule leads to hypertension and also creates a negative potential within the collecting tubule that traps hydrogen and potassium ions, leading to metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia.

Sodium/chloride pumps
A mutation affecting the reabsorption of sodium/chloride at the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) is responsible for Gitelman syndrome. These patients experience metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia (due to a rise in aldosterone, secondary to sodium loss), hypomagnesaemia, hyponatraemia, and hypercalcaemia (due to increased calcium reabsorption). This condition is analogous to long-term thiazide diuretic use.

Sodium/potassium/chloride pumps
A mutation affecting the reabsorption of sodium/potassium/chloride ions in the thick ascending loop of Henle is responsible for Bartter syndrome. These patients experience metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia (due to a rise in aldosterone, secondary to sodium loss) and hypercalciuria. This condition is analogous to long-term loop diuretic use.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with stage 2 chronic kidney disease attends the renal clinic for routine review. She was diagnosed 18 months ago following investigation of microscopic haematuria. Her blood pressure is well controlled on ramipril. Blood tests show: eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73m² (>90) Corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.20-2.60) Phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.80-1.40) PTH 7.2 pmol/L (1.6-6.9) 25-hydroxyvitamin D 22 nmol/L (>50) She reports feeling more tired recently and has generalised muscle aches. What is the most appropriate initial vitamin D supplementation?
explanation:
Cholecalciferol
In early CKD (stages 1-3), vitamin D deficiency should first be corrected using preparations such as ergocalciferol (vitamin D₂) or cholecalciferol (vitamin D₃). Cholecalciferol is the correct answer for this patient with stage 2 CKD and vitamin D deficiency. In early CKD (stages 1-3), native vitamin D preparations such as cholecalciferol (vitamin D₃) or ergocalciferol (vitamin D₂) should be used first-line to correct vitamin D deficiency. These preparations require activation in the liver (to 25-hydroxyvitamin D) and then in the kidneys (to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D or calcitriol) to become active. In early CKD, sufficient renal 1-α hydroxylase activity remains to perform this final activation step. This patient's 25hydroxyvitamin D level of 22 nmol/L indicates significant deficiency (target >50 nmol/L), which likely contributes to her fatigue and muscle aches. The mildly elevated PTH (7.2 pmol/L) is an appropriate physiological response to low vitamin D and does not yet represent true secondary hyperparathyroidism requiring active vitamin D analogues. Correcting native vitamin D deficiency with cholecalciferol is safer, more physiological, and less likely to cause hypercalcaemia compared to active analogues. Standard replacement regimens should be followed, with monitoring of calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D levels.

Alfacalcidol
Alfacalcidol is an active vitamin D analogue (1α-hydroxyvitamin D₃) that requires only hepatic hydroxylation to become fully active. It is reserved for advanced CKD (stages 4-5) when renal 1-α hydroxylase activity is significantly impaired and patients cannot adequately activate native vitamin D. In this patient with stage 2 CKD and preserved renal function (eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73m²), using alfacalcidol would be premature and carries unnecessary risk of hypercalcaemia. The kidneys retain sufficient capacity to activate native vitamin D at this stage. Alfacalcidol would be appropriate later in the disease course when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m² and secondary hyperparathyroidism becomes more problematic despite native vitamin D repletion.

Calcitriol
Calcitriol is the fully active form of vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D₃) and requires no further activation. Like alfacalcidol, it is reserved for advanced CKD (stages 4-5) when the kidneys can no longer perform 1-α hydroxylation effectively. Using calcitriol in stage 2 CKD would bypass the body's normal regulatory mechanisms and significantly increase the risk of hypercalcaemia and vascular calcification. This patient's preserved renal function means her kidneys can still activate native vitamin D appropriately. Calcitriol is typically used when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73m² and there is established secondary hyperparathyroidism requiring suppression of PTH secretion. The current PTH elevation is mild and should respond to native vitamin D replacement.

Cinacalcet
Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic agent that increases the sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells, thereby reducing PTH secretion. It is not a form of vitamin D and does not address vitamin D deficiency. Cinacalcet is used in advanced CKD (typically stage 5 or dialysis patients) with severe secondary hyperparathyroidism that is refractory to vitamin D analogues and phosphate binders. This patient's mildly elevated PTH does not warrant such aggressive therapy, and her primary problem is vitamin D deficiency rather than uncontrolled hyperparathyroidism. Cinacalcet would not correct her low 25hydroxyvitamin D level or address the underlying deficiency causing her symptoms.

Paricalcitol
Paricalcitol is a synthetic vitamin D analogue (19-nor-1,25dihydroxyvitamin D₂) that selectively activates vitamin D receptors with potentially less effect on calcium and phosphate compared to calcitriol. However, like other active vitamin D analogues, it is reserved for advanced CKD with secondary hyperparathyroidism. In stage 2 CKD with preserved renal function, paricalcitol would be inappropriate and unnecessarily expensive. The patient's kidneys retain the ability to activate native vitamin D, making cholecalciferol the safer and more physiological choice. Paricalcitol might be considered in stage 4-5 CKD if there were concerns about hypercalcaemia with other active analogues, but this is not relevant to the current clinical scenario.

stem: A 70-year-old presents with a progressive urge to pass urine. He reports frequently feeling the need to urinate with episodes of urinary incontinence. His symptoms occur throughout the day and night. He is otherwise well and denies any other urinary symptoms. Urinalysis is normal, digital rectal exam reveals a normal size prostate and a prostate-specific antigen test is within normal range, therefore his symptoms are attributed to an overactive bladder. Fluid intake and bladder retraining advice are provided with limited improvement. What first-line medication should now be commenced?
explanation:
An antimuscarinic
Antimuscarinic drugs are useful in patients with an overactive bladder. This patient has presented with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) which are very common in men over the age of 50 years. In this case, the patient has predominately overactive bladder symptoms and therefore conservative measurements such as adjustments to fluid intake and bladder retraining should be trialled. If, however, these approaches fail an antimuscarinic should be offered as first-line medications. Common examples of these drugs include oxybutynin, tolterodine or darifenacin. These medications are thought to affect/block receptors located at the detrusor muscles that make up the bladder, reducing overactive symptoms.

A 5-alpha reductase inhibitor
5-alpha reductase inhibitors are mainly used in the management of LUTS when an enlarged prostate plays the main role in the condition and patients experience voiding issues. Patients with enlarged prostates such as in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) commonly experience voiding symptoms including hesitancy, poor stream, straining and incomplete bladder emptying. 5-alpha reductase inhibitors affect the male hormones resulting in an involution/shrinkage of prostate tissue and therefore they are of little use in patients with prominently overactive bladder symptoms.

A calcium channel blocker
Calcium channel blockers do not play a role in the management of LUTS and instead are known to cause/worsen symptoms when used in the management of conditions such as blood pressure control. As such patients on calcium channel blockers who present with LUTS symptoms should be considered for medication alteration (i.e. changing to another anti-hypertensive) before starting an additional medication for LUTS.

An alpha-blocker
Alpha-blockers, similarly to 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, are mainly used for patients with LUTS secondary to an enlarged prostate. Alpha-blockers relax the smooth muscle in the bladder so again they are of limited use for patients experiencing bladder overactive symptoms and are instead helpful for those with voiding symptoms.

An anti-diuretic
Anti-diuretics such as desmopressin may be used for patients who mainly experience nocturia in an attempt to reduce urine production however they are not normally used as first-line medication and have a limited role in patients with overactive bladder symptoms.

stem: Which one of the following is least associated with retroperitoneal fibrosis?
explanation:
Sulphonamides
Sulphonamides are antibiotics that can cause various adverse effects, including hypersensitivity reactions and crystalluria, but they are not recognised as significant triggers for retroperitoneal fibrosis.

Riedel's thyroiditis
Riedel's thyroiditis is correctly associated with retroperitoneal fibrosis. It is a rare form of chronic thyroiditis characterised by dense fibrosis that replaces normal thyroid parenchyma and often extends beyond the thyroid capsule. Riedel's thyroiditis is considered part of the spectrum of IgG4-related disease, which can manifest as multifocal fibroinflammatory lesions affecting various organs. Retroperitoneal fibrosis is another manifestation of IgG4-related disease, and the association between these conditions is well-established, with approximately 10-15% of patients with Riedel's thyroiditis developing RPF.

Previous radiotherapy
Previous radiotherapy is a recognised cause of retroperitoneal fibrosis. Radiation-induced RPF typically develops months to years after radiotherapy to the abdomen or pelvis. The mechanism involves radiation-induced vascular damage leading to ischaemia, followed by chronic inflammation and excessive fibrosis. This is particularly seen in patients who have received radiotherapy for testicular, cervical, or prostate cancers. The fibrotic process can be progressive and may lead to ureteric obstruction requiring intervention.

Inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm
Inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm has a strong association with retroperitoneal fibrosis. In fact, some experts consider inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm (IAAA) and idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis as different manifestations of the same disease process, sometimes referred to as 'periaortitis.' Both conditions share similar histopathological features, including chronic inflammation with predominant lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates and fibrosis. Approximately 10-20% of patients with RPF have an associated inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm.

Methysergide
Methysergide is classically associated with retroperitoneal fibrosis. It is an ergot alkaloid derivative previously used for migraine prophylaxis. Methysergide-induced RPF typically develops after prolonged use (usually >6 months) and is thought to result from the drug's serotonergic effects on fibroblasts, leading to increased collagen production. The association is so well-recognised that methysergide is now rarely prescribed, and when it is, patients require regular monitoring for the development of fibrosis. The risk of RPF with methysergide is estimated to be approximately 1 in 5,000 patients treated for more than six months.

stem: You review a 42-year-old woman six weeks following a renal transplant for focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Following the procedure she was discharged on a combination of tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisolone. She has now presented with a five day history of feeling generally unwell with anorexia, fatigue and arthralgia. On examination her sclera are jaundiced and she has widespread lymphadenopathy with hepatomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cytomegalovirus
Cytomegalovirus is the most common and important viral infection in solid organ transplant recipients. Ganciclovir is the treatment of choice in such patients.

stem: A 65-year-old man is seen in the Emergency Department complaining of muscle weakness and lethargy. Admission bloods show the following: Na+ 138 mmol/l K+ 6.6 mmol/l Bicarbonate 15 mmol/l Urea 9.2 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l An ECG is done which shows no acute changes. What is the most appropriate initial treatment to lower the serum potassium level?
explanation:
Insulin/dextrose infusion
The correct answer is Insulin/dextrose infusion. This is because insulin promotes the movement of potassium from the extracellular space into cells, effectively lowering serum potassium levels. Dextrose is given alongside to prevent hypoglycaemia which can be caused by insulin. In an emergency situation where hyperkalaemia is present, such as this case with a K+ level of 6.6 mmol/l, rapid reduction of serum potassium levels is crucial to prevent fatal arrhythmias and insulin/dextrose infusion provides this immediate effect.

Intravenous bicarbonate
Intravenous bicarbonate would not be the most appropriate initial treatment in this case. While it can promote a shift of potassium into cells by causing alkalaemia, its effect on serum potassium levels are slower and less predictable than insulin/dextrose infusion and hence not ideal for acute management. Furthermore, the patient's bicarbonate level (15 mmol/l) indicates metabolic acidosis which may have been compensatory to respiratory alkalosis or due to another underlying condition that needs addressing separately.

Haemodialysis
Haemodialysis is effective in removing potassium from the body but it's generally reserved for severe cases of hyperkalaemia that are refractory to medical treatment or when there's an urgent need for removal of other waste products in patients with renal failure. Although our patient has a slight elevation in urea (9.2 mmol/l) and creatinine (110 µmol/l), these values do not indicate severe kidney dysfunction necessitating dialysis.

Intravenous calcium gluconate
The administration of intravenous calcium gluconate does not lower serum potassium levels but instead works by stabilising the myocardial cell membranes against the effects of hyperkalaemia, specifically lifethreatening arrhythmias. It would thus be used as an adjunct treatment rather than primary therapy in managing hyperkalaemia.

Oral calcium resonium
Oral calcium resonium, a cation exchange resin, works by exchanging calcium ions for potassium ions in the gut thereby reducing total body potassium content. However, its onset of action takes several hours and hence it wouldn't be suitable for acute management where immediate reduction of serum potassium levels is needed.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain. This started earlier on in the day and is getting progressively worse. The pain is located on his left flank and radiates down into his groin. He has had not had a similar pain before and is normally fit and well. Examination reveals a man who is flushed and sweaty but is otherwise unremarkable. What is the most suitable initial management?
options: IM diclofenac 75 mg + start bendroflumethiazide to prevent further episodes
explanation:
IM diclofenac 75 mg
Guidelines continue to recommend the use of IM diclofenac in the acute management of renal colic. This man may need to be referred acutely to the surgeons for pain relief and investigations to exclude obstruction.

Immediate abdominal ultrasound
An immediate abdominal ultrasound is not necessary as neither his age nor symptoms point to a diagnosis of abdominal aneurysm.

IM diclofenac 75 mg + start bendroflumethiazide to prevent further episodes
It would not be suitable to start bendroflumethiazide in the initial phase of the first episode.

stem: A 75-year-old male has been scheduled to undergo a coronary angiography for investigation of his ongoing, exertional chest discomfort. The patient has a past medical history of diabetes, hypertension and increased body mass index of 27kg/m2 (weight 78kg, height 170cm). He is currently taking aspirin, metformin and amlodipine. What step should be taken for the 48 hours post-procedure?
options: Give large volume intravenous fluid resuscitation (e.g. 10mL/kg/hr for 12hr pre-contrast)
Monitor renal function only and if no deterioration no further action is required
explanation:
Hold metformin
Patients who are high-risk for contrast-induced nephropathy should have metformin withheld for a minimum of 48 hours and until the renal function has been shown to be normal. The patient is at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy given he is above the age of 70 years. As such he should have his metformin held for a minimum of 48 hours for renal function to be demonstrated normal. This is due to the risk of lactic acidosis associated with metformin in renal impairment.

Give large volume intravenous fluid resuscitation (e.g. 10mL/kg/hr for 12hr pre-contrast)
It is a misconception that large volumes of IV fluids should be used for pre-hydration prior to giving contrast. This is an incorrect management strategy and potentially dangerous for patients. Evidence currently supports the use of IV 0.9% sodium chloride but only at a maintenance rate of 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours pre and post-procedure. Larger volume resuscitation at 10ml/kg/hr in the absence of haemodynamic instability or dehydration can easily result in fluid overload and the associated complications.

Give N-acetylcysteine
Preventive measures such as giving isotonic sodium bicarbonate or N-acetylcysteine have been used in the past to reduce the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy but there is no evidence to support their use.

Hold aspirin
Aspirin is normally continued to reduce the risk of thrombotic complication despite the small risk of bleeding in PCI. Only in very rare cases would aspirin have to be stopped - for instance, if there was continuous, uncontrolled bleeding or complications from an aneurysm.

Monitor renal function only and if no deterioration no further action is required
Renal function should be monitored for a minimum of 48 hours; however, metformin should also be stopped to reduce the risk of lactic acidosis.

stem: A 49-year-old is admitted to hospital with an intensely painful lesion on the right leg. He has a background of end-stage renal failure, hypertension and atrial fibrillation. His regular medications include warfarin, amlodipine, ramipril and paracetamol. On examination, a painful, purpuric lesion is noted, with an area of black necrotic tissue. It appears to have ulcerated somewhat. A biopsy is taken which demonstrates calcium deposition in the lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Calciphylaxis
Calciphylaxis lesion are intensely painful, purpuric patches with an area of black necrotic tissue that may form bullae, ulcerate, and leave a hard, firm eschar. The description of the lesion points towards calciphylaxis, a rare complication of end-stage renal failure. It results in the deposition of calcium within arterioles, leading to microvascular occlusion and necrosis. Usually, it affects the skin (although can affect other organs), presenting as above with painful, purpuric lesions that necrose and may ulcerate. The skin biopsy demonstrating calcium deposition points more towards this diagnosis.

Cholesterol embolisation
Cholesterol embolisation may occur in patients on warfarin, although the history here is more suggestive of calciphylaxis. Release of cholesterol debris leads to emboli, which may create small, infarcted areas, with mottling and purple discolouration of extremities. Non-specific symptoms also include fever and muscle ache.

Cryoglobulinaemia
Cryoglobulinaemia is the presence of cold-sensitive immunoglobulins that become insoluble at reduced temperatures. This can present with purpura and acrocyanosis, but does not fit with the history here, given the presence of end-stage renal failure and calcium deposition in the lesion.

Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum is associated with a number of conditions, such as inflammatory bowel diseases, whereas calciphylaxis is more associated with end-stage renal failure. Pyoderma gangrenosum would instead present with an ulcerating, purple lesion that may have started as a small pustule or blister. A biopsy would demonstrate neutrophilic infiltration rather than calcium deposition.

Warfarin necrosis
Warfarin necrosis is a reasonable differential here - a rare side effect of warfarin use. It presents with single or multiple necrotic lesions and may be difficult to differentiate clinically from calciphylaxis. However, the finding of calcium deposition on biopsy points towards calciphylaxis.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with facial and bilateral leg swelling in the context of a recent viral upper respiratory tract infection. The patient takes no regular or over-the-counter medications. Examination reveals facial, sacral and peripheral pitting oedema. Na+ 137 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.8 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 6.3 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 167 µmol/L (55 - 120) Albumin 13 g/L (35 - 55) Urine Protein:Creatinine Ratio 755 mg/mmol (< 15) A kidney biopsy shows normal appearances on light microscopy and no immune complex deposition on immunofluorescence. Electron microscopy is awaited. What is the definitive treatment for the likely underlying condition?
explanation:
Prednisolone
Minimal change disease - prednisolone. This patient’s clinical presentation is consistent with minimal change disease, with the onset of nephrotic syndrome following a viral upper respiratory tract infection. In minimal change nephropathy, a kidney biopsy shows normal appearances on light microscopy and electron microscopy would demonstrate foot process effacement when available. The correct course of action is to commence prednisolone. The Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guideline recommends starting prednisolone at 1 mg/kg daily unless contraindicated.

Apixaban
Given that the patient is suffering from nephrotic syndrome with a significantly decreased serum albumin level, there is an elevated risk of venous thromboembolic events. Therefore, apixaban, an anticoagulant, might be considered to mitigate this risk. However, treatment of the primary disease with prednisolone takes priority and is a better answer.

Furosemide
While furosemide could help manage the patient’s peripheral oedema, it does not address the underlying pathophysiology of the disease and is therefore not the most appropriate option here.

Ramipril
Although ramipril is important for managing glomerular diseases due to its effectiveness in reducing hypertension and proteinuria, it is a less correct answer as treating the primary pathology takes precedence. ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers play an important role in glomerular diseases as they control hypertension and proteinuria, slowing the progression of chronic kidney disease.

Rituximab
Rituximab, a CD20 inhibitor, is suggested by KDIGO as a potential second-line treatment for minimal change disease when glucocorticoids are contraindicated. In this case, since there are no contraindications to glucocorticoid use, prednisolone remains the more appropriate choice over rituximab.

stem: You are reviewing a 36-year-old woman who has a diagnosis of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). She currently takes losartan 50mg daily and her blood pressure is 122/70 mmHg. Unfortunately her glomerular filtration rate (GFR) has steadily declined in the last 18 months. It is currently 48 ml/min/1.73m2. It has been suggested by her specialist that she should be started on tolvaptan to slow the progression of her disease. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
explanation:
Vasopressin receptor 2 antagonist
Tolvaptan is a vasopressin receptor 2 antagonist. Tolvaptan is recommended as a treatment option to slow the progression of disease in some patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). As a selective and competitive vasopressin 2 (V2) antagonist, it binds to the V2 receptors in the renal collecting ducts to reduce cell proliferation, cyst formation and fluid excretion. This reduces kidney growth and protects renal function.

Aldosterone receptor antagonist
Aldosterone receptor antagonists (e.g. spironolactone) are used in the treatment of heart failure.

Vasopressin receptor 1 agonist
Vasopressin receptor 1 agonists are not the mechanism of action for tolvaptan.

Vasopressin receptor 1 antagonist
Tolvaptan is not a vasopressin receptor 1 antagonist.

Vasopressin receptor 2 agonist
Vasopressin receptor 2 agonists (e.g. desmopressin) are used in the treatment of diabetes insipidus, nocturnal enuresis and von Willebrand disease.

stem: A 6-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by his mother. He presents with a 5-day history of high fever, dysuria and lethargy. The mother states she is encouraging him to drink water but despite this, he is urinating small amounts. Urine dip is positive for leukocytes, nitrates and the pH level is alkaline. The sample is further sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivity, which revealed numerous gram-negative motile rod-shaped bacteria indicating Proteus mirabilis. Which of the following types of renal stones does this infection increase the risk of developing?
explanation:
Struvite stone
Proteus mirabilis infection predisposes to struvite kidney stones. P. mirabilis is a gram negative, facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium which is motile. The likely cause of a patient presenting with alkaline urine is P. mirabilis. This organism produces urease which breaks down urea to carbon dioxide and ammonia resulting in a lower pH. The alkaline urine increases the risk of developing struvite stones.

Cysteine stone
Cysteine stones tend to be related to a genetic defect resulting in a decreased reabsorption of dibasic amino acids which includes cysteine.

Calcium oxalate stone
Calcium oxalate stones are the most common types of stones in adults. Low calcium diets and dehydration increase the risk of the development of these stones.

Uric acid stone
Uric acid stones are the most common stones seen in patients with gout. Dehydration and having acidic urine increase the risk of developing these stones.

Xanthine stone
Xanthine stones are rare. Genetic defects altering xanthine oxidase result in the inability to convert xanthine to uric acid.

stem: A 56-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a one week history of worsening abdominal pain, nausea and diarrhoea. He has a background of end-stage renal failure and is receiving peritoneal dialysis. He is reviewed by the medical registrar on-call, he has a tender abdomen with guarding throughout on examination. There is a raised lactate on his venous blood gas. An urgent erect plain chest radiograph is requested and there is no evidence of consolidation or pneumoperitoneum. Intravenous antibiotics are commenced and a sample of the peritoneal dialysis fluid is sent off to microbiology for cell count, gram stain, culture and sensitivity. Which organism is the most likely cause of his peritonitis?
explanation:
Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus
Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus is the most common cause of peritonitis secondary to peritoneal dialysis. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species, e.g. Staphylococcus epidermidis and Staphylococcus capitis, peritonitis remains a common complication of peritoneal dialysis. Empiric antibiotic therapy usually aims to cover both gram-positive and gram-negative organisms.

Coagulase-positive Staphylococcus
Staphylococcus aureus is another common cause of PD-associated peritonitis worldwide but is not the most common, which is why it is incorrect in this case.

Escherichia coli
Escherichia coli is a leading cause of gram-negative peritonitis and is one of the main ESBL-producing organisms which can potentially cause serious peritonitis in peritoneal dialysis patients. However, it is not the most common cause.

Gram-negative cocci
Gram-negative cocci such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Neisseria meningitidis are uncommon causes of peritonitis, which is why they are incorrect in this case.

Group A streptococcus
Group A Streptococcus pyogenes causing peritonitis can be a life-threatening condition but remains very rare, which is why it is incorrect in this case.

stem: A 22-year-old man is referred with a 3-month history of progressive ankle swelling and facial puffiness. He has also noticed frothy urine but denies haematuria or systemic symptoms. On examination, he has bilateral pitting oedema to the mid-shin and a blood pressure of 148/92 mmHg. 139 mmol/L (135–145) K 4.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.0) Ur 6.5 mmol/L (2.5–7.8) Cr 103 µmol/L (60–110) Complement C3 0.55 g/L (0.75–1.65) Complement C4 0.26 g/L (0.14–0.54) Urinalysis Protein +++ ; Blood ++ Na A renal biopsy reveals dense intramembranous electron-dense deposits on electron microscopy. What is commonly associated with the type 2 variant of the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Partial lipodystrophy
Partial lipodystrophy is correct because the clinical features and biopsy findings are characteristic of mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis (MCGN), also known as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. The patient presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria (protein +++ on urinalysis), microscopic haematuria (blood ++), hypertension, and low serum C3 with normal C4, all typical features of complement-mediated glomerulonephritis. Renal biopsy demonstrating dense intramembranous electron-dense deposits confirms a diagnosis of type 2 MCGN, also called dense deposit disease. In contrast, type 1 MCGN is characterised by subendothelial and mesangial immune complex deposits. Type 2 MCGN has a well-known association with partial lipodystrophy, where complement dysregulation leads to selective loss of subcutaneous fat, typically affecting the face and upper body.

ANCA-associated vasculitis
ANCA-associated vasculitis is incorrect because it causes a pauciimmune glomerulonephritis, typically characterised by minimal or absent immune complex or complement deposition on renal biopsy. In contrast, type 2 membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (now termed dense deposit disease) shows dense intramembranous deposits and is strongly associated with dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway. ANCA-associated vasculitis presents with rapidly progressive renal failure, often with systemic features such as fever, weight loss, or pulmonary involvement—none of which are present in this case. It is not linked to dense deposit disease.

Henoch–Schönlein purpura
Henoch–Schönlein purpura is incorrect because it causes an IgA-mediated small vessel vasculitis, typically presenting with purpura, abdominal pain, arthritis, and renal involvement. Renal biopsy usually shows mesangial IgA deposition, not dense intramembranous deposits. The clinical picture in this case, including the pattern of complement consumption and electron microscopy findings, is not consistent with Henoch–Schönlein purpura.

Hepatitis C virus
Hepatitis C virus is incorrect because while it is strongly associated with type 1 MCGN and mixed cryoglobulinaemia, it is not linked to type 2 MCGN. In hepatitis C-associated renal disease, immune complex deposition results in subendothelial deposits and hypercellularity on biopsy, differing from the dense deposit disease pattern seen in this patient.

Hodgkin lymphoma
Hodgkin lymphoma is incorrect because it is classically associated with minimal change disease, not MCGN. Hodgkin lymphoma may cause nephrotic syndrome through cytokine-mediated podocyte injury, leading to minimal change pathology, which presents differently both clinically and histologically from the findings in this case. Dense deposit disease and complement dysregulation are not features of Hodgkin-associated renal disease.

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with haematuria and oliguria. She has a history of sinusitis over the past few months with associated haemorrhagic discharge. Examination reveals hypertension and urinalysis demonstrates proteinuria and haematuria. Blood tests are performed, with the results below: Na+ 136 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 5.6 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 22.1 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 376 µmol/L (55 - 120) cANCA Positive The patient is referred to the renal team who performs a biopsy as part of their workup. Which of the following biopsy findings is most likely?
explanation:
Glomerular crescents
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, causes: Goodpasture's ANCA positive vasculitis The diagnosis here is that of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) an ANCA-positive vasculitis. The history of recurrent upper respiratory tract symptoms with renal failure and cANCA blood test confirms this diagnosis. By far the most common form of renal failure in this condition is rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, with its severe and rapid loss of kidney function, haematuria and proteinuria. A renal biopsy demonstrates glomerular crescents.

Mesangial hypercellularity
Mesangial hypercellularity would be seen on biopsy in diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis. This is not typically linked with GPA. It is associated with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis in children, and also with systemic lupus erythematosus.

Mesangial immune deposition
Biopsy findings of subendothelial and mesangial immune deposits - a 'tram track' appearance - is indicative of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. This is less likely to be seen in GPA, although would also present with haematuria and proteinuria. Type 1, the most common form, is typically associated with cryoglobulinaemia and hepatitis C.

Podocyte effacement
Renal biopsy demonstrating fusion of podocytes and effacement of foot processes suggests minimal change disease. This is classically seen in children and is usually idiopathic. It also presents with nephrotic syndrome.

Thickened basement membrane
A thickened basement membrane is indicative of membranous glomerulonephritis. This is the most common form of glomerulonephritis, but not typically associated with GPA. It presents with nephrotic syndrome or proteinuria. It is often idiopathic or associated with drugs.

stem: A 33-year-old man presents with a one day history of pain and swelling in the right testicle. Around four weeks ago he returned from a holiday in Spain but reports no dysuria or urethral discharge. On examination he has a tender, swollen right testicle. On examination the heart rate is 84/min and his temperature is 37.1ºC. What is the most appropriate management?
options: IM ceftriaxone stat + oral doxycycline for 2 weeks
explanation:
IM ceftriaxone stat + oral doxycycline for 2 weeks
The correct answer in this case is IM ceftriaxone stat + oral doxycycline for 2 weeks. This combination of antibiotics is appropriate for treating epididymo-orchitis, which is the most likely diagnosis given the patient's presentation with a tender, swollen testicle and recent travel history. Epididymo-orchitis can be caused by sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae, or by urinary tract pathogens like Escherichia coli. Ceftriaxone covers for potential gonococcal infection while doxycycline provides coverage for chlamydial infection.

Oral doxycycline + metronidazole for 2 weeks
Oral doxycycline + metronidazole for 2 weeks would be an inappropriate choice because it does not provide adequate coverage against potential gonococcal infection. Metronidazole is typically used to treat anaerobic bacterial infections and protozoal infections, such as bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis, but it is not effective against N. gonorrhoeae.

Oral trimethoprim for 2 weeks
Oral trimethoprim for 2 weeks is also not an ideal choice in this scenario, as it primarily targets urinary tract pathogens and would not provide coverage against potential STI-causing organisms like C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae.

Oral azithromycin stat dose
Oral azithromycin stat dose would be insufficient treatment because a single dose of azithromycin may not effectively treat epididymo-orchitis caused by either C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae. Furthermore, it does not provide coverage against urinary tract pathogens that could be causing the infection.

Oral ciprofloxacin for 2 weeks
Oral ciprofloxacin for 2 weeks is not recommended for epididymo-orchitis due to increasing resistance of N. gonorrhoeae to fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin. Additionally, it does not provide adequate coverage against C. trachomatis.

stem: A 56-year-old man is referred to the vascular team for the creation of an arteriovenous fistula, after being diagnosed with chronic kidney disease and planning for dialysis. He has been advised that, after its creation, the fistula will take some time to develop before it can be used for dialysis. What time period is needed for development, before use?
explanation:
6 weeks
The time taken for an arteriovenous fistula to develop is 6 to 8 weeks. The normal timeframe quoted before use is 6 to 8 weeks, and so from the options above, 6 weeks is the correct answer.

1 week
The time taken for an arteriovenous fistula to develop is 6 to 8 weeks. 1 week is insufficient for the fistula to mature and be suitable for dialysis.

2 weeks
The time taken for an arteriovenous fistula to develop is 6 to 8 weeks. 2 weeks is insufficient for the fistula to mature and be suitable for dialysis.

4 weeks
The time taken for an arteriovenous fistula to develop is 6 to 8 weeks. 4 weeks is insufficient for the fistula to mature and be suitable for dialysis.

5 weeks
The time taken for an arteriovenous fistula to develop is 6 to 8 weeks. 5 weeks is insufficient for the fistula to mature and be suitable for dialysis.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with haematuria and loin pain. Observations are as follows: heart rate 95 beats per minute, blood pressure 165/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 37.4ºC, and SpO2 98% (on air). An abdominal ultrasound is organised: Abdominal ultrasound 6 cysts are present in the right kidney; 7 cysts are present in the left kidney including one of which has echogenic material within the cyst, without internal blood flow. What is the most common cardiac abnormality associated with this condition?
explanation:
Mitral valve prolapse
Mitral valve prolapse is correct. Mitral valve prolapse is extremely common and is seen in up to 25% of patients with ADPKD.

Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is incorrect. It is in fact aortic regurgitation that is commonly seen in patients with ADPKD.

Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is incorrect. Although this cardiac defect can be associated with ADPKD, it is mitral valve prolapse which is more commonly implicated.

Mitral valve regurgitation
Mitral valve regurgitation is incorrect. Although this cardiac defect can be associated with ADPKD, it is mitral valve prolapse which is more commonly implicated.

Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation is incorrect. Although this cardiac defect can be associated with ADPKD, it is mitral valve prolapse which is more commonly implicated.

stem: A 45-year-old man attends the clinic for genetic counselling. His sister has just been diagnosed with breast cancer and following genetic testing was identified to have a BRCA mutation. The patient's genetic results are as follows: Genetic testing BRCA1 mutation detected What malignancy is this patient at increased risk of developing?
explanation:
Prostate cancer
Men with BRCA mutations have an increased risk of prostate cancer. Male patients with BRCA mutations are at increased risk of prostate cancer as well as breast cancer.

Colorectal cancer
Colorectal cancer is incorrect. Patients with mutations of the APC gene are at increased risk of colorectal cancer.

Melanoma
Melanoma is incorrect. Patients with mutations of the multiple tumour suppressor 1 gene are at increased risk of melanoma.

Retinoblastoma
Retinoblastoma is incorrect. Patients with mutations of the Rb gene are at increased risk of retinoblastoma.

Wilm's tumour
Wilm's tumour is incorrect. Patients with mutations of the WT1 gene are at increased risk of Wilm's tumour.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the nephrology clinic with a history of persistent microscopic haematuria and progressive hearing loss since childhood. He has recently developed worsening fatigue. His maternal uncle required dialysis in his twenties. Urinalysis reveals proteinuria. Renal biopsy electron microscopy shows splitting of the glomerular basement membrane lamina densa. Which genetic inheritance pattern is most likely responsible for his condition?
explanation:
X-linked dominant
Alport's syndrome - X-linked dominant (in the majority) X-linked dominant inheritance is the most common mode for Alport's syndrome, accounting for approximately 85% of cases. This pattern explains why males are more severely affected (as in this scenario) and females are usually carriers with milder symptoms or asymptomatic. The clinical features—microscopic haematuria, progressive renal impairment, sensorineural deafness—and family history affecting male relatives on the maternal side further support this diagnosis. Electron microscopy findings of GBM splitting ('basket-weave' appearance) are characteristic.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive Alport’s syndrome does exist but accounts for only around 10-15% of cases and generally presents with similar features but without a clear X-linked pedigree pattern as described here (maternal uncle affected). It would be less likely given the male predominance and family history presented.

Autosomal dominant
Autosomal dominant inheritance is rare in Alport’s syndrome (<5%). If present, it often results in a milder phenotype and typically affects both sexes equally across generations; this does not fit the scenario provided where there is evidence of X-linked transmission.

Mitochondrial
Mitochondrial inheritance would show maternal transmission to all offspring regardless of sex and is not associated with Alport’s syndrome or its classical renal-auditory-ocular triad.

Y-linked
Y-linked inheritance would affect only males and be transmitted strictly from father to son, which is inconsistent with the maternal uncle being affected in this case. There are no known Y-linked forms of Alport’s syndrome.

stem: A 31-year-old man presents to his GP with a 2-month history of constant abdominal pain and early satiety. He has hypertension for which he takes enalapril. On examination, he is mildly tender in both flanks. Well-circumscribed masses are palpable in both left and right flanks. A soft systolic murmur is heard loudest at the apex. His observations are heart rate 67/min, blood pressure 152/94mmHg, temperature 37.2ºC, respiratory rate 14/min, saturations 97%. Which additional feature is most likely to be found in this patient?
explanation:
Hepatomegaly
ADPKD is associated with hepatomegaly (due to hepatic cysts) The patient in this case has autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). ADPKD often presents with abdominal pain and early satiety as the kidneys occupy a large volume of the abdomen. Traction on the kidney pedicle can also cause pain. The presence of hypertension, bilateral flank masses and a systolic apical murmur (suggesting mitral valve disease) also point towards this diagnosis. Extra-renal features of ADPKD include: Hepatic cysts which manifest as hepatomegaly

Colonic polyps
Colonic polyps are not a feature of ADPKD.

Sensorineural deafness
Sensorineural deafness is associated with Alport's syndrome. Alport's syndrome typically presents with haematuria and progressive renal failure, not renal enlargement.

Angiofibromas
Angiofibromas are a feature of tuberous sclerosis (patients with this disease may have renal cysts). Tuberous sclerosis is usually diagnosed in childhood and is associated with epilepsy and cognitive impairment.

Thrombocytopenia
Thrombocytopenia is not a feature of ADPKD.

stem: A 44-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV presents with a 2-week history of leg swelling. On examination, you note pitting oedema to the mid calves. Observations are as follows: heart rate 85 beats per minute, blood pressure 125/75 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 37.4ºC, and SpO2 98% (on air). Blood results are as follows: Hb 130 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 240 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 6.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 132 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 14.2 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 168 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 2 mg/L (< 5) Urinary protein in 24 hours 4.8g (<0.15) What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is correct. The patient has nephrotic syndrome characterised by >3g of proteinuria over 24 hours. The most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in HIV is focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). It is thought to occur due to direct infection of the kidney cells by HIV, with resulting kidney damage through the viral gene products. Inflammatory cytokines may also be a role. It usually occurs only in advanced HIV disease and approximately 80% of patients with HIVAN have a CD4 count of less than 200.

AA amyloidosis
AA amyloidosis is incorrect. AA amyloidosis can occur due to chronic HIV infection and can result in nephrotic syndrome. However, it is exceedingly rare in comparison to FSGS. Furthermore, amyloid deposition usually occurs in other organs such as the gastrointestinal tract, heart, and nerves. The absence of any other organ involvement makes this a less likely diagnosis.

IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy is incorrect. IgA nephropathy typically presents with macroscopic or gross hematuria that occurs within 24 hours of the onset of an upper respiratory infection. The absence of these clinical features and the presence of HIV infection makes FSGS the most likely diagnosis.

Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephritis is incorrect. Although this is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome it is only rarely seen concomitantly with an HIV infection. Most cases are idiopathic in nature. However, secondary causes commonly include solid organ malignancies.

Minimal change disease
Minimal change disease is incorrect. Although this is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome it is only rarely seen concomitantly with an HIV infection.

stem: A 66-yea-old man presents with abdominal pain and fatigue. On examination, he is jaundiced and an ultrasound scan of his liver shows obstructive cholecystitis secondary to likely liver metastases of unknown primary. He does not have any past medical or surgical history and takes no regular medications. In his family history, he has a mother who recently died from metastatic breast cancer and a sister who has been found to have a breast cancer (BRCA) gene mutation conferring high cancer risk. What primary cancer is this man most likely to have?
explanation:
Prostate
Men with BRCA mutations have an increased risk of prostate cancer. Prostate is the correct answer. Prostate cancer in males is strongly associated with the BRCA genes. In the above case, the presentation is that of liver metastasis in a man who has a strong family history of BRCA genetic predisposition; this means that the prostate is a likely primary, which can metastasize to bone, lymph nodes, or liver most commonly.

Brain
Brain cancer is incorrect because this cancer does not likely metastasize to the liver, most commonly the spread is the converse; liver to brain.

Colon
Colon cancer is an incorrect answer. Although colon cancer commonly metastasises to the liver, the BRCA genetic predisposition, in this case, is more indicative of a prostate or breast primary. Colon cancer has various genetic predispositions, including familial adenomatous polyposis.

Lung
Lung cancer is incorrect in this case as there are no lung symptoms or signs to point towards this diagnosis and lung cancers are not associated with BRCA mutations.

Retinoblastoma
Retinoblastoma is incorrect because this type of cancer primarily stays in the eye and very rarely metastasises to the liver. Moreover, retinoblastoma is associated with the retinoblastoma 1 gene mutation which occurs in utero and not the BRCA gene mutation which occurs later on in life.

stem: A 35-year-old man is receiving dialysis following a childhood diagnosis of an inherited condition. He initially presented with microscopic haematuria, progressive renal failure and bilateral sensorineural deafness. He was diagnosed following genetic testing and a renal biopsy which showed longitudinal splitting of the lamina densa of the glomerular basement membrane with a 'basket-weave' appearance. How is the underlying condition inherited in the majority of cases?
explanation:
X-linked dominant
Alport's syndrome is inherited in an X-linked dominant fashion in 85% of cases. The condition is caused by a defect in the gene which codes for type IV collagen resulting in an abnormal glomerular-basement membrane. The disease is more severe in males with females rarely developing renal failure. The patient in this vignette presents classically for this condition, with childhood progressive renal failure becoming dialysis dependent in mid-life. Examples of cases of Alport's syndrome inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion are rarely reported. However, this question asks for the mechanism of inheritance in the majority of cases.

Autosomal dominant
10-15% of cases of Alport's syndrome are inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion. However, this question asks for the mechanism of inheritance in the majority of cases.

Autosomal recessive
10-15% of cases of Alport's syndrome are inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion. However, this question asks for the mechanism of inheritance in the majority of cases.

Mitochondrial
Mitochondrial disorders are inherited down the maternal line, therefore, males with mitochondrial disease are not at risk of transmitting the disorder. Alport's syndrome is not a mitochondrial disorder. One example of a mitochondrial disorder is Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, which causes bilateral visual loss.

X-linked recessive
X-linked recessive inheritance is a mode of inheritance in which there is a mutation on the X chromosome which causes the disease in males only as they only have one X chromosome. Females with one affected X chromosome are carriers. Typical examples of X-linked recessive disorders include red-green colour blindness and haemophilia A and B. Alport's syndrome is not inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 2-hour history of excruciating back pain. He describes pain that began suddenly and now radiates from his flank to his groin. The patient says that the pain comes and goes in waves. He had a previous kidney stone 2 months previously. A CT kidneys, ureters, and bladder demonstrates a hyperdense calculus in the left ureter. Serum Ca2+ 2.1 mmol/L (2.2-2.6) Urine Ca2+ 9.2 mmol/24hours (2.5-7.5) What is the most appropriate drug to reduce further risk of renal stones?
explanation:
Bendroflumethiazide
In a patient with hypercalciuria and renal stones, calcium excretion and stone formation can be decreased by the use of thiazide diuretics. The correct answer is bendroflumethiazide, as thiazide diuretics may be used in the management of patients with renal stones and hypercalciuria. The patient's hypercalciuria is indicated by their urinary calcium which is above the normal range.

Bumetanide
Bumetanide is incorrect. Bumetanide is a loop diuretic and does not play a role in the management of hypercalciuria and renal stones. Bumetanide may be used in fluid overload associated with heart failure.

Denosumab
Denosumab is incorrect. Denosumab is an antibody used in the treatment of hypercalcaemia associated with malignancy. Denosumab is not used in the management of renal stones.

Furosemide
Furosemide is incorrect. Furosemide is a loop diuretic and does not play a role in the management of hypercalciuria and renal stones. Furosemide may be used in fluid overload associated with heart failure.

Spironolactone
Spironolactone is incorrect. Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic and is not used in the management of renal stones associated with hypercalciuria.

stem: A 26-year-old man with loin pain and haematuria is found to have autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. A defect in which one of the following genes is likely to be responsible?
explanation:
PKD1 gene
Most cases of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) are due to a mutation in the PKD1 gene. The PKD1 gene encodes for a polycystin-1, a large cell-surface glycoprotein of unknown function

Polycystin gene
The Polycystin gene is not the primary gene associated with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). The PKD1 gene is the most commonly involved gene.

stem: A 72-year-old man with heart failure and stage 4 CKD is reviewed. His medications include ramipril and spironolactone. An ECG shows sinus rhythm. He is given an insulin/dextrose infusion for hyperkalaemia. K+ 6.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.3) He is commenced on sodium zirconium cyclosilicate to promote potassium removal. What is the primary mechanism of action of this agent?
options: Intracellular shift via beta-2 adrenoceptor agonism
explanation:
Gastrointestinal cation exchange
Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate acts as a non-absorbed inorganic cation exchanger. It acts as an inorganic cation exchanger, trapping potassium ions in the gastrointestinal tract in exchange for sodium and hydrogen ions. This process prevents the absorption of potassium and promotes its faecal excretion, thereby lowering the total body potassium. This is a key strategy for long-term management after initial measures have been taken to shift potassium intracellularly, as has been done for this patient with an insulin/dextrose infusion.

Cardiac membrane stabilisation
Cardiac membrane stabilisation is the mechanism of intravenous calcium gluconate. It is administered in cases of severe hyperkalaemia (typically >6.5 mmol/L) or when there are ECG changes, to antagonise the cardiotoxic effects of potassium. It does not lower the serum potassium level. In this scenario, the ECG is normal, so while important to consider, this is not the mechanism of the drug in question.

Inhibition of the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter
Inhibition of the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter describes the action of loop diuretics, such as furosemide. By blocking this cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, they increase the delivery of sodium to the distal tubule, which promotes potassium excretion. While loop diuretics are used to remove potassium, this is not the mechanism of sodium zirconium cyclosilicate.

Intracellular shift via beta-2 adrenoceptor agonism
Intracellular shift via beta-2 adrenoceptor agonism is the mechanism of nebulised salbutamol. It stimulates the Na+/K+-ATPase pump on cell membranes, driving potassium from the extracellular to the intracellular space. This is a temporary measure to lower serum potassium, similar to the insulin/dextrose infusion the patient has already received, but it does not remove potassium from the body.

Aldosterone receptor antagonism
Aldosterone receptor antagonism is the mechanism of drugs like spironolactone and eplerenone. These medications block the action of aldosterone in the distal nephron, which leads to decreased potassium excretion and can cause or worsen hyperkalaemia. This patient is already taking spironolactone, which is a likely contributor to his hyperkalaemia.

stem: What is the most likely outcome following the diagnosis of minimal change nephropathy in a 10-year-old male?
options: Chronic kidney disease requiring renal replacement therapy within 30 years
Full recovery and no further episodes
Full recovery but with later relapses
Chronic kidney disease not requiring renal replacement therapy
Chronic kidney disease requiring renal replacement therapy within 10 years
explanation:
Full recovery but with later relapses
As 1/3 of patients have infrequent relapses and 1/3 of patients have frequent relapses a majority (2/3) will have later recurrent episodes. It is important however to stress to patients that generally speaking the longer term prognosis in minimal change glomerulonephritis is good.

Full recovery and no further episodes
It is important however to stress to patients that generally speaking the longer term prognosis in minimal change glomerulonephritis is good, but a majority (2/3) will have later recurrent episodes.

stem: A 31-year-old man was found unconscious on the street and brought by ambulance to the emergency department. He has a background of epilepsy and intravenous drug abuse. On examination he is lethargic but no signs of focal neurology. Pupils normal size and both equally reactive to light. Blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, heart sounds normal. His left calf was mildly swollen and warm to touch. He was catheterized and a residual volume of 340 ml of dark urine was collected. Ultrasound of his renal tracts was normal. Hb 136 g/l Platelets 136 * 109/l WBC 6.85 * 109/l Na+ 134 mmol/l K+ 3.9 mmol/l Urea 9.1 mmol/l Creatinine 235 µmol/l Urinary Na+ 58 mmol/l Which of the following investigations is more useful to identify the cause of his acute kidney injury?
options: Liver function test and coagulation test
Blood cultures and midstream specimen of urine
CT-angiogram renal arteries and left lower limb
explanation:
Serum creatine kinase (CK)
Rhabdomyolysis can cause parenchymal acute kidney injury and is characterised by elevated plasma creatine kinase (CK). The most likely cause for the acute kidney injury in the scenario is the deposit of myoglobin. Creatine kinase is released into blood stream in case of a muscle injury, prevalent after seizures, crush syndromes, traumatic muscle injections, fall, drugs such as statins, malignant neuroleptic syndrome or rheumatological diseases such as dermatomyositis. It is a marker of possible acute kidney injury but what physically damage the glomerulus and kidney tubules is the deposit of myoglobin. It is characterised by dark urine and strong positivity for 'Blood' in urine dipstick, although it is not blood. This positivity is due to similar heme group that myoglobin and haemoglobin share.

Anticonvulsants serum levels
Some deranged levels of anticonvulsants can indeed cause renal impairment but unlikely in this acute scenario.

Liver function test and coagulation test
Liver function test and coagulation could provide information on liver failure but not useful to identify the most likely cause of his acute kidney injury if there is no history of hepatitis or liver cirrhosis.

Blood cultures and midstream specimen of urine
Blood cultures and midstream specimen of urine are unlikely to account for his raised creatinine unless in the presence of sepsis.

CT-angiogram renal arteries and left lower limb
A CT-angiogram is useful if bilateral renal arteries stenosis is suspected, especially if the patient's creatinine raises after being commenced on an angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitor.

stem: You are called to see a 54-year-old man due to the sudden onset of right arm pain in the renal ward. The patient reports the pain came on in his right arm over a matter of minutes whilst he was resting in bed. There is no apparent history of traumatic injury. He has been recently admitted following the development of significant oedema throughout his body, including periorbital oedema. On examination, his right arm is pale, cool to touch, has a capillary refill time of 6 seconds, and no palpable radial pulse. However, his brachial pulse is intact. He is currently having daily blood tests to monitor his renal function. His urine dipstick on presentation showed heavy proteinuria. He was further investigated with a 24-hour urine collection which has just been reported: Protein 6.2g/L What is the likely cause of his right arm pain?
options: Omission of prophylactic low molecular weight heparin
explanation:
Antithrombin III deficiency
Nephrotic syndrome is associated with a hypercoagulable state due to loss of antithrombin III via the kidneys. The lack of a radial pulse and cool limb are more suggestive of arterial pathology. Renal loss of protein S does contribute to this but not as potently as the loss of antithrombin III, as such this is the correct answer.

Factor V Leiden deficiency
Factor V Leiden deficiency, the omission of low molecular weight heparin, and immobility in hospital are all general risk factors for venous thromboses with no association to this current case.

Immobility in hospital
Factor V Leiden deficiency, the omission of low molecular weight heparin, and immobility in hospital are all general risk factors for venous thromboses with no association to this current case.

Omission of prophylactic low molecular weight heparin
Factor V Leiden deficiency, the omission of low molecular weight heparin, and immobility in hospital are all general risk factors for venous thromboses with no association to this current case.

Protein S deficiency
Renal loss of protein S does contribute to this but not as potently as the loss of antithrombin III.

stem: Why do patients with chronic kidney disease have a raised phosphate level?
explanation:
Decreased renal excretion
The correct answer is Decreased renal excretion. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) often leads to a decreased ability of the kidneys to excrete phosphate, which results in elevated serum phosphate levels. This is due to a decline in glomerular filtration rate, impairing the removal of phosphate from the body. The kidneys are the primary regulators of phosphate homeostasis and any impairment in their function can lead to disruptions in this balance.

Increased gut absorption
The option Increased gut absorption is incorrect. While it's true that phosphate absorption occurs primarily in the gut, CKD does not typically result in increased gut absorption of phosphate. In fact, patients with CKD are often advised to limit their dietary intake of phosphate-rich foods to help manage their serum phosphate levels.

Hypervitaminosis D
Hypervitaminosis D is also an incorrect answer. Hypervitaminosis D refers to a condition where there's too much vitamin D in the body, leading to high levels of calcium and potentially causing damage to bones, tissues, and other organs. However, it doesn't directly cause raised phosphate levels.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
The option Primary hyperparathyroidism is another incorrect choice. Although primary hyperparathyroidism can result in increased blood calcium levels due to the overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH), it generally does not cause elevated phosphate levels. Instead, PTH typically promotes renal excretion of phosphate which would lower serum phosphate levels rather than raise them.

Decreased 25-alpha hydroxylation of vitamin D
Finally, Decreased 25-alpha hydroxylation of vitamin D is also not correct. This process takes place predominantly in the liver and converts vitamin D into its active form - calcidiol (25-hydroxyvitamin D). While this step is crucial for calcium homeostasis and bone health, its decrease would not directly lead to raised serum phosphate levels. It could potentially contribute indirectly by reducing intestinal absorption of calcium and therefore stimulating parathyroid hormone secretion which increases renal excretion of phosphate but this would still not result in raised serum phosphates as seen in chronic kidney disease.

stem: A 34-year-old man has 1 week of rapidly worsening fatigue, haemoptysis, and haematuria. He has a longstanding history of chronic sinusitis and over the last few days, has had blood-tinged nasal discharge. His blood pressure is 153/96 mmHg, and his oxygen saturation is 92% breathing air. Auscultation reveals scattered crackles, and he has palpable purpura on his legs. A urine dipstick is positive for blood and protein, and urinalysis reveals red cell casts. Investigations: Urea 12.1 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 392 µmol/L (55 - 120) A renal biopsy is performed. Which option is the most likely biopsy finding?
explanation:
Glomerular crescents
This patient’s one-week history of worsening fatigue, haematuria, haemoptysis, blood-tinged nasal discharge, and chronic sinusitis indicates a systemic vasculitis affecting both kidneys, lungs, and upper respiratory tract, features characteristic of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). The urinalysis shows red cell casts and proteinuria, suggesting active glomerulonephritis, and the raised creatinine and urea confirm acute kidney injury. Palpable purpura indicates small-vessel involvement. GPA typically causes necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis, in which glomerular crescents— proliferation of parietal epithelial cells in Bowman’s space due to severe capillary wall damage—are the hallmark finding. These crescents are associated with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN), the pathological correlate of this presentation. The systemic involvement, acute deterioration, and biopsy pattern make glomerular crescents the most likely finding.

Glomerular sclerosis
Glomerular sclerosis is incorrect because it reflects chronic, irreversible scarring of glomeruli and is inconsistent with the patient’s acute, rapidly progressive illness. The patient has a one-week history of worsening symptoms, red cell casts, and an abrupt rise in creatinine, all indicating active glomerular inflammation rather than longstanding damage. Glomerular sclerosis involves extracellular matrix deposition and obliteration of capillary lumens, typically seen in chronic diseases like diabetic nephropathy, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, or advanced focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). These conditions present with slow renal decline, persistent proteinuria (often nephrotic range), and relatively inactive urinary sediment. This option may be correct in a patient with a gradual onset of symptoms over months to years and no systemic vasculitic features.

Immune complex deposits
Immune complex deposits is incorrect because GPA is a pauci-immune vasculitis, meaning it shows minimal or no immune complex deposition on immunofluorescence. This patient’s presentation with pulmonary-renal syndrome, red cell casts, purpura, and chronic sinusitis aligns with GPA, which causes necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis without immune complex formation. Instead, immune complex deposits are typical in diseases like lupus nephritis, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Those conditions often present more insidiously and have other distinguishing features, such as a malar rash or arthritis in lupus, or timing relative to infections in IgA nephropathy or PSGN. In such cases, biopsy would show granular deposits of immunoglobulins and complement. This option may be correct if the patient had features suggestive of SLE or a different immune complex disease.

Linear IgG deposition
Linear IgG deposition is incorrect because it is characteristic of antiglomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease, not GPA. Although anti-GBM disease can present with haemoptysis, haematuria, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, it does not explain the chronic sinusitis or upper airway involvement seen in this patient. GPA is an ANCA-associated vasculitis that produces pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis, with minimal or no immunoglobulin deposition on immunofluorescence. Linear IgG staining, caused by anti-GBM antibodies targeting type IV collagen, is specific to Goodpasture’s syndrome. This option may be correct if the patient had pulmonary-renal syndrome without upper respiratory tract symptoms like sinusitis or epistaxis.

Linear IgM deposition
Linear IgM deposition is incorrect because it is not a recognised feature of GPA or any specific glomerular pathology, and GPA is pauci-immune by definition. IgM deposition generally reflects chronic or nonspecific glomerular injury rather than acute inflammation. The patient's acute systemic illness, with red cell casts, haematuria, purpura, and pulmonary symptoms, is not consistent with the chronic disease patterns where linear IgM may be seen. Weak, segmental linear IgM staining can occur in hypertensive nephrosclerosis, diabetic nephropathy, or other chronic glomerular conditions without crescents or systemic vasculitic features. This option may be correct in a patient with longstanding renal impairment without signs of systemic vasculitis or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to general practice with a 3 month history of progressive dyspnoea, 6kg of unintentional weight loss and a productive cough of white sputum. Upon further questioning, he admits bone and joint pain with some constipation and polyuria. His medical history includes: hypertension, benign prostatic hyperplasia. His hypertension was well controlled until 3 months ago. On examination there is digital clubbing, coarse bibasal crackles and mild epigastric pain, with suprapubic dullness. There is a left-sided varicocele that enlarges on standing. His observations were as follows: Blood pressure - 180/109 mmHg, heart rate - 95 beats per minute, temperature - 37.1 ºC, oxygen saturation - 95% on air, respiratory rate 22 breaths per min. He was referred to the emergency department, where blood tests revealed: Hb 94 g/L Male: (135-180) Platelets 231 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 14.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Calcium 2.9 mmol/L (2.1-2.6) Urinalysis reveals: blood 4+, protein 2+. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Renal cell carcinoma
Renal cell carcinoma can metastasise to the lungs, and remains an important differential in the setting of hypertension, hypercalcaemia and haematuria. Renal cell carcinoma presents with the classic triad only 10% of the time, and so requires recognition of the other features that are specific to the pathophysiology of the disease. Other paraneoplastic syndromes of renal cell carcinoma include polycythaemia and amyloidosis. Chest X-ray in this patient would show pulmonary cannonball metastases with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. This patient's epigastric pain is likely due to peptic ulcer disease secondary to hypercalcaemia, his suprapubic dullness likely due to chronic urinary retention secondary to his benign prostatic hyperplasia. The paraneoplastic effects are evidenced by hypertension (renin overproduction) and hypercalcaemia (parathyroid-related protein overproduction). The growth of the nephron compressing the left internal spermatic vein results in left-sided pampiniform plexus enlargement and consequent varicocele.

Mesothelioma
Mesothelioma would explain the respiratory symptoms, weight loss and clubbing. However it does not explain the hypercalcaemia nor the varicocele.

Prostatic cancer
Prostatic cancer often causes bony metastasis, with potential subsequent hypercalcaemia, alongside with haematuria. While it can metastasise to the lungs, it would not explain varicocele nor refractory hypertension.

Small cell lung cancer
Small cell lung cancer commonly causes paraneoplastic syndromes, including Cushing's syndrome, SIADH, Lambert Eaton, and cerebellar degeneration. However, squamous cell cancer is the cause of hypercalcaemia of malignancy, and it does not explain the varicocele nor the haematuria.

Phaeochromocytoma
Phaeochromocytoma would cause resistant hypertension, but would not explain the other symptoms.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the emergency department intoxicated. He has a history of alcohol excess and type 2 diabetes. He takes metformin. A recent HbA1c was 44 mmol/mol and blood sugar on arrival was 5.1 mmol/L. The examination is unremarkable other than the patient being intoxicated and frequently needing to go to the bathroom to urinate. Bloods: Creatinine 66 µmol/L (55 - 120) What is the mechanism driving the patient's polyuria?
options: ADH suppression in the posterior pituitary gland
Reduction of principal cells in the collection duct
explanation:
ADH suppression in the posterior pituitary gland
