Ultrasound is the screening test for adult polycystic kidney disease. Ultrasound is the most common and least costly screening method for adult polycystic kidney disease.

Computed tomography (CT)
Computed tomography (CT) is more sensitive, however, it involves radiation or may also require iodinated contrast dye which, can be toxic to the kidney and therefore best avoided initially.

Direct DNA sequencing
Direct DNA sequencing requires only a single sample from you (the person being tested). This method is a direct analysis of the DNA sequences of the PKD1 and PKD2 gene.

Gene linkage testing
Gene linkage can determine if you have PKD with a 99% probability in those with a family history. However, blood samples must be obtained from the person being tested as well as several (typically three or more) family members including those affected and unaffected by PKD. Detailed family history is also required.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may be used to look at complications like bleeding into a cyst or a suspected kidney stone. They may also be used to detect small cysts as needed. However, this form of investigation is not considered first-line in screening for adult polycystic kidney disease.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents with a 1-month history of a painful lesion on his forehead. He feels the lesion has grown in size over the past month. His past medical history includes a renal transplant six years ago due to autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPCKD). He is currently taking tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone. On examination, there is a two-cm, firm, keratotic nodule on the right side of his forehead. What is the most appropriate management of the lesion?
explanation:
Surgical excision and biopsy
The optimum management is excision and biopsy of the lesion to confirm the diagnosis and ensure complete removal.

Cryotherapy
Cryotherapy would not guarantee complete removal of the lesion, and it would not provide histological proof of SCC.

Increase dose of prednisolone
Increasing dose of prednisolone does not confer any benefit. Rather, they put the patients at greater risk of adverse effects from glucocorticoid use.

Topical 5-fluorouracil cream
Topical 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) cream is used for actinic keratosis. While actinic keratosis is also commonly found on sun-exposed sites, it is more slow-growing than the lesion described.

Topical imiquimod
Topical imiquimod is commonly known by its brand name Aldara in the United Kingdom. It is prescribed for superficial basal cell carcinoma and actinic keratosis. Superficial basal cell carcinoma is slow-growing and presents with a thin, translucent rolled border which is not seen here.

stem: A 29-year-old man who is being investigated for haemoptysis and a chronic cough has a blood screen: Hb 12.9 g/dl Plt 248 * 109/l WBC 5.4 * 109/l ESR 11 mm/hr Na+ 138 mmol/l K+ 5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate 19 mmol/l Urea 14.0 mmol/l Creatinine 178 µmol/l Urine dipstick shows blood ++. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Goodpasture's syndrome
The correct answer is Goodpasture's syndrome. Goodpasture's syndrome, also known as anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, is a rare autoimmune condition that affects both the kidneys and lungs. It presents with haemoptysis and a chronic cough due to pulmonary haemorrhage, as well as renal impairment (evidenced by raised creatinine) and haematuria (blood ++ on urine dipstick). The blood screen of the patient indicates these findings.

Wegener's granulomatosis
The first incorrect option is Wegener's granulomatosis, now more commonly referred to as Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). While it can cause similar symptoms to Goodpasture's syndrome, such as haemoptysis, cough and renal impairment, it would typically also present with systemic features such as fever, weight loss and malaise. Furthermore, GPA often leads to an elevation in inflammatory markers like ESR or CRP which is not evident in this case.

Lung cancer with renal metastases
Lung cancer with renal metastases is another incorrect option. Although lung cancer could potentially explain the haemoptysis and chronic cough, it would be highly unusual for lung cancer to metastasise to the kidneys leading to haematuria. Metastatic spread of lung cancer typically involves other organs such as the brain, bones or liver.

Churg-Strauss syndrome
Churg-Strauss syndrome, or Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), is another form of vasculitis that can affect the lungs and kidneys but it predominantly causes eosinophilia which isn't indicated in this case. EGPA also tends to present with asthma and peripheral neuropathy which are not reported here.

Renal cancer with lung metastases
Finally, renal cancer with lung metastases is unlikely given the presentation. While renal cell carcinoma can present with haematuria (blood in urine), it rarely leads to lung symptoms unless there are advanced metastases. Even then, coughing up blood would be less common than other symptoms such as shortness of breath or chest pain.

stem: A 62-year-old man attends your clinic. He has a history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation for which he is anticoagulated with warfarin. A urine dipstick taken 8 weeks ago during a routine hypertension clinic appointment showed blood + with leucocytes +. Initial urine microscopy and culture shows no growth. The urine dipstick has been repeated on two further occasions with the same finding. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Send a 24-urine sample for protein estimation
explanation:
Refer to urology
The incidence of non-visible haematuria is similar in patients taking warfarin to the general population, therefore, these patients should be investigated as normal. Most haematuria protocols suggest sending younger patients (e.g. < 40 years) to nephrology initially but as this patient is older he should be sent to urology for a cystoscopy.

Take no further action
Taking no further action is inappropriate as the patient has persistent non-visible haematuria, which requires further investigation.

Send a 24-urine sample for protein estimation
Sending a 24-urine sample for protein estimation is not the most appropriate action in this case. The primary concern is the persistent haematuria, which should be investigated by a urologist.

Refer to nephrology
Referring to nephrology is not the most appropriate action for this older patient. Most haematuria protocols suggest sending younger patients (e.g. < 40 years) to nephrology initially, but this patient should be referred to urology.

Send a further urine microscopy
Sending a further urine microscopy is not the most appropriate action. The patient has already had urine microscopy and culture, which showed no growth, and the persistent haematuria requires further investigation by a urologist.

stem: A 62-year-old man with chronic kidney disease secondary to diabetes mellitus is reviewed. When assessing his estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), which one of the following variables is not required by the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) equation?
explanation:
Serum urea
The correct answer is serum urea. The Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) equation is a widely used formula to estimate the glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in patients with chronic kidney disease. It requires four variables: age, serum creatinine, ethnicity, and gender. Serum urea is not included in the MDRD equation.

Age
Age is an essential variable in the MDRD equation because the eGFR declines naturally with age. Therefore, it's crucial to adjust for age when calculating eGFR to avoid overestimating kidney function in older individuals.

Serum creatinine
Serum creatinine is a key component of the MDRD equation since it's a marker of kidney function. Creatinine is a waste product generated by muscle metabolism and excreted by the kidneys. When kidney function declines, serum creatinine levels rise, indicating reduced eGFR.

Ethnicity
Ethnicity also plays a role in the MDRD equation as certain ethnic groups, particularly those of African descent, have been found to have higher average muscle mass and consequently higher baseline serum creatinine levels. Therefore, incorporating ethnicity into the equation helps ensure accurate estimation of eGFR across different populations.

Gender
Gender is another important variable in the MDRD equation since men typically have more muscle mass than women and thus produce more creatinine. Including gender allows for more accurate estimation of eGFR by accounting for these differences between males and females.

stem: A 20-year-old Nigerian female presents to the Emergency Department with chest pain. She reports a long history of fatigue and joint pains. Examination reveals a pericardial rub and bilateral pitting oedema. Observations show only that she has a low grade pyrexia 37.7ºC and blood pressure 170/100 mmHg. Urinalysis shows haematuria and nephrotic-range proteinuria. A urine pregnancy test is negative. ECG shows saddle-shaped ST-elevation in all leads. Of interest, her blood results show: Urea 8.2 mmol/l Creatinine 212 µmol/l eGFR 33ml/m/m² Which of the following histopathological findings is most likely on renal biopsy?
explanation:
Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis
The most common histological pattern seen in lupus nephritis is diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents to the emergency department with right flank pain radiating from loin to groin. He reports no past medical history and consumes 25 units of alcohol per week. On examination, he appears extremely restless and has experienced vomiting due to the pain, which is relieved by diclofenac administered rectally. The following investigations have been arranged: 24 hour urinary calcium 723 mg (100-300) Serum urate 320 mmol/L (< 420) What treatment can reduce the risk of this problem recurring?
explanation:
Indapamide
In a patient with hypercalciuria and renal stones, calcium excretion and stone formation can be decreased by the use of thiazide diuretics. Indapamide is the correct answer. The patient presents with abdominal pain that radiates from the loin to the groin, suggestive of renal colic secondary to nephrolithiasis. Moreover, there is evidence of hypercalciuria. In such cases, thiazide diuretics like indapamide are beneficial in preventing further stone formation by reducing urinary calcium levels through enhanced reabsorption in the distal tubules.

Allopurinol
Allopurinol is not the correct choice in this scenario. Allopurinol is indicated for the prevention of urate-based renal stones; however, given that serum urate levels are normal, uric acid stones are improbable here.

Furosemide
Furosemide is incorrect. This is likely to cause hypocalcaemia and therefore hypercalciuria and so would not be an appropriate choice to prevent this type of renal stone.

Percutaneous nephrolithotomy
Percutaneous nephrolithotomy is also incorrect. While this surgical intervention is used to remove symptomatic renal calculi, it does not confer any preventive benefit against future stone formation.

Tamsulosin
Tamsulosin does not represent the right answer either. As an alphablocker, tamsulosin aids in the acute management of renal colic by relaxing the ureters and facilitating stone passage; however, it does not prevent stone formation and is typically reserved for assisting in the passage of small stones less than 10mm.

stem: A 33-year-old renal transplant patient was referred to the eye clinic with a large lesion affecting the left upper eyelid. The lesion had developed rapidly over the previous 6 weeks, reaching approximately 20 mm in size. On examination, the lesion appeared erythematous, ulcerated and with a raised crusted surface. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Squamous cell carcinoma
Patients who have received an organ transplant are at risk of skin cancer (particularly squamous cell carcinoma) due to long-term use of immunosuppressants. Squamous cell carcinoma is a common type of non-melanoma skin cancer. It is derived from cells within the epidermis that make keratin. Clinically presenting as scaly or crusted lumps which are tender on palpation and may ulcerate. These features are present in this case and a major risk factor is a long-term immunosuppression which this patient has received due to their solid-organ transplantation.

Basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma is incorrect as they typically present as waxy shiny papules with a central depression and are smooth in appearance. They can have telangiectasia over the surface. It is the most prevalent type of skin cancer but is not being described in this case.

Intradermal naevus
Intradermal naevus is also known as intradermal melanocytic naevus is basically a classic mole or birthmark. It typically appears as an elevated, dome-shaped bump on the skin surface. Therefore, this is unlikely to be the correct answer.

Lentigo maligna melanoma
Lentigo maligna melanoma is a type of invasive skin cancer that usually starts as a tan-brown macule or patch described here or Hutchinson's melanotic freckle. Lentigo maligna is an early form of melanoma whereby malignant cells are confined to the tissue of origin, the epidermis, hence it is known as in situ melanoma. It occurs in sun-damaged skin so is usually seen on the face or neck but not described here in this case.

Merkel cell carcinoma
Merkel cell carcinoma is a rare, aggressive skin cancer. It appears as a painless, flesh-coloured or bluish-red nodule growing on your skin. Whilst it can commonly occur following organ transplantation, it is not described here in this case.

stem: 82-year-old female with a background of rheumatoid arthritis on maintenance dose prednisolone and sulfasalazine is admitted with deteriorating renal function. Urine dip reveals protein +++. She has previously suffered from a distal radial fracture and is currently complaining of numbness and tingling down the lateral 3 1/2 digits of the opposite hand. Renal ultrasound reveals bilaterally enlarged kidneys and a subcutaneous abdominal fat biopsy is positive after Congo red staining. What is the most likely unifying diagnosis?
explanation:
AA amyloidosis
Secondary AA amyloidosis is most likely given the background of rheumatoid arthritis (the second most common cause after juvenile idiopathic arthritis in the UK), heavy proteinuria, and positive Congo red staining.

Diabetes
Diabetes would be a possibility, however, it is not associated with a positive Congo red staining.

AL amyloidosis
AL amyloidosis tends to be associated with an underlying haematological condition as opposed to an inflammatory problem.

Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia
Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia would not cause a positive Congo red staining.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus would not cause a positive Congo red staining.

stem: Which one of the following statements is true regarding autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease?
options: Onset is typically in the third decade
Is due to a defect on chromosome 16
More common than autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
May be diagnosed on prenatal ultrasound
explanation:
May be diagnosed on prenatal ultrasound
The correct answer is 'May be diagnosed on prenatal ultrasound'. Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is a rare genetic disorder that can be detected prenatally. This condition often presents in utero or at birth, and it's characterised by the development of cysts in both kidneys, leading to enlarged kidneys and impaired kidney function. Prenatal ultrasounds can reveal these abnormalities, thus allowing for early diagnosis.

Onset is typically in the third decade
Onset is typically in the third decade' is not accurate. ARPKD usually presents at birth or during infancy, although it can sometimes present later in childhood. It does not typically onset in the third decade of life; this is more characteristic of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).

Liver involvement is rare
Liver involvement is rare' is also incorrect. In fact, liver involvement is common with ARPKD. The disease often affects multiple organ systems and can cause congenital hepatic fibrosis, which leads to progressive liver disease.

Is due to a defect on chromosome 16
Is due to a defect on chromosome 16' is false as well. ARPKD results from mutations in the PKHD1 gene located on chromosome 6, not chromosome 16. A defect on chromosome 16 causes ADPKD.

More common than autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
More common than autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease' isn't true either. ADPKD is one of the most common monogenic disorders and one of the most common causes of end-stage renal disease, affecting about 1 in every 400 to 1000 people worldwide. On the other hand, ARPKD only affects approximately 1 in every 20,000 individuals.

stem: A 32-year-old man has been referred to the clinic due to a two-month history of loin pain and haematuria. He mentions that his family has a history of an inherited condition primarily impacting the kidneys. Several years ago, he was advised to undergo screening tests, but he chose not to. On examination, the patient exhibits bilaterally palpable masses. A renal ultrasound scan reveals the presence of over 10 cysts in both kidneys. What other complication is most associated with the patient's likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hepatomegaly
ADPKD is associated with hepatomegaly (due to hepatic cysts). This patient has presented with multiple features consistent with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), including flank discomfort, enlarged kidneys, and haematuria, along with a strong family history of a renal condition. The diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of over 10 cysts in both kidneys on ultrasound. ADPKD is associated with several common extra-renal complications, including cysts in other organs, such as the liver. Patients can develop multiple hepatic cysts, leading to liver enlargement, hepatomegaly. Unlike kidney cysts, which are primarily associated with mutations in the PKD1 or PKD2 genes, liver cysts in ADPKD have a different genetic basis and mechanism of formation. Liver cysts in ADPKD are typically associated with mutations in the PRKCSH or SEC63 genes.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm
ADPKD is known to be linked with various cardiac complications, including aortic root dilatation and thoracic aorta dissection. However, there have been few reported cases of the condition being associated with abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), and these incidents are likely attributable to concurrent hypertension, a common feature of ADPKD. In contrast, ADPKD is strongly correlated with the development of intracranial aneurysms, with patients having approximately a fivefold greater risk compared to the general population. However, this heightened risk does not extend to AAA. The underlying pathophysiology and the reasons for variations in aneurysm site risk remain unclear.

Phaeochromocytoma
Several genetic syndromic disorders, such as Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN), and neurofibromatosis, are known to be linked with phaeochromocytomas. However, there is no confirmed association between ADPKD and this uncommon adrenal tumour.

Pleural cysts
The formation of non-renal cysts is commonly associated with ADPKD with cysts development in the liver, spleen and ovaries all being linked to the disease. Pleural cysts however remain very rare in patients with ADPKD.

Uveitis
Uveitis is an ocular manifestation of various systemic syndromes and diseases including inflammatory (e.g. inflammatory bowel disease), vasculitic (e.g. Kawasaki disease) and arthritic conditions (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis) however there is no established link between ADPKD and uveitis.

stem: A 39-year-old man presents to his GP with a three-week history of increasing thirst and polyuria. Physical examination is normal. He has a history of bipolar affective disorder for which he started a new medication approximately four weeks ago. The GP conducts laboratory tests to confirm the suspected diagnosis. Water deprivation test results: Serum osmolarity 330 mmol/L (285-295mOsm/kg) Urine osmolarity 100 mmol/L (50-1200 mOsm/kg) Post-desmopressin test results: Urine osmolarity 125 mmol/L (50 -1200 mOsm/kg) What is the underlying mechanism for the likely diagnosis?
options: Desensitisation of the kidney to respond to antidiuretic hormone
Dysfunctional antidiuretic hormone receptor within the kidney
Increased sodium absorption in the proximal tubule of the kidney
Mutation in the gene that encodes the aquaporin 2 channel
explanation:
Desensitisation of the kidney to respond to antidiuretic hormone
Diabetes insipidus in patients taking lithium mechanism: lithium desensitizes the kidney's ability to respond to ADH in the collecting ducts. Desensitisation of the kidney to respond to antidiuretic hormone is the correct answer. The patient presents with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, as evidenced by the initial symptoms of polyuria and polydipsia, coupled with a water deprivation test that demonstrates minimal change in urine osmolarity following administration of desmopressin. The patient's medical history reveals the recent commencement of medication for bipolar affective disorder, which coincided with the onset of symptoms. Considering our understanding of the etiologies of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, it is plausible to attribute the condition in this case to lithium therapy. Lithium is known to cause desensitization of renal responsiveness to antidiuretic hormone within the collecting ducts, leading effectively to a functional impairment of antidiuretic hormone action.

Decreased secretion of antidiuretic hormone
Decreased secretion of antidiuretic hormone is incorrect as well. This represents another pathophysiological basis for cranial diabetes insipidus. In such cases, one would expect a marked increase in urine osmolarity after desmopressin administration because the renal response to antidiuretic hormone remains intact, ensuring appropriate urine concentration. Etiologies might include traumatic brain injury, postoperative states following pituitary surgery, craniopharyngiomas, and infiltrative disorders. However, evidence supporting these causes or corresponding water deprivation test results indicative of cranial diabetes insipidus are absent in this clinical scenario.

Dysfunctional antidiuretic hormone receptor within the kidney
Dysfunctional antidiuretic hormone receptor within the kidney is incorrect. This suggests an inherited disorder causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus due to aberrant receptor structure or function. Patients with such genetic conditions typically present at an earlier age than depicted here. Moreover, this case specifically mentions the initiation of new medication preceding symptom development, which points more convincingly towards lithium as a causative factor.

Increased sodium absorption in the proximal tubule of the kidney
Increased sodium absorption in the proximal tubule of the kidney is incorrect. This is not an underlying mechanism for diabetes insipidus as seen in this patient supported by their symptoms and water deprivation test. Classically the kidneys may reabsorb increased sodium in response to aldosterone that is released by the zona glomerulosa in response to raised angiotensin II, potassium, and ACTH levels. This is not seen in this patient.

Mutation in the gene that encodes the aquaporin 2 channel
Mutation in the gene that encodes the aquaporin 2 channel is incorrect as well. Although this mutation also leads to nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, it is less common than mutations affecting the antidiuretic hormone receptor itself.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the urology outpatient clinic with a 2-year history of weak urinary stream, hesitancy, and nocturia occurring 3-4 times per night. Digital rectal examination reveals a significantly enlarged, smooth prostate estimated at 60g. His International Prostate Symptom Score is 18. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?
explanation:
Tamsulosin and finasteride combination
Tamsulosin and finasteride combination is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient. NICE guidelines recommend combination therapy for men with bothersome moderate-to-severe voiding symptoms (IPSS ≥8) and prostatic enlargement. This patient has an IPSS of 18 (moderate-to-severe symptoms) and a significantly enlarged prostate (60g), making him an ideal candidate for combination therapy. The alpha-1 antagonist (tamsulosin) will provide rapid symptom relief by relaxing smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck, while the 5alpha reductase inhibitor (finasteride) will reduce prostate volume over time and slow disease progression. The MTOPS trial demonstrated superior efficacy of combination therapy compared to monotherapy in preventing disease progression and improving symptoms in men with enlarged prostates.

Tamsulosin
Tamsulosin monotherapy would be appropriate for patients with moderate-to-severe voiding symptoms but without significant prostatic enlargement. While this patient does have qualifying symptoms, the significantly enlarged prostate (60g) indicates he is at high risk of disease progression, making combination therapy more appropriate than alphablocker monotherapy alone.

Finasteride
Finasteride monotherapy is indicated for patients with significantly enlarged prostates at high risk of progression, but it takes up to 6 months to show symptomatic improvement. Given this patient's bothersome symptoms, starting with finasteride alone would leave him symptomatic for an extended period when combination therapy could provide both immediate relief and long-term benefits.

Tolterodine
Tolterodine is an antimuscarinic agent used when storage symptoms persist after alpha-blocker treatment. This patient primarily presents with voiding symptoms (weak stream, hesitancy) rather than storage symptoms, making this an inappropriate first-line choice.

Doxazosin
Doxazosin is another alpha-1 antagonist that could provide symptom relief, but like tamsulosin monotherapy, it would not address the underlying prostatic enlargement or prevent disease progression in this high-risk patient.

stem: A 6-year-old boy is seen in clinic with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. His mother reports frequent episodes of fever and loin pain since early childhood. His blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg, and an abdominal examination reveals no organomegaly. Urinalysis reveals proteinuria, but no leukocytes, glucose, or nitrites. Investigations: Urea 8.5 mmol/L (1.6 - 6.0) Creatinine 95 µmol/L (29 - 53) Which investigation is most likely to be diagnostic?
explanation:
Micturating cystography
Micturating cystography (MCUG) is correct. This patient has features of vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) with reflux nephropathy. The history of recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) and episodic fever with loin pain, combined with hypertension, proteinuria, and impaired renal function (elevated urea and creatinine), suggests kidney damage secondary to repeated episodes of pyelonephritis caused by VUR. The absence of leukocytes and nitrites at presentation suggests that the patient currently has no infection. MCUG is the gold standard for diagnosing VUR as it directly visualises retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureters and kidneys during voiding.

CT urogram
CT urogram is incorrect as this is primarily used in imaging the kidneys, ureters, and bladder to evaluate urological malignancies, stones, or anatomical abnormalities. It is unsuitable for detecting VUR and does not demonstrate the dynamic retrograde flow of urine from the bladder to the ureters during voiding.

Dimercaptosuccinic acid scan
Dimercaptosuccinic acid scan (DMSA scan) is incorrect as this detects renal tissue scarring rather than identifying retrograde urine flow. In contrast, MCUG directly visualises reflux during voiding, which aids the diagnosis of VUR. A DMSA scan could instead be considered if the diagnosis of VUR is already established and the aim is to assess the extent and severity of renal scarring.

Renal ultrasound
Renal ultrasound is incorrect. While this is a non-invasive and widely available imaging tool, it is more useful for identifying gross anatomical abnormalities such as hydronephrosis or renal scarring, but it cannot provide functional information about urinary reflux. Ultrasonography could instead be considered as an initial test to screen for obstructive uropathy or structural abnormalities before proceeding to MCUG, however, the focus of this question is on the diagnostic test for VUR.

Urodynamic testing
Urodynamic testing is incorrect as this evaluates bladder storage and voiding dynamics rather than detecting retrograde urine flow. In contrast, MCUG directly visualises urine reflux while voiding, which aids the diagnosis of VUR. Urodynamic testing could be considered if there were concerns about bladder dysfunction, such as neurogenic bladder or urinary incontinence, which is not the case here.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents to the urology clinic. He has suffered from recurrent episodes of renal colic. CT scans have shown multiple stones and 24-hour urine collection reveals high urinary calcium. What is the single best medication that might reduce his stone formation?
explanation:
Thiazide diuretic
Thiazide diuretics may help in this scenario. Thiazides can increase distal tubular calcium resorption and therefore decrease calcium in the urine and stone formation.

Allopurinol
Allopurinol works as a xanthine oxidase inhibitor which works to reduce uric acid production. It, therefore, decreases uric acid stones rather than calcium stones.

Cholestyramine
Cholestyramine reduces urinary oxalate secretion and can decrease oxalate stones, not calcium stones.

Oral bicarbonate
Oral bicarbonate can increase the alkalization of the urine and decrease uric acid stones rather than calcium stones.

Pyridoxine
Pyridoxine may reduce oxalate stones rather than calcium stones by reducing urinary oxalate secretion.

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents to the clinic with growth retardation, polyuria, and muscle weakness. His blood tests reveal the following results: Na + 147 mmol/L (136–146), K+ 3 mmol/L (3.5–5.0), Cl - 100 mmol/L (95–105), HCO3 - 18 mmol/L (22-28). Further urine tests indicate: Glucose in urine 5 mmol/24 hours (< 2.78 mmol/24hours), Phosphate in urine 70 mmol/24 hours (15 -50 mmol/24 hours). Which part of the renal tubule is the reabsorptive defect most likely to be located?
options: Ascending limb of loop of Henle
Descending limb of loop of Henle
explanation:
Proximal convoluted tubule
Fanconi syndrome is a reabsorptive defect in PCT where there is increased excretion of nearly all amino acids, glucose, bicarbonate, and phosphate. The presentation of increased urinary glucose and phosphate and a decrease in potassium levels combined with growth retardation and muscle weakness strongly suggest Fanconi syndrome. This condition predominantly affects the proximal convoluted tubule, which explains the increased urinary excretion of glucose and phosphate and decreased serum bicarbonate.

Ascending limb of loop of Henle
Ascending limb of loop of Henle is not the correct option. While the ascending limb of the loop of the Henle does play a significant role in the absorption of sodium, chloride, and potassium ions, it can contribute to the resorption of magnesium and calcium ions. However, glucose and phosphate reabsorption primarily occur within the proximal convoluted tubule. The increased urinary excretion of these substances indicates Fanconi syndrome's impact on the proximal convoluted tubule.

Collecting duct
Collecting duct is an incorrect option. Water and sodium reabsorption occur within the collecting duct. The increased urinary excretion of glucose and phosphate indicates a defect in the proximal convoluted tubule where their reabsorption occurs. Additionally, hypokalemia, growth retardation, and muscle weakness further support a diagnosis of Fanconi syndrome.

Descending limb of loop of Henle
Descending limb of loop of Henle is an inappropriate choice. Water is reabsorbed from this segment via osmosis. It does not facilitate the reabsorption of glucose or phosphate. These processes are compromised in Fanconi syndrome, which affects the proximal convoluted tubule. Growth retardation, polyuria, and muscle weakness, along with hypokalemia with concomitant increases in urinary excretion of glucose and phosphate, further support the diagnosis of Fanconi syndrome.

Distal convoluted tubule
Distal convoluted tubule is an incorrect option. Reabsorption of sodium and chloride occurs in the distal convoluted tubule across its apical membrane but does not participate significantly in glucose and phosphate reabsorption. Excessive urinary excretion of these substances suggests a defect within the proximal convoluted tubule rather than the distal convoluted tubule; when considered together with growth retardation, muscle weakness, and hypokalemia – all indicate Fanconi syndrome.

stem: Which one of the following factors is most associated with an increased risk of developing bladder cancer?
explanation:
Aniline dye exposure
The correct answer is Aniline dye exposure. Aniline dyes are aromatic amines used in various industries such as the rubber, chemical, textile and leather industries. Numerous studies have shown a strong association between exposure to aniline dyes and an increased risk of developing bladder cancer. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has classified some aromatic amines including benzidine and 2-naphthylamine, which are types of aniline dyes, as Group 1 carcinogens, meaning there is sufficient evidence of their carcinogenicity in humans.

Strongyloides stercoralis infection
Strongyloides stercoralis infection is not typically associated with bladder cancer. This parasitic infection primarily affects the intestines and can cause abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and rash. In severe cases or in immunocompromised individuals, it can lead to hyperinfection syndrome or disseminated disease affecting multiple organs but it does not increase the risk of bladder cancer.

Beryllium salt exposure
Beryllium salt exposure has been linked to lung disease and lung cancer but there's no significant evidence associating it with bladder cancer. Beryllium is a metal used in various industries such as aerospace, nuclear weapons production, electronics and dental appliances manufacturing. Chronic beryllium disease (CBD), a granulomatous lung disorder caused by inhalation of beryllium particles or fumes, can lead to pulmonary fibrosis but not bladder cancer.

Aflatoxin exposure
Exposure to Aflatoxin, a mycotoxin produced by the fungi Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus, has been strongly associated with liver cancer but not bladder cancer. Aflatoxin contamination often occurs in crops like peanuts, maize and cottonseed that are stored in warm humid conditions conducive for fungal growth.

Long term phenytoin use
Long-term use of the antiepileptic drug Phenytoin has been associated with several side effects including gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, folate deficiency and osteomalacia but there's no established link between phenytoin use and increased risk of bladder cancer. Phenytoin may induce chronic liver disease due to its hepatic metabolism which could potentially increase the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma but this association remains controversial.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is seen in clinic with a history of recurrent renal stones. She has no history of bone pain or fractures, and has no family history. A non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder (KUB) reveals multiple radiopaque renal calculi. Investigations: 24-hour urinary oxalate excretion 0.25 mmol/24h (0.2 – 0.45) 24-hour urinary calcium excretion 8.75 mmol/24h (< 6) Serum calcium 2.2 mmol/L (2.2 - 2.6) Serum phosphate 1.4 mmol/L (0.8 - 1.5) Serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) 4.5 pmol/L (1.6 - 6.9) Serum vitamin D 75 nmol/L (50 - 150) Which drug is most likely to decrease her risk of future stone formation?
explanation:
Indapamide
In a patient with hypercalciuria and renal stones, calcium excretion and stone formation can be decreased by the use of thiazide diuretics. Indapamide is correct. This patient most likely has idiopathic hypercalciuria, causing recurrent calcium nephrolithiasis. This is supported by the presence of multiple radiopaque calculi on a noncontrast KUB, consistent with calcium-containing stones, and a significantly elevated 24-hour urinary calcium excretion, despite normal serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH levels. Indapamide, a thiazide-like diuretic, reduces urinary calcium excretion by enhancing distal tubular calcium reabsorption, thereby lowering the risk of further stone formation.

Allopurinol
Allopurinol is incorrect as it reduces uric acid levels, which would likely be more useful for uric acid stones secondary to hyperuricemia. Uric acid stones tend to be radiolucent on imaging, unlike the radiopaque stones seen here. Additionally, hyperuricemia may be associated with a history of gout, such as acute 1st metatarsophalangeal joint inflammation or gouty tophi, which are not seen here.

Cinacalcet
Cinacalcet is incorrect as this reduces calcium levels in primary hyperparathyroidism, where surgery is contraindicated or in secondary hyperparathyroidism in end-stage renal disease on dialysis. This patient's serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH levels are normal, and they lack features like bone pain and fractures, making hyperparathyroidism less likely.

Furosemide
Furosemide is incorrect as this increases urinary calcium excretion by inhibiting the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, promoting calciuria. This would hence increase the risk of calcium stone formation. In contrast, thiazide-like diuretics like indapamide reduce urinary calcium excretion, which can reduce the risk of calcium-containing renal stone formation.

Pyridoxine
Pyridoxine is incorrect as this reduces the amount of urinary oxalate secretion, reducing the risk of calcium oxalate stones. While these can also be radiopaque, this patient's 24-hour urinary oxalate secretion is normal, making hyperoxaluria less likely.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents to her GP, anxious to be 'checked out' because her older brother recently passed away from a haemorrhagic stroke. She was told that his autopsy showed cerebral aneurysmal rupture. The patient is well currently, with no fever, weight loss, headache or dysuria but has been treated for recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) over the past 3 years. Her father had a history of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and passed away from a stroke at age 65. What is the most appropriate investigation for diagnosis of this patient's condition?
options: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen with contrast
explanation:
Renal ultrasound scan (USS)
Ultrasound is the screening test for adult polycystic kidney disease. Given the patient's personal and family history, she has an increased risk of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), the most common genetic cause of CKD. Mutations of PKD1/PKD2 genes lead to cystic degeneration of renal parenchyma, resulting in enlargement of the kidneys, hypertension, recurrent UTIs, haematuria and flank pain. ADPKD is also associated with extrarenal manifestations such as pancreatic/hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse, aortic regurgitation and intracranial aneurysms (a cause of haemorrhagic stroke). Renal ultrasound (USS) is the preferred screening modality as age-dependent diagnostic criteria have high sensitivity and specificity and because of its low cost, no exposure to radiation and widespread availability.

Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen with contrast
CT scan of the abdomen can diagnose ADPKD but is inappropriate for screening, considering USS is a relatively cheaper, safer and more widely available option.

Cranial magnetic resonance angiography
This patient needs screening for ADPKD and has no signs of an intracranial aneurysm (e.g. headache). Considering her strong family history of ADPKD-associated intracranial aneurysms she may benefit from aneurysmal screening if she ever develops a headache or neurological symptoms, using cranial magnetic resonance angiography.

Kidneys, ureters and bladder (KUB) X-ray
A KUB X-ray cannot detect polycystic kidneys. However, it is used commonly as the first-line investigation for urolithiasis.

Molecular genetic testing
Genetic testing is less cost-efficient than USS. It is also not a useful screening tool for ADPKD since current genotypic testing can only identify approximately 70% of the known pathogenic intragenic PKD1 and PKD2 mutations.

stem: A 40-year-old man with a history of psychiatric problems and epilepsy comes for review. He complains that he is drinking excessive amounts of water and having to urinate frequently. He has not lost any weight and states that he is compliant with his current medications. Blood tests show the following: Na+ 145 mmol/l K+ 4.1 mmol/l Urea 6.3 mmol/l Creatinine 101 µmol/l Glucose (random) 6.2 mol/l Which one of the following medications is most likely to be responsible for this presentation?
explanation:
Lithium
This patient has probably developed nephrogenic diabetes insipidus secondary to lithium therapy. Polyuria, polydipsia and a high-normal sodium are pointers towards this.

stem: A 55-year-old female presents with polyuria and polydipsia, which has been on-going for 11 weeks. She has hypertension and bipolar disorder and is currently taking amlodipine and lithium. A water deprivation test is carried out: Pre-test urine osmolality 250 mOsm/kg (500-850) Post-test urine osmolality 274 mOsm/kg (500-850) What is the pathogenesis of the likely diagnosis?
options: Lithium desensitizes the ability of the anterior pituitary gland to respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
Lithium desensitizes the ability of the posterior pituitary gland to respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
Lithium desensitizes the kidney's ability to respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in the collecting ducts
Lithium desensitizes the kidney's ability to respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in the distal convoluted tubule
Lithium desensitizes the kidney's ability to respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in the proximal convoluted tubule
explanation:
Lithium desensitizes the kidney's ability to respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in the collecting ducts
Diabetes insipidus in patients taking lithium mechanism: lithium desensitizes the kidney's ability to respond to ADH in the collecting ducts. The water deprivation test results, along with the clinical symptoms of polyuria and polydipsia, indicate that this patient has diabetes insipidus. As the patient is on lithium and has no clinical features suggesting a cranial cause of diabetes insipidus, he most likely has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. The exact molecular mechanism by which lithium causes dysfunction at the collecting duct is still to be fully determined, but it is currently accepted that lithium desensitises the kidney's ability to respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH).

Lithium desensitizes the ability of the anterior pituitary gland to respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
The anterior pituitary gland secretes 7 hormones: follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, prolactin, endorphins, and growth hormone. An anterior pituitary tumour often presents with bilateral hemianopia. This does not explain the pathogenesis of diabetes insipidus in this patient.

Lithium desensitizes the ability of the posterior pituitary gland to respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
The posterior pituitary is the site of ADH release. Dysfunction at the posterior pituitary would cause cranial diabetes insipidus. Although cranial diabetes insipidus can be idiopathic, it classically presents after head trauma or pituitary surgery. This does not apply to the patient's condition.

Lithium desensitizes the kidney's ability to respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in the distal convoluted tubule
The distal convoluted tubule is the site of action for thiazide diuretics. Thiazides are used to treat nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. However, the primary site of lithium's effect is the collecting duct, not the distal convoluted tubule.

Lithium desensitizes the kidney's ability to respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in the proximal convoluted tubule
Dysfunction of the proximal renal tubule can cause Fanconi syndrome; the proximal renal tubular cells are unable to absorb glucose, amino acids, uric acid, phosphate, and bicarbonate. This is not the mechanism of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus caused by lithium.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the renal clinic with a 3-month history of ankle swelling. Examination reveals pitting oedema to the mid-shins. Investigations show: Urinary protein 5.2 g/24h (<0.15) Serum albumin 28 g/L (35-50) Creatinine 92 μmol/L (59-104) Total cholesterol 6.8 mmol/L (<5.0) Renal biopsy shows thickened glomerular basement membrane with subepithelial deposits creating a 'spike and dome' appearance on silver staining. Which antibody is most likely to be detected in this patient's serum?
explanation:
Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor
Idiopathic membranous glomerulonephritis is related to antiphospholipase A2 antibodies. This patient presents with nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria >3.5g/24h, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hypercholesterolaemia) and has renal biopsy findings characteristic of membranous glomerulonephritis (thickened basement membrane with subepithelial deposits creating a 'spike and dome' appearance). The most likely antibody to be detected in this case is anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) antibody. Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibodies are present in approximately 70-80% of patients with primary (idiopathic) membranous glomerulonephritis. These autoantibodies target the PLA2R antigen expressed on podocytes, leading to in situ immune complex formation, complement activation, and subsequent podocyte injury. The presence of these antibodies helps distinguish primary from secondary forms of membranous nephropathy. Anti-PLA2R antibody levels often correlate with disease activity and can be used to monitor response to treatment. The absence of other systemic symptoms or signs in this middle-aged man, along with the classic biopsy findings, strongly supports primary membranous nephropathy as the diagnosis.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane
Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are associated with anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture's syndrome), which typically presents with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and often pulmonary haemorrhage. The renal biopsy in anti-GBM disease shows a crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane, not the subepithelial deposits seen in this case.

Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic
Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) are associated with small vessel vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. These conditions typically present with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and renal biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis without immune complex deposition, unlike the findings in this case.

Anti-double stranded DNA
Anti-double stranded DNA antibodies are characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). While lupus nephritis can cause membranous nephropathy (Class V lupus nephritis), it typically shows 'full house' immunofluorescence with deposits of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q. This patient has no mentioned systemic features of SLE, making this antibody less likely.

Anti-C1q
Anti-C1q antibodies can be found in patients with SLE, particularly those with lupus nephritis, and in patients with hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis. They are not specifically associated with idiopathic membranous glomerulonephritis. The absence of other clinical features of these conditions makes anti-C1q antibodies an unlikely finding in this case.

stem: A 58-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on haemodialysis attends a routine clinic. He reports worsening generalised bone pain and myalgia. His latest blood results are shown below. Ca2+ (adjusted) 2.18 mmol/L (2.20 - 2.60) Phosphate 1.95 mmol/L (0.8 - 1.5) PTH 75 pmol/L (1.6 - 6.9) Alkaline Phosphatase 250 U/L (30 - 130) He is already taking a phosphate binder. Which is the most appropriate additional treatment to manage his condition?
explanation:
Alfacalcidol
Alfacalcidol is used as a vitamin D supplement in end-stage renal disease because it does not require activation in the kidneys. This patient has end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and the clinical and biochemical features of severe secondary hyperparathyroidism, also known as chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD). The key features are hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, and a markedly elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) level, leading to high-turnover bone disease (indicated by the raised alkaline phosphatase and bone pain). A crucial step in vitamin D metabolism is the conversion of inactive 25hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) by the enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the kidneys. In ESRD, this enzyme's activity is severely diminished. Alfacalcidol is 1-alpha-hydroxyvitamin D3; it only requires hydroxylation in the liver to become active calcitriol, thereby bypassing the deficient renal activation step. This active form then helps to suppress PTH secretion, increase intestinal calcium absorption, and correct hypocalcaemia.

Cholecalciferol
Cholecalciferol is vitamin D3. It is an inactive form of vitamin D that requires hydroxylation first in the liver and then, crucially, in the kidneys to become active calcitriol. As this patient has ESRD, the renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase required for this second activation step is deficient. Therefore, supplementation with cholecalciferol would be ineffective in raising active vitamin D levels and managing his secondary hyperparathyroidism. While it is used to treat vitamin D deficiency in patients with normal renal function or early-stage CKD, it is not appropriate for those with ESRD.

Cinacalcet
Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic agent that increases the sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptors on the parathyroid gland to extracellular calcium. This leads to a reduction in PTH secretion. While it is an effective treatment for secondary hyperparathyroidism, it is not the most appropriate first-line addition in this scenario. According to UK guidelines (NICE), an active vitamin D analogue like alfacalcidol should be offered first to suppress the PTH. Cinacalcet is typically considered if PTH levels remain uncontrolled despite optimal doses of phosphate binders and active vitamin D, or if hypercalcaemia prevents up-titration of vitamin D analogues.

Ergocalciferol
Ergocalciferol is vitamin D2. Similar to cholecalciferol, it is an inactive precursor that requires activation in both the liver and the kidneys. For the same reasons that cholecalciferol is inappropriate, ergocalciferol would be ineffective in a patient with end-stage renal disease due to the lack of renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity. It is therefore not a suitable treatment for this patient's condition.

Calcium carbonate
Calcium carbonate is primarily used as a calcium-based phosphate binder. The question states the patient is already taking a phosphate binder. While it also provides calcium supplementation, simply increasing calcium intake will not address the fundamental problem of deficient active vitamin D. Furthermore, in the presence of significant hyperphosphataemia, administering large amounts of calcium can increase the calcium-phosphate product, raising the risk of dangerous soft tissue and vascular calcification. The primary goal is to suppress PTH with an active vitamin D analogue.

stem: A 3-year-old, originally presented with persistent haematuria, undergoes a renal biopsy showing splitting on the lamina densa resulting in an abnormal glomerular-basement membrane. Whilst under investigation, the child develops swallowing issues and a recurrent cough. CT chest showed the presence of oesophagus and tracheobronchial leiomyomatosis. A potential genetic cause is suspect and testing identifies an X-linked dominant inherited protein defect, confirming the syndrome responsible for the child issues. What other feature is most associated with this child's likely syndrome?
explanation:
Sensorineural hearing loss
Alport's syndrome - sensorineural hearing loss. This child has presented with features in keeping with Alport syndrome. Alport syndrome is caused by an inherited defect in type IV collagen, normally in an X-linked dominant pattern. The condition typically results in progressive renal failure secondary to glomerular-basement membrane abnormality and sensorineural hearing loss. Other features of the syndrome include ocular issues, smooth muscle tumours (leiomyomas) and rarely aortic dissection.

Cardiac defect
As Alport syndrome affects the type IV collagen, cardiac defects, which typically result from defects of the myocardium, are not associated with the condition. In very rare cases of early-onset disease, aortic dissection may occur due to vessel wall defects.

High-arched palate
A high-arched palate is associated with a number of congenital conditions, particularly those affecting the connective tissues such as Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, however, it is not a feature of Alport syndrome.

Learning difficulties
As Alport syndrome is due to a collagen defect, neurological and cognitive issues such as learning difficulties are not associated with the condition.

Lens dislocation
Lenticonus, which is a conical-like protrusion on the lens capsule and underlying cortex, is a well-recognised feature of Alport syndrome and although this can lead to light refractory issues and reduced visual acuity, lens dislocation is not associated with the defect.

stem: A 12-year-old boy is investigated for a purpuric rash on the extensor surfaces of his lower legs. He also has a history of abdominal pain and an urticarial rash. The following results are obtained: Urine dipstick: blood ++ What would be the likely finding on renal biopsy?
explanation:
Mesangial hypercellularity
The correct answer is Mesangial hypercellularity. This finding is consistent with the clinical features and laboratory findings of Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP), which the patient likely has. HSP, also known as IgA vasculitis, commonly presents in children with a tetrad of palpable purpura, arthritis or arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal involvement. The renal involvement typically manifests as hematuria and/or proteinuria. Renal biopsy in HSP often demonstrates mesangial hypercellularity due to the deposition of IgA immune complexes within the mesangium.

Linear IgG deposits
Linear IgG deposits are typically seen in Goodpasture's syndrome, an autoimmune disease characterised by anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies resulting in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary haemorrhage. This does not fit with the patient's presentation.

No change
No change on renal biopsy is typically seen in minimal change disease (MCD). MCD is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children but it does not present with purpuric rash or abdominal pain.

Sclerosis within the glomerulus
Sclerosis within the glomerulus would suggest focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) or diabetic nephropathy. These conditions do not present with a purpuric rash and urticarial rash.

Basement membrane thickening
Basement membrane thickening is a characteristic feature of membranous nephropathy or Alport's syndrome. Neither condition presents with a purpuric rash nor abdominal pain.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to his GP with polyuria, nocturia and polydipsia. He has no past medical history of note. Routine blood tests including Hba1c and random glucose are unremarkable. He undergoes a water deprivation test, which confirms diabetes insipidus. There is no response to nasal desmopressin. Which of the following are a cause of this condition?
options: Inherited mutation in the vasopressin (ADH) receptor
Inherited mutation in the aquaporin 1 channel
explanation:
Inherited mutation in the vasopressin (ADH) receptor
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus may be caused by genetic mutations: the more common form affects the vasopressin (ADH) receptor. The less common form results from a mutation in the gene that encodes the aquaporin 2 channel. In this case, the patient has nephrogenic DI, as there is no response to nasal desmopressin, indicating that the kidneys are insensitive to antidiuretic hormone.

Craniopharyngioma
Craniopharyngioma is a cause of cranial diabetes insipidus, not nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is a cause of cranial diabetes insipidus, not nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Hypocalcaemia
Hypocalcaemia is not a cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Hypercalcaemia, not hypocalcaemia, is a cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Inherited mutation in the aquaporin 1 channel
Inherited mutation in the aquaporin 1 channel is not a known cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. The less common form of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus results from a mutation in the gene that encodes the aquaporin 2 channel.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is referred by the general practitioner as her recent blood test showed elevated creatinine and urea levels. Other blood test results are normal. She is oliguric but could produce enough sample for urine dip. Her urine is negative for red cells, nitrites and leucocytes. She was recently started on Ramipril for hypertension 3 weeks ago. She is otherwise well. Her observations are within normal limits. The renal ultrasound shows two normal-sized kidneys with an unobstructed urinary system. Duplex ultrasound showed stenotic renal arteries. Subsequent MR angiography confirmed the diagnosis with the finding of 'string of beads' appearance of the renal arteries. What is the most likely cause of this presentation?
explanation:
Fibromuscular dysplasia
Consider fibromuscular dysplasia in young female patients who develop AKI after the initiation of an ACE inhibitor. In young female patients who develop AKI after initiation of an ACE inhibitor, fibromuscular dysplasia should be suspected. In older persons, suspect atherosclerosis of renal arteries. Fibromuscular dysplasia describes the proliferation of cells in the walls of the arteries causing the vessels to bulge or narrow. This most commonly affects women. These patients are susceptible to AKI after the initiation of an ACE inhibitor. The classic description is 'string of beads' appearance.

Glomerulonephritis
The normal urine dip results ruled out glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome as the cause of kidney failure. Glomerulonephritis typically presents with haematuria with the presence of red cell casts.

Nephrotic syndrome
The normal urine dip results ruled out glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome as the cause of kidney failure. Nephrotic syndrome presents with heavy proteinuria, oedema and hypoalbuminaemia.

Nephrolithiasis
Nephrolithiasis typically presents with painful loin-to-groin pain. It does not cause acute kidney injury unless both kidneys are affected. This was ruled out by the renal ultrasound.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of passing bright red urine. She reports no dysuria, frequency, or suprapubic pain. She has no significant past medical history and takes no regular medications. Examination is unremarkable. Urine dipstick shows blood 3+ with no leucocytes or nitrites. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Arrange urgent urology referral within 2 weeks
Prescribe empirical antibiotics and review in 1 week
Request urgent CT urogram within 48 hours
Arrange routine urology referral within 6 weeks
explanation:
Arrange urgent urology referral within 2 weeks
Urgent 2 week wait referral is needed for unexplained visible haematuria without UTI. Arrange urgent urology referral within 2 weeks is the correct answer. This patient meets the NICE criteria for urgent cancer referral, being aged ≥45 years with unexplained visible haematuria without evidence of urinary tract infection. The absence of leucocytes and nitrites on dipstick, combined with no urinary symptoms suggestive of UTI, makes this unexplained visible haematuria. NICE guidelines specify that patients aged ≥45 years with unexplained visible haematuria should receive urgent referral within 2 weeks due to the risk of underlying malignancy, particularly bladder cancer. The urgency reflects the need to exclude cancer promptly, as early detection significantly improves outcomes. Even though the patient appears well, visible haematuria in this age group warrants immediate specialist assessment.

Prescribe empirical antibiotics and review in 1 week
Prescribe empirical antibiotics and review in 1 week is incorrect. There are no clinical features or dipstick findings to suggest urinary tract infection. The patient has no dysuria, frequency, or systemic symptoms, and the urine dipstick shows no leucocytes or nitrites. Empirical antibiotic treatment would be inappropriate and could delay necessary investigation of potential malignancy.

Request urgent CT urogram within 48 hours
Request urgent CT urogram within 48 hours is inappropriate as the initial management step. While CT urogram may eventually be part of the urological investigation, the correct pathway is referral to urology services who will coordinate appropriate imaging. Direct imaging requests bypass the specialist assessment needed to determine the most suitable investigative approach.

Arrange routine urology referral within 6 weeks
Arrange routine urology referral within 6 weeks fails to recognise the urgency required. NICE guidelines specifically mandate urgent referral within 2 weeks for this presentation due to cancer risk. A routine referral would represent a significant delay in potentially diagnosing malignancy.

Repeat urine dipstick in 2-3 weeks
Repeat urine dipstick in 2-3 weeks is inappropriate for visible haematuria. This approach might be considered for non-visible haematuria to establish persistence, but visible haematuria in a patient aged ≥45 years requires immediate urgent referral regardless of whether it persists.

stem: A 27-year-old man is diagnosed with Goodpasture's syndrome. Which one of the following does not increase the likelihood of a pulmonary haemorrhage?
explanation:
Dehydration
Dehydration may decrease the likelihood of a pulmonary haemorrhage. Pulmonary oedema is associated with an increased risk.

stem: Which of the following types of renal stones are said to have a semiopaque appearance on x-ray?
explanation:
Cystine stones
The correct answer is Cystine stones, which have a semi-opaque (or faintly radiopaque) appearance on plain radiography. Cystine stones form in patients with cystinuria, an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by impaired renal tubular reabsorption of cystine and other dibasic amino acids. These stones have a characteristic appearance on X-ray with moderate radiodensity, appearing as homogeneous, groundglass opacities that are typically described as semi-opaque. They account for approximately 1-2% of all urinary calculi and often form large, staghorn calculi that may recur despite treatment.

Calcium oxalate
Calcium oxalate stones are incorrect. These stones are the most common type of renal calculi, accounting for approximately 70-80% of all kidney stones. They are highly radiopaque (radio-dense) on X-ray due to their calcium content, appearing as distinct white opacities against the soft tissue background. They are not semi-opaque but rather fully opaque and easily visualised on plain radiography.

Urate stones
Urate stones are incorrect. Uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain radiography, meaning they are not visible on X-ray. This is because they lack calcium and other elements that would make them radiopaque. They can only be detected indirectly on X-ray if they cause filling defects in contrast studies or are visualised using other imaging modalities such as CT scanning. Urate stones account for approximately 5-10% of all renal calculi and are associated with conditions causing hyperuricaemia such as gout.

Xanthine stones
Xanthine stones are incorrect. These are extremely rare stones that form in patients with xanthinuria or as a complication of allopurinol therapy in patients with severe hyperuricaemia. Like uric acid stones, xanthine stones are radiolucent and not visible on plain radiography. They would not appear semi-opaque on X-ray.

Triple phosphate stones
Triple phosphate stones are incorrect. These stones, also known as struvite or magnesium ammonium phosphate stones, are associated with urinary tract infections caused by urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus, Klebsiella, and Pseudomonas species. They are fully radiopaque on X-ray due to their mineral content and often form large staghorn calculi that fill the renal pelvis and calyces. They appear distinctly white on X-ray rather than semi-opaque.

stem: A 67-year-old woman attends the dermatology clinic due to a lesion on her left ear which has grown quickly over the last 4 weeks. On examination, there is an ulcerated lesion with an irregular border on the pinna of the left ear. There is some evidence of crusting while the center of the lesion is sunken. She reports this has bled at times and has been slightly painful on occasion. Her past medical history is significant for type 1 diabetes mellitus with nephropathy, for which she underwent a renal transplant 15 years previously. What is the most likely cause of this lesion?
explanation:
Squamous cell carcinoma
Patients who have received an organ transplant are at risk of skin cancer (particularly squamous cell carcinoma) due to long-term use of immunosuppressants. This is likely to be a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Patients who are immunosuppressed following a renal transplant are at particular risk of skin cancer. In contrast to the general population, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is more common than basal cell carcinoma (BCC). As described here, SCC typically presents as a quickly enlarging irregular crusted lesion that can ulcerate and produce pain or bleeding. It is commonly found in sun-exposed areas and can metastasise.

Basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma is less common in renal transplant patients, does not metastasise, and is typically a slow-growing nodule that can bleed and ulcerate. In this case, the speed of onset makes this less likely as well as the epidemiology, with squamous cell carcinoma being more common in renal transplant recipients.

Kaposi's sarcoma
Kaposi's sarcoma typically presents as purplish macular/nodules/papules and does not match the description here.

Malignant melanoma
Malignant melanoma usually starts as an enlarging mole that becomes irregularly pigmented and thickened over time. They may crust and bleed but do not tend to ulcerate. The lack of pigmentation and presence of ulceration, in this case, make this less likely.

Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum usually presents as a rapidly enlarging ulcerated lesion that starts as a small papule, often at the site of trauma. It is typically intensely painful and can be associated with systemic illnesses such as inflammatory bowel disease. In the case described, neither rapid onset nor intense pain is described and there are no other features to suggest a new underlying illness.

stem: A 74-year-old man is admitted to the urology ward with newly diagnosed metastatic prostate cancer. He reports worsening bone pain and urinary retention. He is started on a GnRH agonist. To minimise the risk of tumour flare, which additional medication should be prescribed at initiation?
explanation:
Bicalutamide
Bicalutamide is a non-steroidal anti-androgen that acts by blocking androgen receptors. When starting GnRH agonists for metastatic prostate cancer, there is an initial surge in testosterone ('tumour flare') before suppression occurs, potentially worsening symptoms such as bone pain or urinary obstruction. Bicalutamide blocks androgen receptor activation during this period, thereby preventing tumour flare and its complications. This approach follows UK guidelines for initiating androgen deprivation therapy.

Finasteride
Finasteride is a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor used primarily for benign prostatic hyperplasia and sometimes in low-grade prostate cancer but does not prevent the acute rise in testosterone associated with GnRH agonist initiation. It reduces dihydrotestosterone levels gradually and would not provide immediate blockade of androgen effects needed to prevent tumour flare.

Abiraterone
Abiraterone inhibits androgen synthesis by blocking CYP17; it is reserved for hormone-relapsed metastatic prostate cancer after failure of first-line hormonal therapy or when chemotherapy is not yet indicated. It does not acutely block androgen receptors nor prevent the initial testosterone surge from GnRH agonists.

Tamoxifen
Tamoxifen is an oestrogen receptor modulator used mainly in breast cancer and has no role in preventing tumour flare or treating prostate cancer-related androgen effects.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone may be co-prescribed with some advanced therapies (such as abiraterone) to reduce steroid side-effects but has no direct effect on androgen receptor blockade or prevention of tumour flare following initiation of a GnRH agonist.

stem: A 35-year-old man visits his GP with complaints of peripheral oedema. He has a history of HIV diagnosed six years ago and is on antiretroviral therapy. His blood pressure is 124/67 mmHg. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and blood tests indicate hyperlipidaemia. Na+ 134 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.5 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Bicarbonate 26 mmol/L (22 - 29) Urea 10.2 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 163 µmol/L (55 - 120) What is the most appropriate management for this patient's renal condition?
explanation:
Check adherence to antiretroviral therapy
Antiretroviral therapy is the treatment of choice for HIV-associated nephropathy. HIV-associated nephropathy typically presents with features of nephrotic syndrome, which include proteinuria, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia, accompanied by normotension and reduced renal function. These manifestations are evident in the case described. When antiretroviral therapy has already been initiated, as in this scenario, the most appropriate initial step is to check adherence to antiretroviral therapy.

Cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is an immunosuppressive agent that can be used in the management of certain forms of nephrotic syndrome, such as idiopathic membranous nephropathy in conjunction with glucocorticoids. Cyclophosphamide also serves as a treatment option for steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome of varying causes, including minimal change disease. Nevertheless, given that the patient has HIV infection, HIV-associated nephropathy becomes a more probable diagnosis.

Mycophenolate mofetil
Mycophenolate mofetil is indicated for lupus nephritis treatment and can present with varying clinical pictures ranging from predominantly nephrotic to predominantly nephritic syndromes or an amalgamation thereof depending on its classification. Despite this possibility, there are no additional symptoms indicative of systemic lupus erythematosus in this patient. While it is plausible for patients to exhibit solely renal manifestations initially, the established HIV infection in this patient strongly suggests a diagnosis of HIV-associated renal pathology.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone constitutes first-line management for certain causes of nephrotic syndrome such as minimal change disease and is often employed concomitantly with cyclophosphamide in treating idiopathic membranous nephropathy. However, within the context of HIV-associated nephropathy, antiretroviral therapy is the treatment of choice.

Ramipril
Ramipril, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, represents one therapeutic approach for IgA nephritis which characteristically presents with haematuria. Additionally, ramipril may be considered in cases of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. Nonetheless, for patients with HIV-associated nephropathy like the one under consideration here, antiretroviral therapy remains the cornerstone of treatment.

stem: Which one of the following types of glomerulonephritis is most characteristically associated with partial lipodystrophy?
explanation:
Mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis
Mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis (membranoproliferative) type 2: partial lipodystrophy. Type 2 mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis is associated with partial lipodystrophy.

stem: A 14-year-old is referred to the hospital due to swelling of both legs. Doppler ultrasound is organised which is negative for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) but shows diffuse subcutaneous oedema in both legs. Urinalysis reveals 3+ proteinuria and no other findings. Blood results are as follows. Na+ 144 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 3.7 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22 - 29) Urea 6.8 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 101 µmol/L (55 - 120) Albumin 18 g/L (35-50) What initial course of action is appropriate here?
options: Anticoagulate and repeat Doppler in one week
Contact nephrologist to organise renal biopsy
explanation:
Commence oral prednisolone
Minimal change disease - prednisolone. The correct answer is to commence oral prednisolone. This patient has developed nephrotic syndrome which in children is most commonly due to minimal change disease. The majority of cases are responsive to corticosteroids and this is recommended as the first-line treatment on suspicion of the diagnosis.

Anticoagulate and repeat Doppler in one week
Repeat Doppler could be considered if there is a high suspicion of DVT but in this case, there is a clear alternative diagnosis causing the leg swelling. Repeat doppler after a negative scan rarely shows DVT, with only 2% positivity in one review.

Contact nephrologist to organise renal biopsy
Renal biopsy in children is reserved for failure of steroid treatment, high suspicion of an alternative diagnosis, or declining renal function on a calcineurin inhibitor. It is not without risk so should be used in more complex cases. Nephrotic syndrome in young patients is usually due to minimal change disease and empirical treatment with steroids if recommended without proceeding to biopsy.

Organise plasma exchange
Plasma exchange is not a treatment for minimal change disease. It is used for antibody-mediated renal diseases such as anti-GBM disease and ANCA-associated vasculitis. These would be very unusual in a patient of this age.

Start IV cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is incorrect. This may be used as a steroid-sparing agent later in management, but would not be the first-line treatment for minimal change disease.

stem: A 45-year-old man is seen in the Nephrology clinic after an abnormality was identified in some routine blood tests taken by his GP. He has no significant past medical history, and does not take any regular medications. On examination, the only abnormality is moderate peripheral oedema extending to the knees bilaterally. His investigation results are as follows: Hb 140 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 335 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 6.8 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 138 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.8 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 11.2 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 158 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 5 mg/L (< 5) Albumin 25 g/L (35 - 50) 24h urinary protein collection Renal biopsy: 4.2g 'The basement membrane is thickened with subepithelial electron dense deposits, creating a 'spike and dome' appearance.' Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be positive in this patient?
explanation:
Anti-phospholipase A2 antibodies
Idiopathic membranous glomerulonephritis is related to antiphospholipase A2 antibodies. This patient has presented with nephrotic syndrome, as evidenced by hypoalbuminaemia, renal impairment, and nephrotic range proteinuria (> 3.5g/24h). Of the diseases leading to nephrotic syndrome, the most likely culprit is membranous glomerulonephritis (GN). This is supported by a first presentation during adulthood (minimal change disease most commonly first presents during childhood), and the classic pathological findings of a 'spike and dome' appearance of the basement membrane due to subepithelial deposits. The absence of precipitants for membranous GN in the history, such as culprit drugs like NSAIDs, recent infections or a history consistent with malignancy make idiopathic membranous GN the most likely diagnosis. Idiopathic membranous GN is associated with antiphospholipase A2 antibodies.

Anti-liver-kidney microsomal type 2 antibodies
Anti-liver-kidney microsomal type 2 antibodies are associated with drug-induced hepatitis (whereas anti-LKM type 1 antibodies are associated with autoimmune hepatitis).

Anti-p62 antibodies
Anti-p62 antibodies are associated with primary biliary cirrhosis.

Anti-Ri antibodies
Anti-Ri antibodies are associated with opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome, often in the context of breast cancer.

Anti-GQ1b antibodies
Anti-GQ1b antibodies are associated with Miller-Fisher syndrome, a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome characterised by ataxia, ophthalmoplegia and areflexia.

stem: A 69-year-old woman is admitted with a third episode of urinary tract infection over the past 12 months, proven on urine culture to be due to Proteus mirabilis. She also has right loin pain. She has a past history of hypertension and a previous creatinine tested one month earlier was elevated at 145 micromol/l. A plain x-ray to display kidneys ureters and bladder and an ultrasound of the urinary tract reveal a right staghorn calculus. What is the stone likely to be composed of?
explanation:
Magnesium ammonium phosphate
Magnesium ammonium phosphate, (also known as struvite), kidney stones are formed by urea-splitting bacteria, of which Proteus is an example. Magnesium ammonium phosphate stones can form very large calculi known as staghorn calculi which may significantly impact on renal function due to chronic obstruction and failure to clear urinary tract infection adequately. Treatment of the underlying urinary tract infection, coupled with a urology consult to assess the need for removal of any larger stones are the cornerstone of management.

Calcium phosphate
Calcium phosphate renal stones are associated with hyperparathyroidism, and urate stones are associated with gout.

Urate
Urate stones are associated with gout.

Cystine
Cystine stones are seen in patients with inherited cystinuria.

Oxalate
Oxalate stones are primarily associated with short bowel syndrome.

stem: A 63-year-old man is admitted with severe right sided loin pain to the Emergency Department. A urine dipstick shows blood +++, leucocytes +, protein +. An abdominal radiograph is therefore ordered which shows a stag-horn calculus in the right renal pelvis. What are stag-horn calculi normally composed of?
explanation:
Magnesium ammonium phosphate
