methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide. What other treatment
should be initiated?
options: anti-GBM disease in patients with pulmonary haemorrhage those with renal involvement who do not require renal replacement therapy at presentation (the indication in this case) Tacrolimus
explanation:
Anti-GBM (Goodpasture's) disease classically presents with haematuria
and a rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis due to the production of an
antibody that targets the basement membrane in the kidney. This
antibody can also target the basement membrane in the lung leading to
pulmonary haemorrhage. Left untreated there will be a rapid decline in
renal function leading to end-stage renal failure. Treatment has three
main principles:
Remove any identifiable cause of antibody production. Exposure to
organic solvents, hydrocarbons, metal dust and smoking are known
to increase the risk of developing the disease.
Stop further antibody production using immunosuppressive
medication (cyclophosphamide and methylprednisolone).
Removal of the anti-GBM antibodies rapidly by plasmapheresis to
prevent further damage. This is, therefore, the correct answer to this
question.
Plasmapheresis is the removal of the patient's plasma from the blood
and replacement with another fluid. It is designed to remove large
molecular weight molecules from the blood and therefore will remove
the circulating anti-GBM antibodies. Plasmapheresis is indicated in the
following:
selected patients who may require dialysis but present acutely, are
young and have a proportion of viable glomeruli on renal biopsy.
Other conditions where plasma exchange is indicated include Guillain-
Barre syndrome, hyperviscosity in monoclonal gammopathies and
thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
Tacrolimus is used in solid organ transplantation to prevent rejection but
is not used to treat acute autoimmune conditions. This patient's
haemoglobin is acceptable and she, therefore, does not require a blood
transfusion. There is no evidence of infection and antibiotics are not
routinely given in anti-GBM disease. A three-way catheter and irrigation
is used in haematuria with clot retention and is, therefore, incorrect in
this case.
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM)
disease (Goodpasture's syndrome)
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease (previously known
as Goodpasture's syndrome) is a rare type of small-vessel vasculitis
associated with both pulmonary haemorrhage and rapidly progressive
glomerulonephritis. It is caused by anti-glomerular basement membrane
(anti-GBM) antibodies against type IV collagen. Goodpasture's syndrome
is more common in men (sex ratio 2:1) and has a bimodal age
distribution (peaks in 20-30 and 60-70 age bracket). It is associated with
HLA DR2.

explanation:
The correct answer is paracetamol. This is the only option associated
with a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis. This specific entity caused
by paracetamol is known as pyroglutamic acidosis. This results from
reduced levels of glutathione, resulting in the accumulation of 5-
oxoproline. It is more common in women and has also been associated
with chronic renal insufficiency, malnourishment and co-administration
of some medications such as flucloxacillin.
Acetazolamide is incorrect. This is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
sometimes used in the treatment of benign intracranial hypertension and
has been associated with metabolic acidosis. However, this is generally
a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.
Diarrhoea is incorrect. Gastrointestinal losses, such as diarrhoea, are
associated with normal anion gap acidosis. This results from the loss of
bicarbonate.
Renal tubular acidosis is incorrect. This refers to a spectrum of
disorders where the kidneys do not effectively remove acid from the
blood. Type 4 RTA is the most common and is associated with
hyperkalaemia. This patient's potassium is normal, making this less
likely. RTA is also a cause of normal anion gap acidosis, rather than the
raised anion gap this patient has developed.
Sepsis is incorrect. Sepsis is a common cause of metabolic acidosis,
usually resulting from tissue hypoperfusion and lactic acidosis. Although
this would cause a raised anion gap, this patient's inflammatory markers
and lactate are normal, excluding this as a diagnosis.
Chronic paracetamol use can lead to raised anion gap metabolic
acidosis caused by 5-oxoproline

A 32-year-old gentleman presented to your acute medical unit with right
flank pain. The pain started 2 weeks ago and has been constant. He has
tried paracetamol tablets but this has not relieved the pain. He denies
any dysuria and is otherwise fit and well. He is a smoker and tells you
that his sister recently died from a subarachnoid haemorrhage, which
was caused by a berry aneurysm.
He is tachycardic at 110 bpm but other observations are normal. Urine
dipstick has 2+ blood, nil else. His blood tests reveal a Sodium 141
mmol/l, Potassium 4.6 mmol/l, Urea 3.6 mmol/l, Creatinine 84mol/l, CRP
34mg/l. His FBC is normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Adult polycystic kidney disease is an autosomal dominant condition.
Patients typically present with flank pain, gross haematuria and/or
palpable kidneys. The flank pain is thought to be caused by stretching of
the wall of the cysts in the kidneys or pressure on other organs nearby.
The condition is also associated with berry aneurysms which may
rupture to cause a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Some patients may also
have liver and pancreatic cysts.
Given he was a young male with a 2-week history of constant pain and a
family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage, the most likely answer here
would be polycystic kidney disease.
Renal stone would typically present with a shorter history of pain and
would be colicky in nature. Patients with pyelonephritis tend to be more
unwell and have raised inflammatory markers. Wilms' tumour affects
children. Renal cell carcinoma would be more likely if he had weight loss
and was older.

A 42-year-old woman of Afro-Carribean ethnicity is admitted to hospital
after a two-week history of non-specific fatigue and worsening lower
limb swelling. She was diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus 6
years ago and over the 6 months, her creatinine has been slowly rising
from 120 µmol/l to 260 µmol/l.
On examination, her blood pressure is 180/118 mmHg, she has
significant swelling of ankles and feet, with periorbital oedema. A urine
dip demonstrated 4+ protein and a 24 hour urine collection collected
4.6g protein. She undergoes a renal biopsy under the renal physicians,
demonstrating membranous lupus nephritis. In addition to angiotensin-
converting enzyme inhibitors, statins and anti-hypertensives, what is the
most appropriate immediate treatment?
explanation:
Abnormal renal function is extremely common in patients with SLE with
up to 75% of all patients displaying either haematuria or proteinuria on a
routine urine dip. A classification for lupus nephritis was produced in
2004, with 6 classes of possible overlapping histological findings on
renal biopsy . In the case of this patient, renal biopsy has demonstrated
membranous lupus nephritis, when glomerular walls are thickened and
significant subepithelial immune deposits are seen, classified as class V
lupus nephritis.
The treatment of lupus nephriits is guided by the class of renal histology.
While more focal and mild lesions can be treated less aggressively with
oral steroids alone. However, nephrotic syndrome and advanced diffuse
severe lupus nephritis, as in the case of this patient, warrants early and
aggressive immunosuppresion, involving both intravenous
methylprednisolone and intravenous cyclophosphamide as endorsed by
the KDIGO (Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes) guidelines .
There is no role for plasmaphoresis in lupus nephritis . Treatment must
be started promptly with appropriate induction followed by maintenance
therapy to ensure best long-term prognosis. Monitoring alone is not
appropriate.

glomerulonephritis in systemic lupus erythematosus revisited. Kidney
Int. 2004;65(2):521

Guideline.pdf
3. Lewis EJ, Hunsicker LG, Lan SP et al. A controlled trial of
plasmapheresis therapy in severe lupus nephritis. The Lupus Nephritis
Collaborative Study Group. N Engl J Med. 1992;326(21):1373

attacks, hypertension, and obesity. She takes hydroxychloroquine,
clopidogrel and ramipril regularly.
The renal team is planning to perform a renal biopsy to look for evidence
of lupus nephritis and has requested an ultrasound prior to the
procedure.
Renal
ultrasound
The right renal pelvis appears dilated raising concerns for hydronephrosis.
There is no visible obstruction or underlying collection. Both kidneys appear
atrophic.
What is an absolute contraindication to the procedure?
explanation:
Before a renal biopsy is performed, patients should have a renal
tract ultrasound. The presence of polycystic kidneys, obstruction of
the urinary tract, or hydronephrosis are regarded as absolute
contraindications to biopsy
Of the five options above, only hydronephrosis is an absolute
contraindication to renal biopsy. Other absolute contraindications
include polycystic kidneys, urinary tract obstruction, uncontrolled
hypertension, significant renal malignancy, and significant bleeding
disorders.
Antiplatelet therapy is a relative contraindication to biopsy. Ideally,
antiplatelets should be discontinued prior to biopsy (dependent on the
antiplatelet used, e.g. 24 hours for aspirin, 5 days for clopidogrel),
however, biopsies can still take place despite antiplatelet therapy is the
benefits outweigh the risks of bleeding.
Hypertension is neither a relative contraindication nor an absolute
contraindication. It is uncontrolled hypertension that is an absolute
contraindication due to the increased risk of severe bleeding.
Obesity is a relative contraindication due to the difficulty in performing
the biopsy.
Renal atrophy is also a relative contraindication to renal biopsy. A biopsy
can go ahead if the benefits outweigh the risk of impaired renal function.

explanation:
Tolvaptan is a vasopressin receptor 2 antagonist that has been shown to
slow progression of autosomal polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). It
has been recommended for use by NICE in England and Wales since
2015 for patients with ADPKD and CKD stage 2 or 3 and evidence of
rapidly progressing disease, as in this case. The main side effects are
polyuria and polydipsia. Patients need regular monitoring of renal
Tolvaptan has been shown to reduce the rate of CKD progression in
ADPKD (and is approved by NICE)
function and liver function tests during treatment.
There is no evidence that dual therapy with ACE inhibitors plus
angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) offers any benefit over
monotherapy, especially as this patient's blood pressure is already well
controlled.
Statins are not a specific treatment for ADPKD.
Nephrectomy is not indicated in this patient, as he is asymptomatic.
Nephrectomy is sometimes considered for patients with cyst
complications, such as infection, pain or bleeding.
Renal transplantation is not required as he does not have end-stage

explanation:
IgA nephropathy management
This patient's history is highly suggestive of IgA nephropathy -
haematuria classically following 1-2 days of an upper respiratory tract
infection (URTI). Patients may also have a degree of proteinuria,
although this is rarer in IgA nephropathy than in post-streptococcal
glomerulonephritis. The severity dictates management. In this case,
there is some proteinuria, but the renal function is preserved as per the
blood tests, and so ramipril, an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)
inhibitor, should be initiated.
If there were severe renal impairment, significant proteinuria, and
haematuria, and it was not responding to steroids, then
cyclophosphamide may be added. This is an aggressive
immunosuppressant with significant side effects.
No treatment is inappropriate in this scenario. Renal function is
preserved, but there is some proteinuria present. If the proteinuria were
minimal instead, observation would be appropriate.
Phenoxymethylpenicillin would likely be given if the diagnosis were
post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). There is some overlap
between IgA nephropathy and PSGN, but the main symptom in PSGN
tends to be proteinuria rather than haematuria. There is typically a much
longer interval between the URTI and renal symptoms - 1-2 weeks as
opposed to days.
Prednisolone, an oral steroid, would be appropriate if the renal function
was dropping, or the patient was not responding to an ACE inhibitor. In
this scenario, an ACE inhibitor should be tried first as renal function is
preserved.

Lactic acidosis occurs due to tissue hypoxia. Tissue hypoxia occurs
due to one of four main mechanisms: 1. Hypoxaemia (e.g.
respiratory pathology), 2. Toxic (e.g. carboxyhemoglobinemia, or
cyanide poisoning), 3. Perfusional (e.g. shock), or 4. Severe
anaemia
The patient is acidotic. The anion gap = (Na + K) - (HCO3 + Cl) = 21.9.
Therefore the patient has a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA).
Common causes of HAGMA include ketoacidosis, uraemia, lactic
acidosis and toxins (e.g. salicylates, ethylene glycol and methanol).
The normal glucose level makes diabetic ketoacidosis highly unlikely.
Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, Addison's disease and renal tubular
acidosis are all causes of normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.
Therefore the most likely answer is lactic acidosis. The cause of this
should be sought. Lactic acidosis occurs due to tissue hypoxia. Tissue
hypoxia occurs due to one of four main mechanisms:
1. Hypoxaemia (e.g. respiratory pathology)
2. Toxic (e.g. carboxyhemoglobinemia, or cyanide poisoning)
3. Perfusional (e.g. shock)
4. Severe anaemia
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic acidosis is commonly classified according to the anion gap.
This can be calculated by: (Na  + K ) - (Cl  + HCO ). If a question
supplies the chloride level then this is often a clue that the anion gap
should be calculated. The normal range = 10-18 mmol/L

explanation:
The anaemia, reticulocytosis, and presence of schistocytes on blood film
are highly suggestive of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA).
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) is correct. HUS is characterised by
the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA),
thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. The patient thus fulfils all
these criteria.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is incorrect. The
coagulation profile makes DIC extremely unlikely. DIC classically
presents with prolonged PT, prolonged APTT, extremely high D-dimers,
and a low fibrinogen.
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is incorrect. ITP usually
presents with an isolated thrombocytopenia. The other features in this
case (e.g. renal failure) make this a less likely diagnosis.
Megaloblastic anaemia is incorrect. Although the patient is folic acid
deficient (likely as a consequence of red cell haemolysis and increased
red cell turnover) there are no other features of megaloblastic anaemia
(e.g. hypersegmented neutrophils on blood film). Furthermore, renal
failure would not be expected in this condition.
Normocytic anaemia, thrombocytopaenia and AKI following
diarrhoeal illness - consider HUS
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is incorrect. TTP is
classically defined by the pentad of fever, thrombocytopenia, MAHA,
neurological symptoms (i.e., headaches, altered mental status, seizures,
and visual disturbance), and renal failure. In contrast to HUS, the degree
of renal impairment is usually mild. ADAMTS13 levels are usually < 10%
in TTP. In this case, the ADAMTS13 level > 10%, the presence of oliguric
renal failure, and the lack of fever or neurological disturbance favour the
diagnosis of HUS.
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is generally seen in young children and
produces a triad of:
acute kidney injury
microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA)
thrombocytopenia
Most cases are secondary (termed 'typical HUS'):
classically Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) 0157:H7
'verotoxigenic', 'enterohaemorrhagic'
this is the most common cause in children, accounting for over
90% of cases
pneumococcal infection
HIV
rare: systemic lupus erythematosus, drugs, cancer
Primary HUS ('atypical') is due to complement dysregulation.

breath. Urinalysis revealed nephrotic range proteinuria. A clinical

Which of the following conditions is most commonly associated with
nephrotic syndrome?
explanation:
Nephrotic syndrome consists of heavy proteinuria >3 g/day, low serum
albumin <25 g/L and oedema. It can also lead to hyperlipidaemia,
venous thromboembolism (including renal vein thrombosis) and
increased susceptibility to bacterial infections.
There are many causes of nephrotic syndrome.The commonest causes
can be remembered by the acronym 'MMF' (Minimal change disease,
Membranous nephropathy, and Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis).

previously been controlled with diet alone, this was unsuccessful, and
the following medicines were started two weeks ago: amlodipine,
irbesartan and metformin.
Urinalysis is negative for blood, protein and nitrites.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A rapid deterioration in renal function soon after starting an angiotensin-
2 receptor blocker should raise concerns over possible renal artery
stenosis. While the association is more typically described for
angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, there is significant risk of
deteriorating renal function in patients with renal artery stenosis with the
use of angiotensin-2 receptor blockers as well.
There is also an association between renal artery stenosis and
neurofibromatosis.
Renal vascular disease
Renal vascular disease is most commonly due to atherosclerosis (> 95%
of patients). It is associated with risk factors such as smoking and
hypertension that cause atheroma elsewhere in the body. It may present
as hypertension, chronic renal failure or 'flash' pulmonary oedema.
Another common presentation is a sharp rise in creatinine following the
initiation of ACE inhibitor therapy (e.g. hypertension that may itself be
linked to the underlying renal artery stenosis).
ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II levels, which normally constrict
the efferent arterioles in the glomerulus to maintain glomerular
filtration pressure, especially in states of decreased renal perfusion
- when an ACE inhibitor is introduced, the reduction in angiotensin II
levels leads to dilation of the efferent arterioles
in patients with renal artery stenosis, this change can significantly
reduce the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), causing a sharp rise in
serum creatinine
In younger patients however fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) needs to be
considered. FMD is more common in young women and
characteristically has a 'string of beads' appearance on angiography.

explanation:
This patient presents with ocular disturbances, and renal impairment
consistent with Alport syndrome. If tested, we would expect audiometry
Think of Alport syndrome when renal failure, sensorineural hearing
loss and ocular abnormalities develop in a child
to reveal bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment. There is no specific
treatment for Alport syndrome. However, as with any progressive
glomerular disease, management of blood pressure and proteinuria
should be optimised with ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers,
and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors.
Fabry disease is an X-linked multisystem disorder resulting from a
deficiency of the enzyme α-galactosidase. It typically presents in
adolescence with skin, cardiac, and neurological involvement. Although
renal impairment does occur, it usually develops later (typically between
ages 30 and 50). The ocular manifestations of Fabry disease include
corneal opacities and dystrophy, and sensorineural hearing loss can
occur but at later stages. The lens protrusion and early onset of kidney
impairment are more consistent with Alport syndrome.
Hyperoxaluria is an autosomal recessive condition caused by defective
enzyme pathways that lead to an accumulation of oxalate. Clinically, it
presents in childhood with calcium oxalate calculi and nephrocalcinosis.
There is also significant oxalate deposition in the heart, vasculature, and
joints, leading to morbidity. It doesn't typically cause eye problems, as
seen in this case. The treatment of choice is a combined liver and kidney
transplant.
Nail-patella syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant condition, with
renal involvement occurring in 50% of patients. It is caused by a gene
mutation in the LMX1B gene on chromosome 9, which codes for a
transcription factor essential for maintaining the glomerular basement
membrane. Nails may be absent, dysplastic, discoloured, misshapen, or
have ridges. Patellae may be absent, leading to early-onset
osteoarthritis. Renal features typically present in adolescence, including
microscopic haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, and chronic kidney
disease. However, it does not cause the ocular features presenting in
this case.
Thin basement membrane disease is a common autosomal dominant
condition caused by mutations in the COL4A3 and COL4A4 genes. This
results in partial failure of the glomerular basement membrane, and
some clinicians consider it a milder form of Alport syndrome. It presents
with microscopic haematuria, but renal function is generally normal.
Alport's syndrome
Alport's syndrome is usually inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern*. It
is due to a defect in the gene which codes for type IV collagen resulting
in an abnormal glomerular-basement membrane (GBM). The disease is
more severe in males with females rarely developing renal failure.
A favourite question is an Alport's patient with a failing renal transplant.
This may be caused by the presence of anti-GBM antibodies leading to a
Goodpasture's syndrome like picture.
Alport's syndrome usually presents in childhood. The following features
may be seen:
microscopic haematuria
progressive renal failure
bilateral sensorineural deafness
lenticonus: protrusion of the lens surface into the anterior chamber
retinitis pigmentosa
renal biopsy: splitting of lamina densa seen on electron microscopy
Diagnosis
molecular genetic testing
renal biopsy
electron microscopy: characteristic finding is of the longitudinal
splitting of the lamina densa of the glomerular basement
membrane, resulting in a 'basket-weave' appearance
*in around 85% of cases - 10-15% of cases are inherited in an autosomal
recessive fashion with rare autosomal dominant variants existing

requiring laparotomy and an incisional hernia that has not been repaired.
You discuss renal replacement therapies with him. He is very keen for
the least lifestyle-restricting option if at all possible but understands that
'his health comes first'. A recent ultrasound of his renal tract
demonstrates bilateral atrophic kidneys with extensive bilateral iliac
vessel calcification. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
Annual follow up
Haemodialysis
Peritoneal dialysis
Renal transplant

Question 55 of 186
A 74-year-old male is reviewed in the renal outpatient clinic. Over the
past 4 years, his renal function has slowly deteriorated, with his
creatinine rising to 482 µmol/l and estimated glomerular filtration rate at
7 ml/min. He has noted the amount of urine he passes to be
deteriorating over the past 3 months. His past medical history includes
hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, duodenal ulcer 35 years ago
requiring laparotomy and an incisional hernia that has not been repaired.
You discuss renal replacement therapies with him. He is very keen for
the least lifestyle-restricting option if at all possible but understands that
'his health comes first'. A recent ultrasound of his renal tract
demonstrates bilateral atrophic kidneys with extensive bilateral iliac
vessel calcification. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
explanation:
This question examines the different options of renal replacement
therapy. This patient has deteriorating renal function and requires renal
replacement therapy. The decision is which one, palliation and annual
follow-up are definitely inappropriate. It would be inappropriate to rule
out the patient for renal transplant on age alone: it is a common
misconception that there is an age threshold for transplant. A recent
review of transplanted patients revealed at least 13% of recipients to be
over 70 years old. A contraindication may be limited life expectancy such
as malignancy or degenerative diseases, which does not appear to be
the case in this patient. However, the patient has a surgical
contraindication to transplant: his significant bilateral renal artery
calcification would prevent successful transplantation.
Although peritoneal dialysis is the renal replacement therapy that would
be in keeping with his wish of 'least lifestyle-restricting' option, his
previous history of laparotomy and unrepaired abdominal hernia are
contraindications. Haemodialysis, via AV fistula or tunnelled catheter
line, would be the most appropriate option.
1. National Kidney Foundation KDOQI Guidelines 2000
Renal replacement therapy
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a relatively common condition, affecting
1 in 8 people in the UK. Around 10% of those with CKD will go on to
develop renal failure, which is defined as a glomerular filtration rate of
less than 15ml/min. For patients with renal failure, the management
options are renal replacement therapy (RRT), to take over the physiology
of the kidneys, or conservative management, which will be palliative.
There are several types of renal replacement therapy available to
patients:
haemodialysis
peritoneal dialysis
renal transplant
The decision about which RRT option to pick should be made jointly by
the patient and their healthcare team, taking into account the following:
predicted quality of life
predicted life expectancy
patient preference
co-existing medical conditions
Haemodialysis is the most common form of renal replacement therapy.

The clinical picture of polyuria, polydipsia, and nocturia, and the
biochemical profile is consistent with diabetes insipidus. Diabetes
insipidus is diagnosed with a water-deprivation test. A lack of response
(failure to concentrate the urine) to desmopressin would suggest
nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Up to 20% of patients taking lithium
develop impairment of urinary concentration due to dysregulation of the
aquaporin system in the collecting duct. This is usually, but not always,
reversed on stopping the lithium.
In cranial diabetes insipidus, the urine osmolality increases with the use
of desmopressin. The random blood glucose is not in the diabetes
range. For primary polydipsia and pre-renal acute kidney injury, urine
osmolality will be >600mosm/kg after water deprivation test.
Diabetes insipidus
Diabetes insipidus (DI) is a condition characterised by a deficiency in the
action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also known as arginine
vasopressin (AVP). ADH is synthesised by the magnocellular neurons in
the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and
stored in the posterior pituitary.
A deficiency in ADH secretion is known as cranial (central) DI, often
referred to as arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D), whereas
insensitivity of the kidney to ADH is known as nephrogenic DI (arginine
vasopressin resistance, AVP-R).
Causes of cranial DI
idiopathic
Lithium is a recognised cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

a 4-month history of palpitations. Upon further questioning, he also
notes an unintentional 7 kg weight loss and some heat intolerance over
the same time frame.
Clinical examination reveals mild thyromegaly, fine tremor, brisk reflexes,
and bilateral lid lag. He does not have any exophthalmos and the rest of
the examination is unremarkable. He denies any family history of thyroid
disease. He has thyroid function tests which reveal a low Thyroid-
stimulating Hormone (TSH), elevated Free thyroxine (FT4) and Free
Triiodothyronine (FT3), and negative anti-TPO antibodies. Thyroid uptake
scan demonstrates diffusely increased uptake.
At a follow-up visit to discuss the above results he reports that he may
have discovered a mass on his testicle. Your exam confirms this finding.
At this point, in addition to basic labs and imaging to further evaluate
this testicular mass, what laboratory test would be necessary to further
evaluate the aetiology behind his hyperthyroidism?
TSH

Thyroid Stimulating Antibodies

and bilateral lid lag. He does not have any exophthalmos and the rest of

disease. He has thyroid function tests which reveal a low Thyroid-
stimulating Hormone (TSH), elevated Free thyroxine (FT4) and Free
Triiodothyronine (FT3), and negative anti-TPO antibodies. Thyroid uptake
scan demonstrates diffusely increased uptake.
At a follow-up visit to discuss the above results he reports that he may
have discovered a mass on his testicle. Your exam confirms this finding.
At this point, in addition to basic labs and imaging to further evaluate
this testicular mass, what laboratory test would be necessary to further
evaluate the aetiology behind his hyperthyroidism?
explanation:
With hyperthyroidism and a testicular mass, this patient may have a
germ cell tumour causing his hyperthyroidism. These tumours have the
potential to secrete hCG, LDH, and/or AFP. hCG is homologous to TSH in
structure and therefore can lead to hyperthyroidism. This patient has
negative TPO antibodies so it is unlikely that he has autoimmune thyroid
disease such as Graves Disease, which would have positive thyroid-
stimulating Antibodies (TSA). Thyroglobulin level would be unhelpful in
this setting and is frequently used in patients with thyroid cancer to
assess for any residual thyroid tissue after thyroidectomy and ablation.
And while this patient should certainly have LDH and AFP levels checked
they are unlikely to offer further information regarding his thyroid
disease.
Testicular cancer
Testicular cancer is the most common malignancy in men aged 20-30
years. Around 95% of cases of testicular cancer are germ-cell tumours.
Germ cell tumours may essentially be divided into:
seminomas
non-seminomas: including embryonal, yolk sac, teratoma and
choriocarcinoma
Non-germ cell tumours include Leydig cell tumours and sarcomas.
The peak incidence for teratomas is 25 years and seminomas is 35
years. Risk factors include:
infertility (increases risk by a factor of 3)
cryptorchidism
family history
Klinefelter's syndrome
mumps orchitis
Features
a painless lump is the most common presenting symptom
pain may also be present in a minority of men
hydrocele
gynaecomastia

A 56-year-old man with long-standing hypertension medicated with
enalapril and diuretics presents with right flank pain. Temperature is
37.2°C, blood pressure is 145/95 mmHg.
On examination: Tenderness in right costovertebral angle and bilaterally
enlarged kidneys. Urine dip-stick noted micro-haematuria.
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
explanation:
The findings of hypertension with bilaterally enlarged kidneys is
suggestive of autosomal dominant (adult) polycystic kidney disease,
where hypertension is frequently the initial presenting sign. A positive
family history may be noted. Ultrasound of the kidneys is the initial
diagnostic procedure of choice as it is very sensitive for detecting cystic
formation within the kidneys.

The most appropriate next step in management is to restart
antiretroviral therapy. This patient presents with classic features of HIV-
associated nephropathy (HIVAN): nephrotic syndrome (evidenced by
significant proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, and
oedema), normal blood pressure, and normal-sized kidneys with
increased echogenicity on ultrasound. The patient has stopped his
antiretroviral therapy 8 months ago, which has likely led to the
development of HIVAN, as indicated by his high viral load and low CD4
count. Antiretroviral therapy is the cornerstone of treatment for HIVAN
and has been shown to improve renal function, reduce proteinuria, and
prevent progression to end-stage renal disease. By suppressing viral
replication, antiretroviral therapy can directly address the underlying
cause of the nephropathy. Early reinitiation of antiretroviral therapy is
crucial to preserve remaining renal function and improve outcomes in
this patient.
Starting prednisolone is not the first-line treatment for HIVAN. While
some studies have suggested that corticosteroids may reduce
proteinuria in HIVAN, the evidence is limited, and any potential benefit is
significantly less than that of antiretroviral therapy. Additionally,
corticosteroids can further compromise the patient's already suppressed
immune system, increasing the risk of opportunistic infections.
Corticosteroids might be considered as an adjunctive therapy in specific
cases, but only after antiretroviral therapy has been initiated.
Starting furosemide would only provide symptomatic relief for the
oedema but would not address the underlying cause of the nephropathy.
While loop diuretics may be used as supportive therapy to manage fluid
overload in nephrotic syndrome, they do not modify the disease process
in HIVAN. Furthermore, diuretic therapy alone could worsen the patient's
renal function by causing intravascular volume depletion and pre-renal
acute kidney injury.
Antiretroviral therapy is the treatment of choice for HIV-associated
nephropathy
Starting ramipril, an ACE inhibitor, might be considered as an adjunctive
therapy for proteinuria reduction in chronic kidney disease. However, in
HIVAN, antiretroviral therapy should be initiated first. ACE inhibitors may
be added later as part of a comprehensive management plan to reduce
proteinuria and slow progression of renal disease, but they are not the
primary treatment for HIVAN.
Performing a renal biopsy is not immediately necessary in this case.
The clinical presentation, laboratory findings, and imaging results
strongly suggest HIVAN in this non-adherent HIV-positive patient. While
a renal biopsy would provide definitive diagnosis by demonstrating focal
segmental glomerulosclerosis with collapsing features characteristic of
HIVAN, it would delay the initiation of antiretroviral therapy, which is the
most urgent intervention. A biopsy might be considered if the patient
fails to respond to antiretroviral therapy or if there is suspicion of an
alternative diagnosis.

Renal vascular disease
Renal vascular disease is most commonly due to atherosclerosis (> 95%
of patients). It is associated with risk factors such as smoking and
hypertension that cause atheroma elsewhere in the body. It may present
as hypertension, chronic renal failure or 'flash' pulmonary oedema.
Another common presentation is a sharp rise in creatinine following the
initiation of ACE inhibitor therapy (e.g. hypertension that may itself be
linked to the underlying renal artery stenosis).
ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II levels, which normally constrict

This gentleman has chronic kidney disease. In this situation, with a
ferritin of <200, then ensuring he is iron replete is the first step, prior to
consideration fo EPO-stimulating agents. A blood transfusion would be
avoided if possible in order to avoid antigen-sensitisation should he

investigation for other causes of blood loss - such as gastrointestinal -

testing is used only in the context of the screening programme and is
not useful in the investigation of iron deficiency anaemia.

explanation:
E. coli 0157 is an infectious gastroenteritis that can prove fatal
particularly in the young and the elderly. Complications include
haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) and TTP. It may cause a spectrum
of presentations from asymptomatic infection to haemorrhagic colitis
and HUS. Thrombocytopenia and fragmented erythrocytes suggest the
onset of HUS.
Although no clues are given in the question as to the source of this
patient's infection, it is often the case that there has been contact with
farm animals. Other routes of infection include person-to-person contact
and from contaminated water e.g. contaminated
lakes/streams/swimming pools/non-chlorinated water supply.
Management is supportive and cases need to be reported to a
consultant in communicable disease control (CCDC).
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is generally seen in young children and
produces a triad of:
acute kidney injury
microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA)
thrombocytopenia
Most cases are secondary (termed 'typical HUS'):
classically Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) 0157:H7
'verotoxigenic', 'enterohaemorrhagic'
this is the most common cause in children, accounting for over
90% of cases
pneumococcal infection
HIV
rare: systemic lupus erythematosus, drugs, cancer
Primary HUS ('atypical') is due to complement dysregulation.

The diagnosis is membranous glomerulonephritis which could be

The main difference in the management of membranous
glomerulonephritis and the other glomerulopathies is that high dose
steroids and azathioprine are not associated with any significant
benefits in the former. The main treatment strategy involves control of
blood pressure with ACE inhibitors and immunosuppression with either
cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, ciclosporin or mycophenolate mofetil
along with prednisolone. Rituximab has also been shown to have a
benefit in the short term.
Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephritis is the commonest type of
glomerulonephritis in adults and is the third most common cause of end-
stage renal failure (ESRF). It usually presents with nephrotic syndrome or
proteinuria.

risk of contrast nephropathy, there is no role for mannitol, which
produces a greater incidence of adverse events .

However, given its cheap cost and ready availability, it is recommended
in the 2012 KDIGO guidelines for prevention of contrast nephropathy in
high-risk patients. It is not, however, routinely used as a treatment after
contrast nephropathy. The next most appropriate step in this patient is
monitoring of renal dysfunction, which should spontaneously reverse in

foci of high grade activity involving the spine, ribs, sternum, pelvic and
femoral bones. The findings are in keeping with multiple osteoblastic

Question 74 of 186
A 67-year-old man with chronic kidney disease secondary to diabetes
mellitus is seen in the clinic. He reports no new symptoms and has good
glycaemic control.
His current medications are metformin 1g BD, aspirin 75mg OD,
bisoprolol 1.25mg OD On examination, there is mild peripheral oedema
and his blood pressure is 135/80mmHg; this has been confirmed by
ambulatory blood pressure monitoring.
What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
The most appropriate next step in this scenario is to add in ramipril
1.25mg OD PO. This is the correct answer because the patient has
chronic kidney disease (CKD) secondary to diabetes mellitus and
hypertension. In such patients, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors
(ACEIs) like ramipril are recommended as first-line treatment for blood
pressure control and renal protection, according to UK guidelines. ACEIs
have been shown to slow down the progression of CKD in diabetic
patients by reducing proteinuria, lowering blood pressure, and providing
direct renal vasodilatory effects.
Monitor blood pressure alone would not be sufficient in this case, as the
patient's blood pressure is above the target range for someone with CKD
and diabetes (ideally below 130/80 mmHg). Additionally, monitoring
without intervention may lead to further deterioration of his renal
function.
Adding atorvastatin 40mg ON PO might be beneficial for this patient's
cardiovascular risk profile due to his age, diabetes, and CKD; however, it
would not directly address his elevated blood pressure or provide renal
protection. Statins are mainly used for lipid-lowering purposes and
primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular events.
Add furosemide is not the best choice in this situation. Furosemide is a
loop diuretic that can help reduce peripheral oedema but does not offer
significant renal protection compared to ACEIs or angiotensin II receptor
blockers (ARBs). Furthermore, furosemide may cause electrolyte
imbalances which could exacerbate CKD if not monitored closely.
Lastly, increase bisoprolol to 2.5mg OD would help lower the patient's
blood pressure but would not provide optimal renal protection compared
to adding an ACEI like ramipril. Bisoprolol is a beta-blocker, which can be
used in combination with ACEIs or ARBs for blood pressure control, but
it does not have the same renoprotective effects.

Abdominal examination reveals a significant swelling in his left scrotum,

swelling is noted to the top of both thighs. A urine dip reveals pH 6.5 4+
blood 1+ protein 1+ leucocyte 1+ nitrite. An initial chest radiograph
reveals multiple round opacities in both lung fields. Blood tests are
awaited.
Which investigation is most likely to reveal the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
There are a number of worrying features with this patient: flank pain and
haematuria, associated with round opacities in the lungs, a left
varicocoele and bilateral limb swelling point towards a malignancy and
unlikely to be explained by tuberculosis alone. Renal cell carcinoma
(RCC) should be strongly suspected.
Be aware that while the classic triad of haematuria, abdominal mass and
flank pain is frequently described in textbooks, this combination of
features only present in 9% of RCC patients.
A left-sided varicocele should raise suspicion of compression on the left
testicular vein. Bilateral lower limb oedema in the absence of overt right
heart failure should alert you to obstruction of the inferior vena cava, a
classic site of malignant tracking from renal cell carcinoma towards
metastases in the lungs.
While miliary tuberculosis producing bilateral lung features with cystitis
and sterile TB pyuria is possible, IVC obstruction features and bilateral
rounded lung opacities would be atypical.
Renal cell cancer
Renal cell cancer is also known as hypernephroma and accounts for 85%
of primary renal neoplasms. It arises from proximal renal tubular
epithelium. The most common histological subtype is clear cell (75 to 85
percent of tumours).

explanation:
This gentleman has acute pain and swelling in his fistula arm in the
absence of infective symptoms. The fistula is still working but dialysis is
painful. This points to a diagnosis of a stenosis.
Cellulitis is unlikely with normal inflammatory markers. A diagnosis of
superior vena cava obstruction is more likely in someone with a
tunnelled dialysis line and is typically associated with bilateral arm and
face swelling, shortness of breath and widened mediastinum on x-ray.
Lymphoedema of the arm is more common following surgery to axillary
lymph nodes and is unlikely to present this late. A thrombosis
associated with the fistula is possible although there is no history.
However, the fistula itself is not totally thrombosed given the thrill and
bruit.

Renal replacement therapy
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a relatively common condition, affecting
1 in 8 people in the UK. Around 10% of those with CKD will go on to
develop renal failure, which is defined as a glomerular filtration rate of
less than 15ml/min. For patients with renal failure, the management
options are renal replacement therapy (RRT), to take over the physiology
of the kidneys, or conservative management, which will be palliative.

explanation:
Goodpasture syndrome, also known as Anti-GBM disease, involves
rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage
caused by autoantibodies against the basement membrane in the
kidneys and lungs. Dyspnoea, cough, haemoptysis, and bibasal
consolidations on CT suggest alveolar haemorrhage. Laboratory findings
of acute kidney injury (creatinine 378 µmol/L, urea 14 mmol/L),
haematuria with dysmorphic RBCs, proteinuria, hyperkalaemia (K+ 6.1
mmol/L), and anaemia (Hb 100 g/L) indicate renal dysfunction.
Diagnosis is confirmed by testing for anti-GBM antibodies and, if needed,
renal biopsy.
Cryoglobulinaemia-associated glomerulonephritis typically presents
with systemic manifestations, including purpura, arthralgia, and
weakness (Meltzer's triad), which are absent in this case. Additionally, it
is commonly associated with hepatitis C infection.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, previously known as Wegener's
granulomatosis, often presents with upper airway involvement—such as
nasal crusting, sinusitis, or a saddle-nose deformity—none of which is
described in this patient. Although it can cause lung and kidney issues,
the absence of nasal findings or granulomatous features makes this
diagnosis less likely.
Polyarteritis nodosa is a medium-vessel vasculitis that primarily leads to
renal ischemia rather than direct glomerular damage; hence, it typically
does not present with red blood cells in the urine. Additionally, lung
involvement is usually spared in polyarteritis nodosa, which further
reduces the probability of being diagnosed by this patient.
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can cause glomerulonephritis

photosensitivity, none of which are reported. Furthermore, serological
markers like ANA and anti-dsDNA are necessary for diagnosis, and their
absence in this case makes SLE less likely.
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM)
disease (Goodpasture's syndrome)
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease (previously known
as Goodpasture's syndrome) is a rare type of small-vessel vasculitis
associated with both pulmonary haemorrhage and rapidly progressive
glomerulonephritis. It is caused by anti-glomerular basement membrane
(anti-GBM) antibodies against type IV collagen. Goodpasture's syndrome
is more common in men (sex ratio 2:1) and has a bimodal age
distribution (peaks in 20-30 and 60-70 age bracket). It is associated with
HLA DR2.

A difficult question: the patient has presented with fairly non-specific
symptoms and a raft of metabolic abnormalities. The easiest approach
is to consider each of the diagnoses in turn.
The history of bone pain combined with the presence of an underlying
'antibody disorder' could point you toward a diagnosis multiple myeloma.
This is supported by the large discrepancy between the total protein and
albumin, indicating that the patient's globulins are grossly elevated.
However, the blood tests also reveal the presence of normal
haemoglobin, calcium, and renal function. Taken together, these
abnormalities point instead to a diagnosis of monoclonal gammopathy
of uncertain significance (MGUS).
Diabetes mellitus would explain the polyuria, polydipsia, and glycosuria,
however, the normal fasting glucose makes this unlikely.
Pseudohypoaldosteronism is due to aldosterone resistance and leads to
renal salt wasting and hyperkalaemia. This is inconsistent with the
biochemistry in the vignette.
Fanconi syndrome is a generalised disorder of proximal renal tubular
function. Reabsorption of filtered solutes is impaired and as a result,
large quantities of bicarbonate, potassium, phosphate, glucose, uric acid
and amino acids are lost in the urine. It is associated with the
development of type 2 (proximal) renal tubular acidosis, as indicated by
the elevated chloride and low bicarbonate in the patient's blood results.
The remaining metabolic abnormalities can all be explained by the loss
of these solutes in the urine, which in turn explain the presence of
glucose and protein on urine dipstick.
A number of congenital and acquired conditions can lead to the
development of Fanconi syndrome. although onset in later life suggests
an acquired cause. In this case, MGUS is likely to be the predisposing
factor.
The clinical features that cause patients to seek treatment are usually
polydipsia and polyuria secondary to the osmotic effect of the urinary
solute load. Bone pain due to osteomalacia and muscle weakness due
to hypophosphataemia may also occur. Hypokalaemia may cause
palpitations and can occasionally result in sudden death due to cardiac
arrhythmia.
Cystinuria causes recurrent renal calculi that typically present in the first
decades of life. The diagnosis was historically made by the sodium
nitroprusside test, which is included here as a red herring and is positive
due to the generalised aminoaciduria associated with Fanconi
syndrome.
Fanconi syndrome
Fanconi syndrome describes a generalised reabsorptive disorder of renal
tubular transport in the proximal convoluted tubule resulting in:
type 2 (proximal) renal tubular acidosis
polyuria
aminoaciduria
glycosuria
phosphaturia
osteomalacia

This patient has hypernatraemia secondary to nephrogenic diabetes

water reabsorption, thereby diminishing the water delivery to the ADH

excessive free water loss - renal (diabetes insipidus, diuretics,
osmotic diuresis as with hyperglycaemia), GI (diarrhoea, vomiting),
skin (sweating, burns)
reduced thirst - seen in very old and very young patients.
Treatment is aimed at the underlying cause. An acute hypernatraemia
can be corrected quickly but if chronic (>24hours) then it should be
corrected at <0.5mmol/L/hr. Fluid resuscitation should involve oral

A urine dipstick test showed micro-haematuria with mild proteinuria. The
patients urea and electrolytes were within normal range. Serum IgA was

explanation:
The patient's presentation is consistent with Berger disease (or IgA
nephropathy). Micro-haematuria or mild proteinuria can occur
incidentally or following recurrent upper respiratory/intestinal infections
after 1-2 days. This is distinct from post-infectious glomerulonephritis,
which commonly occurs 1-2 weeks after infection by group A
Streptococcus (pharyngitis or impetigo) and manifests with nephritic
syndrome. Haematuria found in the setting of IgA nephropathy however,
is concomitant with an upper respiratory tract infection (known as
synpharyngitic haematuria).

non-self human leukocyte antigens (HLA), the blood recipient is at risk of
sensitisation to HLA through the development of anti-HLA antibodies.

transfusions should be avoided if at all possible in this cohort. If the
patient has worsening anaemia despite adequate ion replacement and
an ESA, then of course a transfusion may be deemed necessary.

options: Oral pre-hydration is superior to intravenous pre-hydration
Intravenous fluids should be administered with a diuretic
Intravenous N-acetylcysteine is superior to oral N-acetylcysteine
Prophylactic haemofiltration should be undertaken post-scan
Intravenous pre- and post-hydration should only be undertaken with isotonic fluid
explanation:
The only evidence showing benefit in intravenous pre- and post-hydration
is for isotonic fluids.
There is evidence that oral fluids may be as efficacious as intravenous
fluids in certain populations (e.g. CKD Stage 1 and 2), however in higher-
risk groups this has not been proven and hence intravenous fluids are
the the preferred option.
There is no evidence that co-administration of a diuretic improves
outcomes, and evidence that some diuretics (e.g. furosemide, mannitol)
may cause harm.
There is no evidence to show that intravenous is superior to oral N-
acetylcysteine (NAC). Since intravenous NAC is associated with
increased frequency of drug reactions, the oral route is preferred if
possible.
The evidence suggests no benefit for prophylactic haemodialysis or
haemofiltration pre- or post-procedure in CKD Stage 3 and Stage 4.
In addition to these measures, it is of course advisable to stop
nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs) and metformin.
Nephrotoxicity due to contrast media
Contrast media nephrotoxicity may be defined as a 25% increase in
creatinine occurring within 3 days of the intravascular administration of
contrast media. Contrast-induced nephropathy occurs 2 -5 days after
administration.
Risk factors include
known renal impairment (especially diabetic nephropathy)
age > 70 years
dehydration
cardiac failure
the use of nephrotoxic drugs such as NSAIDs

diffuse renal damage and is linked to HIV, sickle cell anaemia and
intravenous heroin abuse, not marijuana.

Minimal change disease nearly always presents as nephrotic syndrome,

Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (DI) is a relatively common side effect of

dehydration only presents if patients have struggled to keep up with the
oral intake as is the case here.
Unlike cranial DI, nephrogenic DI is not usually responsive to low doses
of desmopressin (DDAVP) although mild to moderate cases have been
successfully treated with high doses.
The patient is clearly very dehydrated, therefore fluid restriction is likely
to worsen her condition. Equally, in view of her hypernatraemia, the use
of hypertonic saline will likely worsen this.

a low urine osmolality
Observation is likely to result in further deterioration. Ideally, the case
should be discussed with the psychiatrists and the lithium discontinued
and she should be encouraged to drink plenty of fluids.
As she is markedly dehydrated and affected by her DI, treatment with
thiazide diuretics (which produce a paradoxical concentration of the
urine) and amiloride has been shown to be effective. This is, therefore,

the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and
stored in the posterior pituitary.

on histology, of which there are many causes.
Although he gives a history of throat infection, his ASOT titre is normal,
which points away from a post-infectious GN.
Penicillin typically causes an acute interstitial nephritis without nephrotic
syndrome.
Phospholipase A2 is highly specific for idiopathic membranous

Although systemic lupus and anti-phospholipid syndrome are both
known to cause membranous GN, this gentleman does not display
typical symptoms associated with either condition. His arthralgia and

systemic lupus to be associated with low complement levels and anti-

Reference: Fervenza FC, Sethi S, Specks U. Idiopathic Membranous
Nephropathy: Diagnosis and Treatment. CJASN 2008:3(3);905-919.
Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephritis is the commonest type of
glomerulonephritis in adults and is the third most common cause of end-
stage renal failure (ESRF). It usually presents with nephrotic syndrome or
proteinuria.
Renal biopsy demonstrates:
electron microscopy: the basement membrane is thickened with
subepithelial electron dense deposits. This creates a 'spike and
dome' appearance
Causes
idiopathic: due to anti-phospholipase A2 antibodies
infections: hepatitis B, malaria, syphilis
malignancy (in 5-20%): prostate, lung, lymphoma, leukaemia
drugs: gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs
autoimmune diseases: systemic lupus erythematosus (class V
disease), thyroiditis, rheumatoid
Management
all patients should receive an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin II
receptor blocker (ARB):
these have been shown to reduce proteinuria and improve
prognosis
immunosuppression
as many patients spontaneously improve only patient with
severe or progressive disease require immunosuppression
corticosteroids alone have not been shown to be effective. A
combination of corticosteroid + another agent such as
cyclophosphamide is often used
consider anticoagulation for high-risk patients

explanation:
Struvite is the correct answer. The patient presents with symptoms
suggestive of renal colic and a urine dipstick demonstrating blood. She
also has evidence of alkaline urine with a pH of 8.4. In the setting of
chronic urinary tract infections, this suggests her stone is likely to be
struvite in origin. Struvite stones are formed in the presence of increased
urinary ammonia and alkaline urine (>7.2). These occur as a result of
urease producing bacteria (and are thus associated with chronic
infections).
Calcium oxalate is incorrect. This is the most common cause of a renal
stone and would be the likely answer if it were not for the presence of
alkaline urine and chronic infections. Hypercalciuria is a risk factor.
Calcium phosphate is incorrect. These are typically associated with
renal tubular acidosis, which is absent in this case.
Cystine is incorrect. This type of stone is caused by an inherited disorder
and therefore we would not expect the first episode at 53.
Uric acid is incorrect. These stones typically precipitate when urinary pH
is low rather than high. They are associated with gout, malignancy and
inborn errors of metabolism, which are absent here.
Struvite stones are formed in the presence of increased urinary
ammonia and alkaline urine (>7.2).

Renal impairment, flank masses, hypertension → ?ADPKD
This patient presents with a history consistent with autosomal dominant
polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). The combination of renal
impairment, flank masses (bilateral ballotable kidneys), haematuria, and
hypertension should prompt consideration of this diagnosis. Although
there is no reported family history, up to 25% of patients with ADPKD
have no family history. Given the patient's advanced kidney disease at a
young age, a mutation in the PKD-1 gene, located on chromosome 16, is
most likely. PKD1 mutations account for about 85% of ADPKD cases and
are associated with earlier onset and more rapid progression of kidney
disease compared to PKD2 mutations.
Mutations in the CTNS gene on chromosome 17 are responsible for
cystinosis, inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. This condition
impairs the export of cystine from lysosomes, causing cystine
accumulation in target organs. Patients typically present with growth
failure, Fanconi's syndrome, and progressive renal impairment during
childhood.
Mutations in the PKD-2 gene on chromosome 4 also cause ADPKD. PKD-
2 mutations are less common than PKD-1 mutations and result in a
milder form of the disease, with end-stage renal failure occurring
approximately 15 years later than in PKD-1 mutations. Given the patient's
advanced kidney disease at a young age, a PKD-1 mutation is more
likely.
Tuberous sclerosis is a multisystem disorder characterised by
hamartomatous lesions. Mutations in the TSC1 gene on chromosome 9
and the TSC2 gene on chromosome 16 are pathogenic. The condition
typically presents with neurological manifestations, such as
developmental delay and seizures, as well as skin disease. Renal
manifestations include angiomyolipomas, cystic disease, and renal cell
carcinoma.
Several renal disorders are caused by mutations on the X chromosome,
leading to diseases predominantly affecting men. Examples include
Alport syndrome, characterised by a triad of progressive nephropathy,
sensorineural hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities, and Fabry's
disease, which involves skin, cardiac, neurological, ocular, pulmonary,
and renal symptoms.

impairing fibrinolysis.

for acute coronary syndrome. The nature of the pain is not suggestive of
aortic dissection. Musculoskeletal pain is a possibility but in the
presence of the clinical and biochemical findings pulmonary embolism
must be ruled out first.

This patient presents with nephrotic syndrome secondary to focal
segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). He has nephrotic-range
proteinuria (>3.5g/day) with oedema and hypoalbuminaemia. His biopsy
is suggestive of FSGS - typically sclerosis or scarring is seen in only
parts of the glomeruli (segmental) in only some of the glomeruli (focal).

causes including HIV and heroin use. The overall incidence is higher in
African-Americans. The first-line treatment is with steroids. Patients who
are resistant to steroids are treated with immunosuppressive therapy
such as calcineurin inhibitors.
Untreated FSGS has a <10% chance of spontaneous remission so whilst
supportive therapy should accompany active treatment, it is not
appropriate in isolation.

Whilst this patient has recently travelled from a TB-endemic area,

are not in keeping with this as the cause of his deterioration in renal

ultrasound (significant asymmetry, such as a size discrepancy of >1.5cm

equal peak flow velocities on doppler. Therefore revascularisation is not
the correct answer.

haemodialysis (e.g. treatment-resistant acidosis, hyperkalaemia,

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a cause of nephrotic
syndrome and chronic kidney disease. It generally presents in young
adults.

Secondary (AA) amyloidosis can be related to chronic inflammatory

the incidence has decreased significantly with improvements in
treatments for inflammatory arthritides.
Hepatitis C infection and cryoglobulinaemia can cause nephrotic
syndrome but are typically associated with membranoproliferative
glomerulonephritis.

A 61-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit with
community-acquired pneumonia and stage 2 acute kidney injury from
reduced oral intake. She is being treated with intravenous antibiotics and
intravenous fluids. Her past medical history includes mild COPD, type 2
diabetes mellitus and hypertension for which she takes metformin,
ramipril and regular inhalers.
During her admission, she complains of chest discomfort and
palpitations. Her observations are within normal limits. An ECG is taken,
as shown below:
© Image used on license from Dr Smith, University of Minnesota
What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
Calcium chloride is correct. This patient has features of hyperkalaemia
on her ECG including tall T waves seen in leads II, III, aVF and V3-V6.
There are also associated broad QRS complexes which are another
feature of hyperkalaemia. Given the admission presentation of
pneumonia and an acute kidney injury and ramipril ingestion,
hyperkalaemia is quite likely to be present. The management of
hyperkalaemia and ECG changes includes immediate administration of
intravenous calcium chloride or calcium gluconate to stabilise the
cardiac membrane and prevent deterioration into life-threatening
arrhythmias.
Aspirin is incorrect. This patient's ECG shows peaked T waves, indicative
of hyperkalaemia. Aspirin would be indicated if there were signs of
ischaemic heart disease (e.g. ST-segment elevation, depression or T
wave inversion).
Insulin and dextrose solution is incorrect. Although this is the treatment
of choice to lower the serum potassium level, this patient has signs of
ECG changes that are characteristic of hyperkalaemia and, therefore,
stabilisation of the cardiac membrane with calcium chloride or calcium
gluconate is required.
Intravenous sodium chloride is incorrect. Intravenous fluids are not used
in the treatment of hyperkalaemia.
Salbutamol nebuliser is incorrect. Similarly to insulin and dextrose,
although this treatment can be used to lower the serum potassium level,
this patient has signs of ECG changes that are characteristic of
hyperkalaemia and, therefore, stabilisation of the cardiac membrane
with calcium chloride or calcium gluconate is required.

has clinical features relating to the organs involved heart failure,
nephrotic syndrome with proteinuria. Given her background of multiple
myeloma, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, heart failure and proteinuria,
the answer that accounts for all of this is amyloidosis.
Although this lady has heart failure based on her clinical history and
chest x-ray findings, it does not explain all of her symptoms.
Membranous nephropathy is less likely to account for this lady's
symptoms as it tends to be associated with lymphoma or chronic
lymphoid leukaemia rather than multiple myeloma. Minimal change
disease is most common in children and renal function is usually
preserved. This pattern of findings is also unlikely to be associated with
treatment.

which requires aggressive increases in immunosuppression, and post-
transplant lymphoproliferative disorder, which requires a reduction in
immunosuppression with possible chemotherapy. In short, PTLD
frequently demonstrates clonal populations of T or B cells in significant
lymphoid disruption of renal architecture, EBV antigen present in many
cells with significant immunoglobulin light chain expression. This is not
the case in this patient, who demonstrates clinical and histological
evidence of allograft rejection. The initial treatment would involve pulsed
intravenous methylprednisolone before changing doses of maintenance
immunosuppression such as tacrolimus after at least 3 days of steroids.
There is no evidence of a post-renal obstruction and hence
percutaneous nephrostomy is not indicated. There is no acute indication
for starting a second immunosuppressant.

Contrast CT abdomen and chest is the correct answer. An older man
with a new-onset left varicocele and intermittent loin pain raises concern
for a possible renal origin, such as a tumour compressing the left renal
vein. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and chest provides a
detailed evaluation of both renal and thoracic structures, allowing for the
identification of any suspicious mass or other pathology.
Abdominal ultrasound, while non-invasive, would not provide sufficient
detail of the retroperitoneal structures and could miss small renal
masses or other pathology causing venous obstruction. Since the
patient has a confirmed left-sided, new-onset varicocele, it is
recommended to proceed to contrast imaging to detect the underlying
cause (which is likely renal cell carcinoma, given the age of this man).
Contrast MRI abdomen and chest could provide similar information to
CT but is generally less readily available and may take longer to perform.
It would be a reasonable alternative if CT is contraindicated.
Intravenous pyelography is not the correct choice. This technique
involves administering intravenous contrast to delineate the kidneys,
ureters, and urinary bladder. It is useful in assessing renal stones and
congenital anomalies, evaluating renal function, and investigating

not represent a recommended approach for imaging suspected cases of

fatigue, hypertension and evidence of thrombotic microangiopathy

further evidence of haemolysis with low haptoglobin. In the setting of a
recent diarrhoea illness, this is likely to represent haemolytic uraemic
syndrome (HUS) caused by Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli

features but it is the association with a diarrhoeal illness that
characterizes HUS.
Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome is incorrect. This shares many of
the same features as HUS but is not caused by STEC but has a genetic
component. It is caused by chronic uncontrolled activation of the
complement system. It can also mimic thrombotic thrombocytopenic
purpura initially. It should be suspected in those patients without a
recent history of a diarrhoeal illness who have severe renal impairment,
fail to respond to plasma exchange (treatment for TTP) and have normal
or near-normal ADAMST13 activity. The treatment is eculizumab, which
is a complement inhibitor. There may be a family history. The history of
diarrhoea, in this case, makes a diagnosis of HUS much more likely than
atypical HUS.
Lupus nephritis is incorrect. This can cause renal failure and proteinuria
and in rare cases thrombotic microangiopathy. However, an antinuclear
antibody result and an absence of other typical features make this
diagnosis unlikely in this case.
Normocytic anaemia, thrombocytopaenia and AKI following
diarrhoeal illness - consider HUS

microangiopathy and hypertension. However, this is associated with a

pentad of renal failure, fever, neurological signs and symptoms,
schistocytes and anaemia. If suspected, plasma exchange should be
commenced without delay as it may be life-saving. Severely reduced
levels of ADAMST13 are typical of TTP and can distinguish it from
atypical HUS. The normal ADAMST13 levels exclude it here. Additionally,
neurological features are often prominent and they are absent here.

explanation:
Eculizumab is a monoclonal antibody against the C5 component of
complement and thereby blocks the complement cascade. Atypical
haemolytic syndrome is a subtype of thrombotic microangiopathies,
which also includes Shiga toxin-producing E.coli haemolytic-uraemic
syndrome and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, which results from
genetic defects in the complement cascade resulting in uncontrolled
activation. Eculizumab has been shown to be efficacious in the
treatment of atypical haemolytic-uraemic syndrome and is currently
recommended by NICE.
Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody against Ig-E and used in certain
types of asthma.
Daratumumab is a monoclonal antibody targeting CD38 and has use in
the treatment of multiple myeloma.
Rituximab is an anti-CD20 and used in certain autoimmune disorders
such as rheumatoid arthritis and malignancies such as certain types of
lymphoma.
Cyclophosphamide is an immunosuppressant used in the treatment of a
variety of rheumatological processes such as types of vasculitis and in
certain chemotherapy regimens.
Eculizumab (a C5 inhibitor monoclonal antibody) has evidence of
greater efficiency than plasma exchange alone in the treatment of

The most appropriate advice would be to advise weight loss and a trial

Trial of sildenafil is appropriate unless contraindicated for erectile
dysfunction, regardless of underlying aetiology
psychological stress, but could also potentially be due to an endocrine
cause or due to worsening diabetes. Regardless of the cause, advising
weight loss and a trial of sildenafil is recommended. In the presence of

support in the future.
Erectile dysfunction
Erectile dysfunction (ED) is the persistent inability to attain and maintain
an erection sufficient to permit satisfactory sexual performance. It is a
symptom and not a disease and the causes can broadly be split into
organic, psychogenic and mixed.
It is important to try and differentiate between organic and psychogenic
causes of erectile dysfunction.

options: Intrarenal vasoconstriction secondary to ACE inhibitor
explanation:
Muddy brown casts are indicative of acute tubular necrosis (ATN). ATN
occurs due to damage to renal epithelial cells. This may be ischaemic or
toxic in its aetiology. Ischaemic causes are prolonged hypotension such
as during surgery or sepsis. Toxic causes include myoglobin from
rhabdomyolysis/massive haemolysis, IV contrast, hyperuricaemia
(tumour lysis syndrome), poisons (ethylene glycol, mercury) or drugs
(aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, chemotherapy agents etc.). Given the
presence of muddy brown casts and the timeline of events, the likely
diagnosis is acute tubular necrosis and the only cause of this listed is
contrast nephropathy which can occur following the use of IV contrast in
percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).
Intrarenal vasoconstriction secondary to ACE inhibitor is incorrect as,
although ACE inhibitors can cause AKI, the mechanism is not via ATN
and therefore not correct in this instance.
Acute interstitial nephritis is not characterised by muddy brown casts
and there is no causative agent listed in this history and therefore not
correct. Common causes of acute interstitial nephritis include
antibiotics, NSAIDs, aciclovir, omeprazole and infections - though there
are many more.
Cardio-renal syndrome is characterised by decreased kidney function,
diuretic-resistant heart failure with congestion, and worsening kidney
function during treatment for heart failure. As there is no history of heart
failure for this patient this is incorrect.
Acute kidney injury following a percutaneous coronary
intervention→ ?contrast-induced nephropathy
Though prolonged hypotension is a cause of ATN, there is no significant
history of prolonged hypotension in this case and therefore, the most
likely cause of the ATN in this instance is contrast nephropathy following
PCI.
Nephrotoxicity due to contrast media
Contrast media nephrotoxicity may be defined as a 25% increase in
creatinine occurring within 3 days of the intravascular administration of
contrast media. Contrast-induced nephropathy occurs 2 -5 days after
administration.
Risk factors include
known renal impairment (especially diabetic nephropathy)
age > 70 years
dehydration
cardiac failure
the use of nephrotoxic drugs such as NSAIDs
Examples of procedures that may cause contrast-induced nephropathy
includes:
CT with contrast
coronary angiography/percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)
around 5% of patients who've undergone PCI develop a
transient rise in the plasma creatinine concentration of more
than 88 µmol/L
Prevention
the evidence base currently supports the use of intravenous 0.9%
sodium chloride at a rate of 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours pre- and
post- procedure. There is also evidence to support the use of
isotonic sodium bicarbonate

explanation:
Mycophenolate is the preferred follow-on agent in lupus nephritis
once there has been a response to the initial therapy
This case describes a woman with known SLE developing significant
kidney dysfunction, most likely secondary to lupus nephritis. Her renal
biopsy has shown diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis which is class
IV lupus nephritis on the WHO classification.
Lupus nephritis is initially managed with high-dose steroids alongside
either mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide. The preferred treatment for
maintenance is mycophenolate.
Azathioprine is a recognised maintenance treatment, however has a
higher risk of development of end-stage renal disease and is, therefore,
less preferred.
Cyclophosphamide can be used alongside steroids to induce remission,
however is not used for maintenance.
Steroids, as with cyclophosphamide, are only used in the initial treatment
and are not used in long-term management.
Tacrolimus is also a recognised treatment however mycophenolate is
preferred.

A chest x-ray demonstrates bilateral coalescent airspace opacification.
A renal biopsy is undertaken, which demonstrates linear IgG deposits
along the basement membrane.
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide and plasmapheresis is the correct
answer. This elderly smoker presents with haemoptysis, anaemia and
bilateral airspace opacifications (suggestive of pulmonary haemorrhage)
along with a probable acute kidney injury and nephritis
(haematoproteinuria). These findings, together with a characteristic
biopsy, suggest a diagnosis of anti-glomerular basement membrane
disease (anti-GBM). This is an autoimmune disease that targets the
capillary beds of the lungs and kidneys. It is caused by the development
of autoantibodies directed against autoantigens on the basement
membranes of these particular organs. The accepted consensus
treatment for this condition is urgent plasmapheresis to rapidly remove
culprit antibodies and subsequent CYC and prednisolone treatment to
inhibit autoantibody production and resolve inflammation.
Anti-GBM disease is typically managed with a combination of
corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide and plasmapheresis
Corticosteroids is incorrect. This approach has been shown to be
insufficient in anti-GBM disease. Plasma exchange is required to remove
the culprit autoantibodies and further immunosuppression is required
with cyclophosphamide to inhibit further autoantibody production.
Corticosteroids and plasmapheresis is incorrect. Prevention of further
antibody synthesis with CYC is an important component of management
in this condition.
Corticosteroids, rituximab and cyclophosphamide is incorrect. An
accepted component of management of this condition is the urgent
removal of culprit pathogenic autoantibodies by plasma exchange. This
regimen can be used in life-threatening ANCA vasculitis.
Corticosteroids, rituximab and plasmapheresis is incorrect. There is
some suggestion that rituximab may be effective in anti-GBM disease
and it may be an option in relapsing disease. However, it is not first-line
treatment and CYC should be used in preference initially.
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM)
disease (Goodpasture's syndrome)
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease (previously known
as Goodpasture's syndrome) is a rare type of small-vessel vasculitis
associated with both pulmonary haemorrhage and rapidly progressive
glomerulonephritis. It is caused by anti-glomerular basement membrane
(anti-GBM) antibodies against type IV collagen. Goodpasture's syndrome
is more common in men (sex ratio 2:1) and has a bimodal age
distribution (peaks in 20-30 and 60-70 age bracket). It is associated with
HLA DR2.

The vast majority of renal tract calculi are visible on non-contrast CT
scan of the abdomen. This question describes one of the rare instances
in which a radiolucent stone on CT KUB may lead to a missed diagnosis.
Furosemide, acetazolamide, and allopurinol predispose to the formation

Calcium stones are readily visible on both plain x-ray and CT whilst uric

with indinavir can, however, give rise to pure indinavir stones that are
undetectable on both plain x-ray or computed tomography.
Hydration and analgesia are the recommended first-line treatment for
indinavir stones, although temporary or permanent discontinuation of
the drug may be required.

explanation:
This lady has presented with the classical symptoms of
cytomegalovirus(CMV) infection which is a cause of increased morbidity
and mortality in renal transplant patients. CMV infection normally
presents one to four months after renal transplantation or stopping
cytomegalovirus prophylaxis (valganciclovir) as in this case. All renal
transplant patients and donors will have their CMV status checked prior
to transplantation and recipients will receive prophylaxis unless both
they and the donor test negative. CMV infection presents with a
mononucleosis-like syndrome with fever, myalgia and arthralgia. There is
often a leukopaenia, atypical lymphocytosis with a mild rise in
transaminases and graft dysfunction. Specific organ involvement can
lead to hepatitis, pancreatitis, gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding,
pneumonitis, colitis and meningoencephalitis. The diagnosis is
confirmed with CMV polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Treatment for
patients with invasive disease is initially IV ganciclovir.
Although immunosuppression increases the risk of bacterial infections
there are no symptoms of urinary tract infection in the history, making
this diagnosis unlikely. Hepatitis C infection would be unlikely to present
in this manner. An upper respiratory tract infection would not explain the
deranged liver function tests or deterioration in renal function. BK virus is
a polyomavirus which can cause asymptomatic latent infection in renal
tissue in immunocompetent individuals. After renal transplantation this
virus can reactivate causing fever and graft dysfunction. BK virus
infection could account for some of this lady's symptoms, however,
cytomegalovirus infection is more likely and fits the presentation better.

You start the patient on high-dose steroids and mycophenolate with a

explanation:
The clinical features and strongly positive ANA and anti-dsDNA confirm
a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus. The kidney biopsy results
confirm class IV diffuse lupus nephritis.
Mycophenolate is correct. This drug has the best evidence for
preventing the development of end-stage renal disease.
Azathioprine is incorrect. Although azathioprine can be used as
maintenance, new evidence shows that mycophenolate has better
efficacy in preventing end-stage renal disease.
Cyclophosphamide is incorrect. Cyclophosphamide can be used in the
acute phase to induce remission, however, it is not used as
maintenance.
Etanercept is incorrect. This drug is not used to treat lupus nephritis.
There are a growing number of cases of drug-induced lupus as a
consequence of anti-tumour necrosis factor (TNF) alpha drugs.
Steroids is incorrect. Steroids are used in the acute phase to induce
remission, however, they are not used as maintenance.
Mycophenolate is the preferred follow-on agent in lupus nephritis
once there has been a response to the initial therapy

with anaemia of CKD who are iron deficient and who are not receiving
