A bone marrow biopsy wouldn't be indicated at this stage, particularly as
the myeloma screen was negative, but might be considered if the patient
failed to respond to iron and ESA therapy.

A 67-year-old man with a history of heart failure treated with bisoprolol,
ramipril, furosemide and spironolactone comes to the clinic for review.
His heart failure symptoms are stable, but his main complaint is of
painful gynaecomastia that has become more prominent over the past 6
months since he had a medication change. On examination his blood
pressure is 125/80 mmHg, his pulse is 65 beats per minute and regular.
There are only minor basal crackles at both lung bases on auscultation,
and minor pitting oedema of both ankles. Routine blood testing is
unremarkable including creatinine.
Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage his
gynaecomastia?
Change furosemide to bendroflumethiazide
Change spironolactone to eplerenone
Stop bisoprolol
Stop ramipril
Stop spironolactone
Question 132 of 186
A 67-year-old man with a history of heart failure treated with bisoprolol,
ramipril, furosemide and spironolactone comes to the clinic for review.
His heart failure symptoms are stable, but his main complaint is of
painful gynaecomastia that has become more prominent over the past 6
months since he had a medication change. On examination his blood
pressure is 125/80 mmHg, his pulse is 65 beats per minute and regular.
There are only minor basal crackles at both lung bases on auscultation,
and minor pitting oedema of both ankles. Routine blood testing is
unremarkable including creatinine.
Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage his
gynaecomastia?
explanation:
Spironolactone both decreases testosterone production and increases
peripheral conversion of testosterone to oestradiol. Both of these factors
drive gynaecomastia. Eplerenone is a next generation aldosterone
antagonist which doesn't cause gynaecomastia, given he has stable
heart failure, switching is the most appropriate thing to do.
Eplerenone can be used in patients with troublesome
gynaecomastia on spironolactone
Changing furosemide to bendroflumethiazide will not impact on
gynaecomastia and may worsen control of his heart failure. Stopping the
spironolactone altogether will cause worsening of fluid retention Both
bisoprolol and ramipril are associated with improvement in LV function
and symptoms of heart failure, and should not be discontinued.
Spironolactone
Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist which acts in the cortical
collecting duct.

explanation:
In an individual of 15-39 years of age with a family history of ADPKD, a
renal ultrasound with a total of three or more cysts is considered to be
diagnostic of the disease.
The HALT-PKD trial demonstrated that individuals aged 15-49 years with
early ADPKD (eGFR > 90), treatment with an ACE inhibitor that
successfully achieved a blood pressure target of < 110 / 75 mmHg
benefited from a reduction in the annual increase in total kidney volume
and other outcomes compared to higher blood pressure targets.
In England and Wales, tolvaptan is recommended for patients with
rapidly progressive disease at chronic kidney disease stage 2-3.
Simms R. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. BMJ
2016;352:i679.

A 62-year-old man is admitted due a three week history of penile
swelling. He has a past medical history of colorectal cancer, obesity and
asthma. Limited examination demonstrates global pitting oedema and a
mild expiratory wheeze. The FY1 prints off his admission blood tests:
Na+
142 mmol/l
K+
3.6 mmol/l
Urea
6.9 mmol/l (Baseline 4.2 mmol/l)
Creatinine
126 µmol/l (Baseline 84 µmol/l)
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Nephrotic syndrome can commonly present in men with penile swelling.
This particular symptom will have occurred following oedema of other
areas but may be the first noted problem by the patient. The further clue
in this question relates to the patient's history of colorectal cancer. A
significant cause of nephrotic syndrome in older adults is membranous
nephropathy. This can be secondary to a malignancy. Therefore in this
patient it would be prudent to perform lower GI endoscopy.
Churg-Strauss syndrome is a triad of late-onset asthma, vasculitis and
eosinophilia. It is a multi-system disease, with the symptoms presented
dependent on the organs affected; oedema would not be an expected
presenting complaint. The degree of renal impairment may also be
expected to be greater. His co-existing diagnosis of asthma is a
distractor.
Malnutrition may indeed cause gross global oedema. However, this
would not be expected in a patient who is overweight in a Western
society.
Testicular cancer would not be expected to cause oedema.
Mondor's disease is a thrombophlebitis of superficial veins typically in
the breast or anterior chest wall. It may also occur in the penis.

Question 137 of 186
A 27-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease stage 5 secondary to
focal segmental glomerulosclerosis presents with left forearm pain. This
has been getting gradually worse over the past few weeks and is no
longer controlled with a combination of paracetamol and codeine. An x-
ray of the left forearm is shown below:
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the most likely cause of this appearance?
options: The option Fibrous dysplasia is also incorrect. Fibrous dysplasia is a benign condition where normal bone and marrow are replaced by fibrous Sarcoma
explanation:
The correct answer is Secondary hyperparathyroidism. This condition is
a common complication of chronic kidney disease (CKD), particularly in
stage 5. It arises due to phosphate retention and decreased calcium
levels, which stimulate the parathyroid gland to produce more
parathyroid hormone (PTH). Over time, this leads to high PTH levels,
causing bone resorption and subsequent bone pain as well as
radiological changes known as renal osteodystrophy. The x-ray shows a
Brown tumour caused by secondary hyperparathyroidism.
Sarcoma is incorrect because although sarcomas can cause bone pain
and abnormal x-ray findings, they are relatively rare. Moreover, there's no
specific link between CKD and an increased risk of sarcoma. In addition,
the gradual onset of symptoms over weeks is more consistent with a
metabolic or inflammatory process rather than a malignant one.
Osteomyelitis could cause similar symptoms but it's typically associated
with acute onset of severe pain, fever and other systemic signs of
infection which are not mentioned in the scenario. Furthermore, the x-ray
changes seen in osteomyelitis usually show areas of bone destruction
and possible abscess formation rather than generalised alterations in
bone density.
tissue leading to abnormal growth or swelling of bone. However, it does
not have any correlation with CKD nor does it typically present with
progressive pain.
Lastly, Complication of phosphate binder therapy is unlikely because
phosphate binders such as calcium acetate or sevelamer are used to
control high serum phosphate levels in patients with CKD. Although they
can cause side effects like constipation or nausea, they do not directly
cause bone pain or radiological changes seen on the x-ray.

Observations on admission are as follows: heart rate 102 beats per
minute, blood pressure 125/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen
saturations 97% (room air), temperature 37.2ºC. On examination, there is
bilateral loin tenderness, with no evidence of peritonism. Bowel sounds
are active. Urine dipstick confirms blood 2+ with no evidence of nitrites
or leucocytes. An abdominal x-ray is unremarkable.
Which medication is likely to be implicated with the underlying
diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is bromocriptine. This gentleman has presented with
retroperitoneal fibrosis, resulting in secondary hydroureters and
hydronephrosis. Examination findings of bilateral loin pain, with
associated haematuria, is consistent with this. Though not present in
this case, there is an association with inflammatory bowel disease. The
exact pathogenesis has not been clearly described, but evidence
supports the notion that it results from an immunological response to
antigens within atherosclerotic plaques.
Medications associated with retroperitoneal fibrosis include
bromocriptine, beta-blockers and methysergide.
Retroperitoneal fibrosis
Lower back/flank pain is the most common presenting feature. Fever
and lower limb oedema is also seen in some patients.

You are called to see a 34-year-old gentleman following an episode of
haematemesis on the dialysis ward. His haemoglobin has dropped from
101g/L to 69g/L. His blood pressure is 98/54 mmHg, with a heart rate of
100bpm. You note that he is currently awaiting a renal transplant for end-
stage diabetic nephropathy. He has no other past medical history. You
organise an urgent OGD. How would you manage his anaemia?
Hold transfusion and expedite the OGD
Transfuse and inform the transplant team
Increase the dose of erythropoietin
Contact the renal team for advice regarding transfusion
Transfuse and administer terlipressin
Question 139 of 186
You are called to see a 34-year-old gentleman following an episode of
haematemesis on the dialysis ward. His haemoglobin has dropped from
101g/L to 69g/L. His blood pressure is 98/54 mmHg, with a heart rate of
100bpm. You note that he is currently awaiting a renal transplant for end-
stage diabetic nephropathy. He has no other past medical history. You
organise an urgent OGD. How would you manage his anaemia?
options: Hold transfusion and expedite the OGD
Transfuse and inform the transplant team
Contact the renal team for advice regarding transfusion
explanation:
Transfusions in patients awaiting renal transplants are usually avoided
where possible, due to the potential risk of circulating antibodies and
thus organ rejection. In this example, the patient is haemodynamically
unstable and therefore an urgent blood transfusion would be advised in
this instance. The transplant team would need to be informed and the
patient advised that a transplant will be postponed for at least 3 months,
following repeat antibody screening. Terlipressin is only advised in
patients with known oesophageal varices or acute hepato-renal
syndrome. There is no role for increased dose of erythropoietin in the
acute setting.

A 45-year-old female presents to the hyperacute stroke unit with
expressive dysphasia and mild right sided upper limb weakness without
sensory disturbance seven hours after symptom onset. Although she is
outside the thrombolysis window, a hyperacute CT head demonstrates
multiple small infarcts in the left middle cerebral artery territory while a
simultaneous CT angiogram of her extra and intracranial vessels was
reported by the radiologist as a string of beads appearance. What is the
most appropriate next investigation to request to demonstrate the
underlying cause of this young females strokes?
Factor V Leiden
CT angiogram renal arteries
Lupus anticoagulant
MRI head with contrast
MR venogram
Question 140 of 186
A 45-year-old female presents to the hyperacute stroke unit with
expressive dysphasia and mild right sided upper limb weakness without
sensory disturbance seven hours after symptom onset. Although she is
outside the thrombolysis window, a hyperacute CT head demonstrates
multiple small infarcts in the left middle cerebral artery territory while a
simultaneous CT angiogram of her extra and intracranial vessels was
reported by the radiologist as a string of beads appearance. What is the
most appropriate next investigation to request to demonstrate the
underlying cause of this young females strokes?
explanation:
Young patients under 55 years with acute ischaemic stroke should alert
you to an underlying cause beyond arterial atherosclerotic or
cardioembolic disease. In this case, the CT angiography findings
classically describe a patient with fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD), a non-
atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory condition producing segmental
stenoses in all vascular beds. Pathogenesis remains unknown but a
strong genetic predisposition is known to FMD while hormonal
influences are thought to contribute, with significant numbers of females
within child-bearing age being affected. Between 35 to 60% of FMD
patients have carotid artery involvement , hence the frequent
presentation of cerebral ischaemia such as transient ischaemic attacks,
strokes, headache and tinnitus .
However, the most commonly affected vasculature in FMD is the renal
arteries, implicated in up to 70% of FMD patients . As a result of reduced
renal perfusion secondary to renal artery stenoses and consequent
activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, FMD patients
frequently report preceding years of severe or refractory hypertension,
often taking multiple anti-hypertensive agents. While digital subtraction
angiography is the investigation of choice, non-invasive modalities such
as CT and MR angiography are more commonly used.
1. Olin JW, Froehlich J, Gu X, Bacharach JM, Eagle K, Gray BH, Jaff MR,
Kim ES, Mace P, Matsumoto AH, McBane RD, Kline-Rogers E, White CJ,
Gornik HL. The United States Registry for Fibromuscular Dysplasia:
results in the first 447 patients. Circulation. 2012;125(25):3182.
2. Olin JW, Pierce M. Contemporary management of fibromuscular
dysplasia. Curr Opin Cardiol. 2008;23(6):527
Renal vascular disease
Renal vascular disease is most commonly due to atherosclerosis (> 95%
of patients). It is associated with risk factors such as smoking and
hypertension that cause atheroma elsewhere in the body. It may present
as hypertension, chronic renal failure or 'flash' pulmonary oedema.
Another common presentation is a sharp rise in creatinine following the
initiation of ACE inhibitor therapy (e.g. hypertension that may itself be
linked to the underlying renal artery stenosis).
ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II levels, which normally constrict
the efferent arterioles in the glomerulus to maintain glomerular
filtration pressure, especially in states of decreased renal perfusion
- when an ACE inhibitor is introduced, the reduction in angiotensin II
levels leads to dilation of the efferent arterioles

This gentleman clearly has an acute kidney injury. There is nothing in the
history to suggest pre-renal failure and although bilateral ureteric
obstruction is a possibility that needs to be excluded it is probably less
likely than 'intrinsic' renal failure. Given the speed of onset of symptoms
and the grossly elevated creatinine a diagnosis of acute

Goodpasture's syndrome is an autoimmune condition where antibodies
attack the basement membrane found in the glomerulus and the lung.
This results in a glomerulonephritis with acute kidney injury and a
nephritic syndrome, and also pulmonary haemorrhage. Pulmonary
haemorrhage can present with a variety of symptoms such as
breathlessness and chest pain; notably, haemoptysis is by no means
universally present. The chest x-ray findings can help differentiate
pulmonary haemorrhage from pulmonary oedema that might be found in
someone with acute kidney injury with volume overload. The most
important treatment is the removal of the antibodies using
plasmapheresis. High dose steroids can have a role as part of
immunosuppression after initial control and would be used first line if
the aetiology was a small vessel vasculitis such as Wegener's
granulomatosis. Haemofiltration or dialysis may also be necessary in the
interim but there is no indication for immediate use of these services in
this case (refractory acidosis, hyperkalaemia, pulmonary oedema).
Anti-GBM disease is typically managed with a combination of
corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide and plasmapheresis
much help, and given the already raised blood pressure may make
pulmonary oedema more likely.
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM)
disease (Goodpasture's syndrome)
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease (previously known
as Goodpasture's syndrome) is a rare type of small-vessel vasculitis
associated with both pulmonary haemorrhage and rapidly progressive
glomerulonephritis. It is caused by anti-glomerular basement membrane
(anti-GBM) antibodies against type IV collagen. Goodpasture's syndrome
is more common in men (sex ratio 2:1) and has a bimodal age
distribution (peaks in 20-30 and 60-70 age bracket). It is associated with
HLA DR2.

explanation:
Given this patient's history of bladder cancer the most likely answer is
malignant infiltration of the ureters. Urothelial cell cancer of the bladder
can metastasise to the cells lining the ureters, as well as lymph nodes in
the nearby area. This can potentially cause a blockage of urine, thereby
causing hydronephrosis.
Renal tract calculi and ureteric blood clot are unlikely to give bilateral
hydronephrosis.
Urinary tract infection is an extremely unlikely cause of hydronephrosis
but can of course complicate acute hydronephrosis.
Retroperitoneal fibrosis is a potential cause of bilateral hydronephrosis,
but is a rare cause and not the most likely in this context.

options: Renal biopsy is incorrect. Biopsy of a surrogate site is preferred in the initial investigation of amyloidosis due to the increased bleeding risk associated with this condition and greater technical expertise required ESR
explanation:
Abdominal fat aspiration is correct. The patient presents with leg
swelling and evidence of nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria,
hypoalbuminemia) and deranged renal function. In addition, he has
evidence of sensory peripheral neuropathy. Together with his history of
longstanding untreated ankylosing spondylitis, this suggests a diagnosis
of secondary (AA) amyloidosis. This condition is more common in those
patients with chronic levels of systemic inflammation, which causes the
production of a protein called SAA (serum amyloid A protein) in large
amounts. If the inflammation persists, a small amount of SAA protein
(called AA protein) will deposit in affected tissues as AA amyloid. The
diagnosis is confirmed by a biopsy. While it is possible to biopsy the
affected organ (i.e. renal or nerve), a biopsy of a surrogate site (i.e.
abdominal fat) is preferred in the first instance due to its relative ease,
lower risk of complications and great physical comfort.
Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibody is incorrect. This antibody is
associated with idiopathic membranous nephropathy rather than
amyloidosis. This is a cause of nephrotic syndrome. However, it is much
less likely to be associated with peripheral neuropathy and chronic
systemic inflammation and is, therefore, less likely.
ESR is incorrect. This is a non-specific marker of inflammation and may
well be raised in this circumstance. However, it will not confirm or refute
the diagnosis.
Amyloidosis may be confirmed by a biopsy of skin, rectal mucosa,
or abdominal fat
for biopsy.
Transthoracic echocardiogram is incorrect. This may show indirect
evidence of cardiac amyloidosis but is less specific for the diagnosis
when compared with an abdominal fat pad biopsy.

proteinuria.

explanation:
Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome results in cerebral oedema which
can present as focal neurological deficits, papilloedema and a
decreased level of consciousness. It can be treated with mannitol
or hypertonic saline
Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome is a rare but serious complication of
haemodialysis. It is more likely to occur in patients with very high levels
of urea, metabolic acidosis, extremes of age, and central nervous
system diseases. High levels of urea result in fluid shifts in the brain. If
urea is rapidly decreased, the result is a sudden drop in serum
osmolarity, and a fluid shift from interstitial to intracellular
compartments. The end result is cerebral oedema.
Cerebral oedema can present with headaches, focal neurological
deficits, myoclonus, papilloedema and a decreased level of
consciousness.
Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome can be treated with mannitol or
hypertonic saline to increase plasma osmolarity and reduce cerebral
oedema.
Although opioid toxicity can present with myoclonic jerks, the headache
would not be typical, and the history is more suggestive of dialysis
disequilibrium syndrome. Therefore, naloxone is not indicated.
Although the potassium is high, it is important to note that this is pre-
dialysis bloods, and the potassium will be normalised following dialysis.
Therefore, calcium gluconate is not indicated.
Renal replacement therapy
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a relatively common condition, affecting
1 in 8 people in the UK. Around 10% of those with CKD will go on to
develop renal failure, which is defined as a glomerular filtration rate of
less than 15ml/min. For patients with renal failure, the management
options are renal replacement therapy (RRT), to take over the physiology
of the kidneys, or conservative management, which will be palliative.

Observations:

Respiratory rate 18/minute
Oxygen saturations 96% on room air
Temperature 38.4°C
On examination, there is mild abdominal tenderness. Bowel sounds are
present. The dialysate fluid appears cloudy.
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the appropriate antibiotic choice?
explanation:
Peritoneal dialysis peritonitis: treat with intraperitoneal vancomycin
+ ceftazidime
Intraperitoneal vancomycin + ceftazidime is the correct answer. The
patient has peritoneal dialysis peritonitis as evidenced by fever,
abdominal pain and a cloudy dialysate fluid. The appropriate antibiotic
choice is intraperitoneal vancomycin + ceftazidime. The antibiotic choice
should give broad coverage to both gram-positive and gram-negative
organisms. Intraperitoneal administration of antibiotics has been shown
to be safer and more effective when compared with IV in patients with
peritoneal dialysis peritonitis.
IV benzylpenicillin is incorrect. This would only provide coverage against
gram-positive organisms, which would be insufficient in this scenario.
Intraperitoneal ciprofloxacin and intravenous amikacin is incorrect. This
antibiotic choice would provide broad gram-negative coverage. There is
some suggestion that amikacin may have some action against gram-
positive organisms including Staphylococcus aureus and Methicillin-
resistant Staphylococcus aureus but vancomycin would be a preferable
choice and the intraperitoneal route is superior, in addition.
Intravenous ciprofloxacin is incorrect. This would provide insufficient
cover for gram-positive organisms.
Intraperitoneal flucloxacillin and ceftazidime . This would provide good
gram-positive and gram-negative coverage in this scenario. However,
intraperitoneal vancomycin would be preferable to flucloxacillin due to
its activity against MRSA.
Peritoneal dialysis
Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is a form of renal replacement therapy. It is
sometimes used as a stop-gap to haemodialysis or for younger patients
who do not want to have to visit hospital three times a week.
The majority of patients do Continuous Ambulatory Peritoneal Dialysis

was not an option and the patient did not have Alport's syndrome.
Alport's syndrome is associated with a defective type IV collagen
synthesis, which form part of the basement membrane in the kidneys.
The body therefore mounts an immune response towards the type IV
collagen in the transplanted kidneys and patient's develop Goodpasture's
syndrome.
Alport's syndrome
Alport's syndrome is usually inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern*. It
is due to a defect in the gene which codes for type IV collagen resulting
in an abnormal glomerular-basement membrane (GBM). The disease is
more severe in males with females rarely developing renal failure.
A favourite question is an Alport's patient with a failing renal transplant.
This may be caused by the presence of anti-GBM antibodies leading to a
Goodpasture's syndrome like picture.
Alport's syndrome usually presents in childhood. The following features
may be seen:
microscopic haematuria
progressive renal failure
bilateral sensorineural deafness
lenticonus: protrusion of the lens surface into the anterior chamber
retinitis pigmentosa
renal biopsy: splitting of lamina densa seen on electron microscopy

renal biopsy

splitting of the lamina densa of the glomerular basement

What is the absolute contraindication to this patient acting as a living
kidney donor to his daughter?
explanation:
Detailed guidelines exist for living donor kidney transplantation (see
below link). There are few absolute contraindications for an individual to
donate a kidney. In this individual's case, the failure of three agents to
control his blood pressure would render him ineligible to donate. This is
due both to the increased peri-operative risk and also the potential for
nephrectomy to exacerbate hypertension following donation. Other
absolute contraindications include active malignancy, chronic infection,
overt proteinuria, bilateral renal artery atherosclerosis and sickle cell
disease.
Other factors mentioned are relative contraindications that need to be
considered when discussing the risk of nephrectomy for the potential
donor. The donor's pre-operative renal function must be of a level to give
a minimum expected eGFR of 37.5 ml / min / 1.73 m2 at age 80 years
(for this individual at age 60, the minimum eGFR would be considered to
be 68 ml / min / 1.73 m2. There is no upper age limit for an individual to
act as a donor, but pre-operative assessment must be particularly
rigorous for older individuals. Moderate obesity (BMI 30-35 kg / m2)
would also indicate the need for rigorous pre-operative assessment.
Historically, all transplants had to occur between ABO blood groups and
HLA compatible donor and recipient pairs; however, desensitisation
techniques are now available to allow immunologically incompatible
kidney transplants in some cases.

This gentleman has Goodpasture's disease, an autoimmune disease

haemorrhage.

antibiotics. However, this is commonly a precipitant for a pulmonary

This gentleman may require haemodialysis however at present he does
not require acute haemodialysis given his pH and potassium.
CPAP may be used in patients with pulmonary haemorrhage who have a
type 1 respiratory failure. However, his oxygen demand has been
managed successfully with supplementary oxygen and what he requires
is treatment of the underlying condition.
Anti-GBM disease is typically managed with a combination of
corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide and plasmapheresis
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM)
disease (Goodpasture's syndrome)
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease (previously known
as Goodpasture's syndrome) is a rare type of small-vessel vasculitis
associated with both pulmonary haemorrhage and rapidly progressive
glomerulonephritis. It is caused by anti-glomerular basement membrane
(anti-GBM) antibodies against type IV collagen. Goodpasture's syndrome
is more common in men (sex ratio 2:1) and has a bimodal age
distribution (peaks in 20-30 and 60-70 age bracket). It is associated with
HLA DR2.

Commencement of erythropoiesis stimulating agents with a target haemoglobin of 120-140 g/dL
explanation:
Anaemia is commonly seen in chronic kidney disease (CKD). It is well
known that a reduction in haemoglobin is seen with reducing glomerular
filtration rates. It is thought to be secondary to reduced production of
erythropoietin (EPO) by the kidney. Whilst measurements of EPO levels
in CKD are usually normal or slightly reduced they are considered
inappropriately low considering the degree of anaemia. Anaemia is
associated with an increased morbidity and mortality in patients with
CKD.
The introduction of human recombinant EPO has now prevented patients
from becoming iron overloaded as a result of multiple transfusions.
The UK renal association recommends that haemoglobin levels should
be tested at least annually in CKD patients to identify anaemia. CKD
should be considered as a possible cause of anaemia when the
glomerular filtration rate is <60ml/min/1.73m . Other causes of anaemia
such as blood loss, folic acid and vitamin B12 deficiency should be
excluded before the anaemia is attributed to the CKD. The measurement
of EPO levels is not necessary for the diagnosis or management of
anaemia in CKD patients.
The renal association recommends that treatment with erythropoiesis-
stimulating agents (ESAs) should be offered to patients with anaemia of
CKD who may benefit in terms of symptoms, quality of life and in order
to avoid transfusion in patients considered suitable for future
transplantation.
Anaemia in CKD - aim for 10-12 g/dl
Patients with CKD on ESA therapy should achieve a haemoglobin of
between 10-12 g/dL. Adjustments to the patients therapy should be
based on the haemoglobin level. In order for ESA to have their intended
benefit, patients need to have adequate iron stores for effective
erythropoiesis. Less than a third of patients with CKD and anaemia have
a satisfactory iron status (ferritin >100ng/ml, transferrin saturation
>20%). Patients who are being assessed for ESA therapy need to have
their iron status assessed and unless contraindicated are commenced
on a regime of parenteral iron therapy in addition to their ESA.

On examination, there is an arteriovenous fistula in the right forearm.
There is an audible bruit at the fistula. There is no other swelling or
erythema. There is no pain on passive movement of the forearm. The
colour of the hand is normal.
What is the likely diagnosis?
AV fistula infection
AV fistula stenosis
AV fistula thrombosis

Question 161 of 186
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with pain in
the right forearm. He has a past medical history of end-stage renal
failure and hypertension. He takes ramipril, amlodipine and doxazosin.
On examination, there is an arteriovenous fistula in the right forearm.
There is an audible bruit at the fistula. There is no other swelling or
erythema. There is no pain on passive movement of the forearm. The
colour of the hand is normal.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
AV fistula stenosis is the correct answer. Stenosis of an AV fistula can
present with acute limb pain at the site of the fistula.
AV fistula infection is incorrect. Typically, patients with this type of
infection would present with fevers, chills and malaise. There may be
localized erythema over the site of the AV fistula.
AV fistula thrombosis is incorrect. This is classically identified by the
absence of a bruit in the AV fistula. There is a bruit present here so this
Arteriovenous fistula stenosis presents with acute limb pain
is not likely.
AV steal syndrome is incorrect. This syndrome causes ischaemia of the
hand as a consequence of reversal or reduction or reversal of flow
through the arterial segment of the fistula distal to the AV fistula. It may
cause pallor and necrosis of the hand, which are not present here.
Compartment syndrome is incorrect. This is caused by increased
pressure within a muscle compartment causing muscle +/- nerve injury.
Typically this occurs after a significant injury. Furthermore, there is
typically pain on passive movement of the region, which is absent in this
case.
Arteriovenous fistulas
Arteriovenous fistulas are direct connections between arteries and
veins. They may occur pathologically but are generally formed surgically
to allow access for haemodialysis.
They are now regarded as the preferred method of access for
haemodialysis due to the lower rates of complications.
The time taken for an arteriovenous fistula to develop is 6 to 8 weeks.
Potential complications include:
infection
thrombosis
may be detected by the absence of a bruit
stenosis
may present with acute limb pain
steal syndrome

explanation:
Acute graft failure is the correct answer. The patient is not reporting any
symptoms of infection or worsening renal failure. However, we can see
that there is worsening graft function in association with pyuria and
proteinuria. Three months after a renal transplant, worsening renal
function raises the suspicion of acute graft failure, which typically
occurs < 6 months after a transplant.
Chronic graft failure is incorrect. This typically occurs at > 6 months
post-transplant and is caused by both antibody and cell-mediated
mechanisms causing fibrosis to the transplanted kidney (chronic
allograft nephropathy). In some other cases, it may be caused by the
recurrence of original renal disease.
Doxazosin use is incorrect. This is not classically considered a
nephrotoxic medication. If it caused a period of profound hypotension it
may plausibly cause an acute kidney injury but there is no suggestion of
that from this scenario.
Hyperacute graft failure is incorrect. This occurs within minutes to hours
as is due to pre-existing antibodies against ABO or HLA antigens. It is a
type II hypersensitivity reaction and leads to widespread thrombosis of
graft vessels. This causes ischaemia and necrosis of the transplanted
Acute graft failure happens within months, is usually asymptomatic
and is picked up by a rising creatinine, pyuria and proteinuria
organ. No treatment is possible and the graft must be removed.
Urinary tract infection is incorrect. While the patient has some
leucocytes in the urine, he has no symptoms of a urinary tract infection
and nitrites are negative, making this diagnosis unlikely.

The patient is severely dehydrated and is hypotensive and tachycardic
with a lactic acidosis. She needs emergency fluid resuscitation as
treatment for hypovolaemic shock. NICE guidance on intravenous fluid
prescription for adults in hospital recommends an initial fluid bolus of
500 mL of crystalloid (containing 130-154 mmol / L sodium) over 15
minutes.
Reassessment after the initial bolus is recommended with a further
bolus of 250-500 mL crystalloid if patient still requires fluid
resuscitation. If patient still has signs of shock after 2000 mL of fluid
have been given then recommendation is to seek expert help.
Human albumin solution and colloids such as Gelofusine have no place
in the NICE guidance on IV fluid resuscitation.

The prescription of intravenous fluids is one of the most common tasks

underlying pathophysiology is deemed irreversible and eGFR has
deteriorated to less than 30, transplantation should be discussed.
Palliation would be wholly inappropriate.

minor, despite it likely to produce the best genetic match. Renal
transplantation is a rigorous process and donors under 18 years of age
are almost never considered for renal transplantation, on the basis of the
validity of consent and autonomy in such situations . The patient should
thus be placed first on the national register with preparations for renal

injury (AKI), thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolytic
anaemia which points toward a diagnosis of haemolytic uraemic
syndrome. The next investigation of choice is to send a stool
microscopy and culture to confirm the strain Escherichia coli O157.
Urinalysis would be appropriate to send to look for the presence of
haematuria or proteinuria which may appear in early disease. However, it
is not the next best investigation to send.
Faecal calprotectin is an investigation needed for the diagnosis of
inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Whilst cramping abdominal pain,
bloody diarrhoea and weight loss are features of IBD, it does not explain
the AKI, haemolytic anaemic and thrombocytopenia.
A blood culture is a necessary investigation given the presence of fever
but a stool culture is more appropriate in this scenario.
Clostridium difficile is a less likely diagnosis, making stool antigen
testing less appropriate.
Stool culture looking for Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli
should be sent in patients with suspected haemolytic uraemic
syndrome

explanation:
An underlying diagnosis of membranous glomerulonephritis is almost
given in the renal biopsy. This would be consistent with a renal
complication of lymphomatous disease. However, this is insufficient to
explain the acute presentation of flank pain, oedema and varicocele.
Although the precise pathophysiology is unclear, there is a significant
association between nephrotic syndrome and renal vein thrombus. In
this case, the left renal vein thrombus would explain the left varicocele
and flank tenderness. Other causes of glomerulonephritis offered are
unlikely to produce pain. Renal calculi should not produce oedema and
varicocele.
Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephritis is the commonest type of
glomerulonephritis in adults and is the third most common cause of end-
stage renal failure (ESRF). It usually presents with nephrotic syndrome or
proteinuria.
Renal biopsy demonstrates:
electron microscopy: the basement membrane is thickened with
subepithelial electron dense deposits. This creates a 'spike and
dome' appearance
Causes
idiopathic: due to anti-phospholipase A2 antibodies
infections: hepatitis B, malaria, syphilis
malignancy (in 5-20%): prostate, lung, lymphoma, leukaemia

This gentleman has developed post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

specific strands of Streptococcus spp. The latent period is classically
one to two weeks post infection and presents with an acute
glomerulonephritis characterised by haematuria (with dark urine owing

predominantly by haematuria, with an usually excellent prognosis.

membraneous nephropathy is characterised by a nephrotic syndrome.
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis typically occurs 7-14 days
following a group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus infection (usually
Streptococcus pyogenes). It is caused by immune complex (IgG, IgM and
C3) deposition in the glomeruli. Young children are most commonly
affected.

First line treatment for hypertension in this group remains an ACE
inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker.

where the usual NICE hypertension algorithm does not apply for second
line management. Diuretics are used to help excrete salt and diminish
hypertension. In patients with an eGFR <30ml/min loop diuretics, such

presentations of iron deficient patients with renal disease. This is
confirmed biochemically with low ferritin (normal >250 ng/ml) and

a Jehovah's witness. The most appropriate management would be to
correct iron stores, which from experience can produce dramatic clinical
improvements in renal transplant patients even if ferritin and TSAT are
close to normal ranges. Erythropoietin (EPO) is not appropriate until iron
replacement has completed, desaturation of iron stores is one of the
most common causes of EPO resistance.

A 19 year-old man presents with frank haematuria. He had just recovered

antibiotics. His past medical history includes hearing problems from a
young age, for which he wears hearing aids and a recent corneal ulcer.
His observations are stable and urine dipstick reveals protein ++ and
blood +++ in his urine.
It is decided that he will undergo a renal biopsy. What is the most likely
finding under light microscopy?
explanation:
This patient has Alport's syndrome - a combination of nephritis causing
microscopic haematuria with episodic frank haematuria, high frequency
sensorineural deafness and ocular problems which include corneal
ulcers and bilateral lenticonus. Light microscopy is usually unremarkable
and electron microscopy is usually required.

Weekly subcutaneous erythropoietin is used in pre-dialysis patients for
the treatment of renal anaemia. Renal anaemia is typically associated
with an eGFR <30 and with a normal MCV. Once serum ferritin stores are
optimised (using either oral or IV ferritin), erythropoietin would be
considered appropriate. Subcutaneous administration is used in pre-
dialysis patients and the intravenous route is used in patients
undergoing haemodialysis. Blood transfusions are used in patients with
anaemia that is not responsive to erythropoietin when other causes of
anaemia have been excluded.

explanation:
The diagnosis of calciphylaxis is confirmed on skin biopsy. PTH is
sensitive but not specific for calciphylaxis. An arterial ulcer would be an
important differential but the distribution (upper calf) makes this less
likely. Taking a skin swab for bacterial culture is important as there may
be superimposed infection but it does not confirm the underlying
diagnosis. Vasculitis is unlikely, especially given the nature of her
underlying kidney disease.

pulmonary oedema. There are many causes. He is not overtly septic. His
medications which include ACE inhibitors and an NSAIDs can contribute
to renal failure but this would be more likely on initiating or increasing

on a background of a vasculitis with additional features to suggest that.
We know the gentleman has an enlarged prostate with a palpable
bladder on examination. Given his total anuria for two days and enlarged
prostate, it is likely this caused obstruction. Ultrasound can be negative
in 5% of cases of obstructive uropathy and therefore the clinical story is
of great importance in acute kidney injury. The signs of congestive
cardiac failure are similar but there would usually be risk factors such as
an extensive cardiac history and they would be passing urine.

explanation:
The most likely cause here is furosemide abuse as it explains her
hypotension, tachycardia and acute kidney injury (dehydration/ fluids
depletion) and hypokalaemia.
Addison's disease would explain the hyponatraemia and hypotension but
is typically associated with hyperkalaemia. Similarly,
pseudohypoaldosteronism would likely cause high potassium.
Excess aldosterone (either production by adenoma or familial) would
cause hypokalaemia but is far more commonly associated with
hypertension.

Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephritis is the commonest type of
glomerulonephritis in adults and is the third most common cause of end-
stage renal failure (ESRF). It usually presents with nephrotic syndrome or
proteinuria.
Renal biopsy demonstrates:
electron microscopy: the basement membrane is thickened with
subepithelial electron dense deposits. This creates a 'spike and
dome' appearance
Causes
idiopathic: due to anti-phospholipase A2 antibodies
infections: hepatitis B, malaria, syphilis
malignancy (in 5-20%): prostate, lung, lymphoma, leukaemia
drugs: gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs
autoimmune diseases: systemic lupus erythematosus (class V
disease), thyroiditis, rheumatoid

options: A micturating cystogram (MCUG) is used to investigate VUR in the context of recurrent urinary tract infections (UTI), primarily in children, Micturating cystogram (MCUG)
explanation:
In this scenario, the patient presents with microscopic haematuria, sub-
nephrotic range proteinuria, and deranged renal function. The most likely
diagnosis is IgA nephropathy (though another type of glomerulonephritis
is also possible), and therefore, a kidney biopsy is most likely to be
diagnostic. Any patient under 60 years old presenting with haematuria
(provided there are no obvious risk factors for urological malignancy)
should be referred to renal services for further investigation and
management, especially if there is co-existing proteinuria and reduced
kidney function.
A CT kidneys/ureters/bladder would be the investigation of choice for
potential renal calculi and may also be useful for investigating urothelial
malignancy/renal cell carcinoma. Although renal calculi can present with
visible haematuria, they are usually also associated with loin-groin pain,
which is not present in this case.
A dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scan uses radioisotopes to assess
kidney functionality, location, and any evidence of scarring. A DMSA is a
useful test in children, especially for detecting scarring due to
vesicoureteric reflux (VUR), but it has no role in investigating
glomerulonephritis.
In patients presenting with haematuria, urological malignancy must be
considered. For older patients (over 60 years old) or younger patients
(under 45 years old) at high risk of urological malignancy or whose
symptoms have persisted despite treatment of urinary tract infection,
flexible cystoscopy would be an appropriate investigation. However, in
this case, the patient is young and has no reported risk factors for
urological malignancy, making a referral to renal and a kidney biopsy
more appropriate.
Routine renal review may be more appropriate than urgent
urological review in younger patients with haematuria
with limited use in adults. In the context of recurrent UTIs, it would
demonstrate the backflow of urine into the ureters. Since there is no
history of recurrent UTIs in this patient, an MCUG is not indicated.

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most likely finding on kidney
biopsy?
options: Crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear capillary wall IgG and C3
GBM titre is inconsistent with membranous nephropathy, which is Crescentic glomerulonephritis without immune staining
Diffuse GBM thickening with spikes and foot process effacement
Mesangial expansion and glomerular and tubular basement membrane thickening
Mesangial proliferation with IgA and C3 deposition
explanation:
This patient presents with a pulmonary-renal syndrome, characterised by
haemoptysis and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN). The
widespread coarse crackles heard on auscultation likely indicate alveolar
haemorrhage. The primary differential diagnoses are anti-glomerular
basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease and ANCA-associated small
vessel vasculitis. The rapid onset of symptoms and the patient’s age
make anti-GBM disease the more likely diagnosis, which is confirmed by
a positive anti-GBM titre. A kidney biopsy in this condition would reveal
crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear capillary wall IgG and C3.
ANCA-associated vasculitis is a key differential in this case; however, it
typically presents with a less acute clinical course and is associated with
serum ANCA positivity. The presence of a positive anti-GBM titre
strongly supports anti-GBM disease. Classically, ANCA-associated
vasculitis leads to pauci-immune glomerulonephritis, characterised by
the absence of immune deposits on immunofluorescence. Therefore,
crescentic glomerulonephritis without immune staining would be more
indicative of ANCA-associated vasculitis, making it an incorrect answer.
Diffuse GBM thickening with spikes and foot process effacement is the
classical histological feature of advanced membranous nephropathy.
Membranous nephropathy primarily presents with nephrotic syndrome
(in around 80% of cases) rather than RPGN. Additionally, a positive anti-
Anti-GBM disease typically presents with haemoptysis +
AKI/proteinuria/haematuria
typically associated with a positive anti-PLA2R antibody.
Mesangial expansion and glomerular and tubular basement membrane
thickening is characteristic of diabetic nephropathy. Diabetic
nephropathy typically has a gradual onset, with a slow decline in kidney
function and progressively increasing proteinuria, contrasting with the
acute RPGN presentation described here which is consistent with anti-
GBM disease.
IgA nephropathy, the most common primary glomerulonephritis
worldwide, often presents with asymptomatic microscopic urinary
abnormalities. The typical biopsy finding in IgA nephropathy is
mesangial proliferation with IgA and C3 deposition. While IgA
nephropathy can occasionally present with an RPGN-like picture, this is
uncommon, and the current clinical scenario is more consistent with
anti-GBM disease.
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM)
disease (Goodpasture's syndrome)
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease (previously known
as Goodpasture's syndrome) is a rare type of small-vessel vasculitis
associated with both pulmonary haemorrhage and rapidly progressive
glomerulonephritis. It is caused by anti-glomerular basement membrane
(anti-GBM) antibodies against type IV collagen. Goodpasture's syndrome
is more common in men (sex ratio 2:1) and has a bimodal age
distribution (peaks in 20-30 and 60-70 age bracket). It is associated with
HLA DR2.

symptoms associated with diarrhoea and weight loss. There is no
evidence of a 'common' (> 1 in 10) cause of polyuria, for example

is thyroid function tests, particularly in the setting of other possible
symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. Hyperthyroidism is an 'infrequent' cause of
polyuria (> 1 in 100).
While paired serum and urine osmolalities may be indicated they are to
detect diabetes insipidus, a 'very rare' cause of polyuria (< 1 in 10,000)
and are therefore much less likely to make a positive diagnosis of this
patient's polyuria. Desmopressin administration is performed after
identification of diabetes insipidus to distinguish between a cranial or
nephrogenic origin and would not be appropriate at this stage.

This man has rhabdomyolysis, as evidenced by his acute kidney injury,
and markedly raised CK values, secondary to status epilepticus.
Rhabdomyolysis is the clinical syndrome resulting from the breakdown
of muscle cells, resulting in the release of the intracellular contents into
the circulation eg. myoglobin and potassium, resulting in electrolyte
imbalances and acute kidney injury. It can also be caused by crush
injuries, overexertion, compartment syndrome, drugs eg. statins,
neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
In severe cases, it results in metabolic acidosis secondary to raised
serum lactic acid levels from the ischaemic muscle fibres. The serum
lactate is raised which would suggest an acidotic picture over a normal
blood gas picture, ruling out options (b), (d), (e). Option D is a spurious
result - it is alkalotic despite a high pCO2 and low HCO3. Option (c) is a
picture of respiratory acidosis, leaving option (a) as the only correct
answer.

options: Acute kidney injury: NICE guidelines and staging Creatinine >1000 µmol/l
explanation:
We don't yet know what the underlying diagnosis is yet but it is clear that
this patient has an acute kidney injury. We also dont know why she has
had a seizure. Given the normal CT head, the next logical cause for the
seizure would be the uraemia. The renal team decide to dialyse this
patient; the main reason is that they suspect the patient is experiencing
symptomatic uraemia (seizure). An elevated urea in of itself would not
be an indication without the concomitant symptoms. A creatinine >1000
µmol/l , whilst indicating severe renal impairment, is not an indication for
dialysis. A urea of >25 mmol/l is not an indication for dialysis (>27 is the
point you could consider dialysis to prevent uraemic symptoms if
progressive). You would try to medically treat the potassium first before
jumping to dialyse. Potassium >6.5 mmol/l would be an indication. a pH
of 7.34 is not severe enough to warrant dialysis. A pH of <7.1 would be
an indication.

explanation:
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is becoming a more common chronic
condition and management of its eventual sequelae is important.
Mineral bone disease in the context of CKD is often asymptomatic and
this is picked up on routine blood tests.
Hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia are driving the
hyperparathyroidism here. Supplementation like calcium and vitamin D is
important to restore the lack of active vitamin D produced by the kidneys
and restore normal calcium homeostasis.
Management of hyperphosphatemia will begin with limiting dietary
intake of phosphates. The food listed above are examples of food to
avoid. It is worth noting that avoiding all these classes of foods are often
challenging and difficult for patients to adhere to.
Use of phosphate binders is usually reserved for patients who have not
improved on dietary changes. Sevelamer and lanthanum are examples
of such phosphate binders.
Cinacalcet will be useful in the management of secondary
hyperparathyroidism but its use is usually reserved if the secondary
hyperparathyroidism is unresponsive to dialysis.
Lastly, parathyroidectomy will help manage the secondary
hyperparathyroidism but this is usually reserved for cases not
responding to medical management and dialysis.

The first-line investigation of a testicular mass is an ultrasound
It is normal to have some degree of difference between the size of the
two testes.
Ultrasound examination should first be performed to characterise the
lesion and confirm the presence of a mass.
If the mass is suspicious for cancer, then tumour markers should be
measured.
Imaging with MRI may be required for patients with equivocal ultrasound
findings.
Testicular cancer
Testicular cancer is the most common malignancy in men aged 20-30
years. Around 95% of cases of testicular cancer are germ-cell tumours.
Germ cell tumours may essentially be divided into:
seminomas
non-seminomas: including embryonal, yolk sac, teratoma and
choriocarcinoma
Non-germ cell tumours include Leydig cell tumours and sarcomas.
The peak incidence for teratomas is 25 years and seminomas is 35
years. Risk factors include:
infertility (increases risk by a factor of 3)
cryptorchidism
family history
Klinefelter's syndrome
mumps orchitis
Features
a painless lump is the most common presenting symptom
